text:
Introduction

Moussa Diawara, a 57-year-old Malian national who had lived in the United States for approximately 25 years, was deported by American immigration authorities to Ghana in July 2026. Within days, Ghanaian officials allegedly forced him onto a flight to Mali, despite a 2012 ruling by a US immigration judge protecting him from deportation to that country because of the likelihood of persecution. His case raises a question under international law: can the United States deport someone through an intermediate country when the foreseeable consequence may be return to a destination covered by an existing protection order?

International law does not categorically prohibit third-country deportations. States generally retain authority to remove foreign nationals who lack permission to remain, subject to domestic and international obligations. That authority is constrained by the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits certain transfers exposing individuals to persecution, torture, or other legally protected risks. Depending on the applicable treaty, the prohibition may extend to indirect transfers where the receiving state subsequently sends the person to a dangerous destination.

Diawara's case raises substantial questions about American compliance with those obligations. Investigations by CBS News, Reuters, and Human Rights Watch have documented earlier instances in which Ghana returned American deportees to countries covered by US protection orders. Documents examined by CBS also identified Mali as Diawara's destination, although the Department of Homeland Security disputed their significance. These circumstances make the foreseeability of his eventual return a central legal issue. They do not conclusively establish deliberate coordination between American and Ghanaian authorities, and no final judicial determination has established that the United States violated international law in his individual case.

1. Moussa Diawara and the Deportation Through Ghana

Diawara entered the United States on a tourist visa when he was approximately 32 years old. After his authorization to remain expired, he continued living in the country and eventually sought protection against deportation to Mali. By 2026, he had established a family in Texas, married an American citizen, and become the father of two US citizen children. He worked as an Uber driver and held employment authorization under his immigration arrangements (Toboni et al., 2026).

His immigration history was legally significant because an American court had already recognized a barrier to returning him to his country of nationality. The reported decision did not grant unrestricted permission to remain in the United States. It restricted the government's ability to execute a removal order by sending him to Mali, while leaving open the possibility of deportation to another legally permissible destination.

The Trump administration's expanded use of third-country deportations placed individuals with similar protection orders in an uncertain position. Instead of returning them directly to their countries of origin, American authorities arranged transfers to countries with which the deportees sometimes had no previous connection. Those arrangements became contentious when receiving governments subsequently returned individuals to destinations that American immigration judges had previously found unsafe.

1.1 The 2012 Protection Against Deportation to Mali

In 2012, an American immigration judge reportedly determined that Diawara could not be deported to Mali because he would likely face persecution there. According to CBS News's October 25, 2026 investigation, his protection claim concerned his conversion to Christianity and the threats he believed he would encounter in Mali, a predominantly Muslim country affected by an Islamist insurgency.

The protection was identified as withholding of removal. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1231(b)(3), American immigration law generally prohibits removing a person to a country where their life or freedom would be threatened because of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion. The applicable standard ordinarily requires demonstrating that qualifying persecution is more likely than not, subject to specified statutory exceptions.

Withholding of removal differs from asylum and protection under the Convention Against Torture. Asylum provides a separate immigration status, while withholding prevents removal to a particular destination without necessarily preventing removal elsewhere. An individual may qualify as a refugee under international law without receiving asylum under American immigration law, but the legal consequences of these classifications are not identical. The complete 2012 judgment has not been made publicly available, leaving its precise findings and reasoning unclear. The reported protection nevertheless explains why Diawara's eventual return to Mali requires legal examination.

1.2 Arrest, Deportation, and Forced Return to Mali

On July 11, 2026, ICE agents arrested Diawara outside his Houston-area home after he finished working as an Uber driver. He was detained at the Prairieland Detention Center in Texas. On July 29, with legal assistance, he filed a federal habeas corpus petition challenging the government's imminent intention to deport him to Ghana, a country he had never visited and where he had no established ties.

Federal court records establish that Diawara was removed from the United States on July 30. CBS reported that he arrived in Ghana on July 31 aboard a deportation operation involving multiple African destinations. According to his testimony, Ghanaian authorities detained him and other deportees in a guarded hotel, restricted their communications, and forced him onto a flight to Mali within five days of their arrival.

Diawara reported that he was left in Mali without money or identification and feared for his safety. When CBS contacted him in August, he was homeless and hiding. After approximately three weeks, he reportedly escaped to another African country with assistance from local truck drivers. He requested that his subsequent location remain undisclosed because of security concerns. Ghana's government declined to comment on the allegations presented by CBS (Toboni et al., 2026).

2. Why the United States Could Deport Him to Ghana

The existence of a withholding-of-removal order does not necessarily invalidate the underlying deportation order. American immigration law distinguishes the authority to remove someone from the separate question of which destination may lawfully receive that person. Section 241(b)(2) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1231(b)(2), establishes a statutory sequence for selecting countries of removal. That sequence includes provisions concerning the individual's designated country, countries of nationality or other specified connections, and additional destinations where the statutory conditions are satisfied.

Section 1231(b)(3) imposes a separate restriction where removal would expose an individual to qualifying persecution. Regulation 8 C.F.R. § 1208.16(f) preserves the possibility of removal to a third country other than the destination to which removal has been withheld or deferred. Consequently, the reported 2012 decision did not categorically prohibit the United States from deporting Diawara to Ghana.

The Supreme Court addressed an aspect of destination selection in Jama v. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, 543 U.S. 335 (2005). It held that removal under one specified statutory provision, § 1231(b)(2)(E)(iv), did not require advance acceptance by the receiving country's government. The judgment did not establish that every destination may be selected without restrictions or that protection against persecution and torture can be disregarded.

Ordinary third-country removal under § 1231(b)(2) must also be distinguished from a safe-third-country arrangement under the separate asylum provisions of American immigration law. The latter concerns particular statutory arrangements governing access to asylum procedures. Diawara's reported transfer to Ghana arose in the context of executing an existing removal order, not from an established finding that Ghana qualified under the separate safe-third-country asylum mechanism.

Country selection remains subject to applicable procedural and substantive safeguards. The controversy addressed in D.V.D. v. Department of Homeland Security concerned whether DHS procedures provided meaningful notice and opportunities to contest third-country removals on fear-based grounds. These safeguards relate to the practical ability to invoke refugee and asylum-seeker protections before departure.

The United States could potentially select Ghana as Diawara's removal destination without contradicting the country-specific protection against removal to Mali. That possibility does not establish that the particular transfer complied with international law. The decisive question is what American authorities knew or reasonably should have anticipated about the consequences of sending him to Ghana.

3. International Law and the Prohibition of Chain Refoulement

Non-refoulement limits the power of states to transfer individuals to territories where they face specified forms of serious harm. Its principal treaty formulations appear in international refugee law and human rights law. Although these regimes overlap, they differ in their beneficiaries, substantive thresholds, exceptions, and procedures. Those distinctions are essential when evaluating a particular deportation.

The prohibition is not limited to direct transportation to a dangerous destination. Chain refoulement, also described as indirect refoulement, arises when an individual is transferred through an intermediate country before reaching a territory where legally protected risks exist. The legal concern is whether the initial transferring state exposes the person to a sufficiently established and foreseeable process of onward removal.

The assessment is primarily prospective. A prohibited risk may exist before persecution or torture actually occurs. However, the fact that an intermediate country subsequently carries out a wrongful removal does not automatically establish that the first country breached every applicable international obligation. Responsibility depends on the particular rule, the circumstances of the transfer, and the connection between the initial decision and the resulting exposure to danger.

3.1 Article 33 of the Refugee Convention

Article 33(1) of the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees prohibits contracting states from returning refugees to territories where their life or freedom would be threatened because of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion. The United States is not a party to the original Convention but is bound by its relevant substantive provisions through accession to the 1967 Protocol.

The wording and protective purpose of Article 33 are significant for indirect removals. UNHCR has consistently interpreted the principle of non-refoulement as covering transfers to intermediate countries where there is a risk of subsequent return to persecution. This interpretation is authoritative guidance concerning refugee protection, although it must be distinguished from the treaty text itself. The legal concern is the exposure to qualifying danger, not merely which government operates the aircraft carrying out the final transfer.

Article 33(2) recognizes limited exceptions involving danger to the security of the host country or a refugee who, following conviction by a final judgment of a particularly serious crime, constitutes a danger to the community. These are distinct grounds. The absence of a criminal conviction does not independently dispose of the national-security exception, which requires its own legal assessment. CBS reported that Diawara had no criminal record, and the available information does not establish circumstances satisfying either exception.

Applying Article 33 also requires attention to Diawara's status under the Refugee Convention. American withholding of removal and recognition as a Convention refugee involve related legal standards, but they are not legally interchangeable. A person may meet the Convention's refugee definition without having received formal refugee status, while a withholding determination may rest on findings that require closer examination before their international-law implications can be established.

The reported 2012 ruling provides significant evidence that an American immigration judge recognized a serious risk connected to Diawara's return to Mali. It does not independently establish every element of a violation of Article 33. That conclusion requires examining his applicable refugee-law status, whether the feared harm falls within the treaty, and whether the United States' transfer through Ghana exposed him to the prohibited risk.

3.2 Article 3 of the Convention Against Torture

Article 3(1) of the 1984 Convention Against Torture prohibits a state party from expelling, returning, or extraditing a person to another state where substantial grounds exist for believing that the person would be in danger of torture. The United States and Ghana are parties to the Convention. Unlike the Refugee Convention's Article 33(2), this provision contains no exception permitting transfer to a sufficiently established risk of torture on national-security or criminality grounds.

The UN Committee Against Torture addressed indirect removal in General Comment No. 4, adopted in 2017 and issued as an official document in 2018. Paragraph 11 describes substantial grounds in terms of a foreseeable, personal, present, and real risk of torture. Paragraph 12 specifically addresses subsequent deportation through an intermediate state to another country where the individual would face such danger (Committee Against Torture, 2018, paras 11–12).

This interpretation closely corresponds to the legal mechanism alleged in Diawara's case. Its application requires evidence satisfying the torture-related threshold. Article 1 of the Convention defines torture by reference to the intentional infliction of severe pain or suffering for specified purposes, involving public officials or persons acting in an official capacity, including through their consent or acquiescence. Serious mistreatment by non-state actors can engage the Convention where the required connection to public authority is established.

A likelihood of religious persecution does not automatically satisfy the definition of torture. The reported 2012 withholding order concerned persecution, and the available account does not establish that Diawara separately obtained protection under the Convention Against Torture. Evidence concerning the specific threats he faced, their likely perpetrators, the severity of the anticipated harm, and the role or acquiescence of public officials would be relevant to a separate Article 3 assessment.

General Comment No. 4 remains an interpretation issued by a treaty-monitoring committee rather than an additional binding treaty provision. Its analysis nevertheless demonstrates why transferring an individual to an intermediate country does not necessarily satisfy Article 3 if onward deportation to a place of torture remains sufficiently foreseeable.

3.3 Protection Under the ICCPR

Articles 6 and 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights protect the right to life and prohibit torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. The United States ratified the ICCPR in 1992, subject to reservations, understandings, and declarations. The Covenant provides another relevant basis for examining transfers exposing individuals to serious, irreversible harm.

In General Comment No. 31, the Human Rights Committee interpreted the Covenant as requiring states not to extradite, deport, expel, or otherwise remove individuals where substantial grounds exist for believing that a real risk of irreparable harm would arise. Paragraph 12 expressly addresses harm in the immediate receiving country and in any country to which the person may subsequently be removed (Human Rights Committee, 2004, para. 12).

The ICCPR analysis extends beyond the refugee-specific grounds recognized in Article 33 of the Refugee Convention. Its protection against irreparable harm under Articles 6 and 7 is not limited to persecution based on religion, nationality, or another Convention ground. The relevant legal threshold, however, remains demanding. General insecurity, poor economic conditions, or the possibility of hardship do not automatically establish a violation.

The United States has declared the ICCPR non-self-executing and entered reservations and interpretive statements, including concerning Article 7. It has also disputed aspects of the Human Rights Committee's interpretation of the Covenant. These positions affect domestic enforceability and the interpretation of the precise obligation asserted; they do not mean ratification has no international legal consequences.

The Committee's General Comments are influential interpretations, not binding judgments of an international court. Their reasoning forms part of the broader interpretive practice of international human rights law, but cannot be treated as automatically settling every dispute concerning treaty interpretation.

For Diawara, the ICCPR requires a separate assessment of whether transfer through Ghana exposed him to a sufficiently established risk of irreparable harm contemplated by Articles 6 or 7. The reported fear of religious persecution, the security conditions in Mali, and the earlier immigration decision are relevant evidence. Their significance must be evaluated against the Covenant's requirements rather than treated as conclusive by themselves.

4. The Risk Facing Diawara in Mali

Mali's security situation provides important context for the protection Diawara reportedly obtained in 2012. The country has experienced prolonged political instability, armed insurgency, and attacks by militant groups operating across the Sahel. These conditions have affected civilian security and complicated the ability of national authorities to protect people in areas affected by armed violence.

The US Department of State's June 8, 2026 travel advisory maintained Mali at Level 4, advising American citizens not to travel there because of crime, terrorism, unrest, health risks, and kidnapping. The advisory also recorded substantial restrictions on the movement of American government personnel outside Bamako. Although intended to inform travel decisions rather than adjudicate asylum claims, the warning provides official evidence of the broader security environment (US Department of State, 2026).

Diawara's reported conversion to Christianity adds an individualized dimension to those concerns. Persecution connected to religious conversion may fall within the Refugee Convention's protection against threats based on religion, depending on the person's circumstances, the nature of the anticipated harm, and the availability of state protection. Mali's Muslim-majority population does not itself establish a likelihood of persecution. The relevant inquiry concerns Diawara's specific religious identity, reported threats, and the actors capable of harming him.

The earlier immigration decision is consequently more probative of his individual circumstances than the State Department's general travel advisory. According to CBS, an immigration judge had already concluded that return to Mali would expose him to a likelihood of persecution. DHS questioned the credibility of Diawara's stated fears during the October 2026 investigation, but the publicly available account does not establish that his earlier withholding protection had been lawfully terminated.

The complete immigration judgment remains important because the legal assessment depends on its original factual findings and the protection actually granted. It would also be necessary to examine whether circumstances had materially changed before the July 2026 removal. A contemporary assessment could consider the geographical reach of the feared harm, whether protection was realistically available from Malian authorities, and whether any lawful alternative existed within Mali.

International non-refoulement obligations are preventive. They do not generally require an individual to suffer torture or persecution before protection becomes operative. Diawara's reported experience of homelessness and fear after arriving in Mali is relevant to the consequences of his return, but it does not independently prove that he experienced torture or every form of persecution initially feared.

5. Did the United States Know Ghana Would Return Him to Mali?

The most significant unresolved issue concerns what American authorities understood about Ghana's likely treatment of Diawara before his deportation. A transfer to Ghana might have been legally permissible if effective arrangements prevented onward removal to Mali. The position becomes substantially more difficult if the United States knew, or had sufficient reason to anticipate, that Ghana would send him to the country covered by his protection order.

International responsibility cannot be established merely by assuming that American officials must have known what would happen. Evidence concerning earlier deportations, diplomatic communications, destination records, and the government's assessment of Ghana is necessary to evaluate the circumstances. Information available before July 2026 is especially significant because it bears on the foreseeability of onward removal at the time DHS selected Ghana.

Deliberate coordination presents a separate question. Evidence that Ghana's conduct was foreseeable does not automatically prove that American officials ordered the final deportation. Conversely, the absence of proven instructions does not necessarily defeat a non-refoulement claim concerning the foreseeable consequences of the original American transfer.

5.1 Ghana's Earlier Returns of Protected Deportees

On January 16, 2026, Reuters published an investigation into Ghana's treatment of third-country nationals deported from the United States. Lawyers interviewed by Reuters identified at least 22 people who had reportedly been returned to countries where American immigration judges had granted protection against removal. These events occurred months before Diawara's July transfer, establishing that the alleged pattern had already become the subject of public reporting (Corey-Boulet and Bruce, 2026).

One case concerned Rabbiatu Kuyateh, a Sierra Leonean woman who sought protection after expressing fears of torture connected to her father's political associations. An American immigration judge granted withholding of removal. In November 2025, she was deported to Ghana, detained there for six days, and subsequently returned to Sierra Leone against her will, according to Reuters. Her case demonstrated how an intermediate transfer could lead to the precise destination an American protection decision was intended to exclude.

Human Rights Watch's October 8, 2026 report documented additional examples of detention, onward removal, and difficulties obtaining legal protection. Its analysis of ICE records identified 536 third-country nationals transferred from the United States to African countries between January 20, 2025, and August 5, 2026. The report drew on deportation data, judicial records, documentary material, previous reporting, and interviews. Its findings concerning Ghana did not rest on firsthand interviews with every person transferred there (Human Rights Watch, 2026).

CBS supplied further evidence concerning Diawara's own deportation operation. The flight departing Texas on July 30 carried 63 people and stopped in Sierra Leone and the Central African Republic before reaching Ghana. Of 19 individuals transferred to Ghana whom CBS subsequently contacted, 17 said they had been sent against their will to countries covered by American protection orders. These accounts support the reported pattern, although they do not constitute judicial findings concerning each individual case (Toboni et al., 2026).

The earlier incidents materially strengthen the argument that Ghana's conduct was foreseeable by July 2026. Public reporting alone does not establish the actual knowledge of every ICE official involved in Diawara's removal. It does, however, provide a substantial basis for examining the risk assessments, operational instructions, and diplomatic communications that informed the decision to select Ghana.

The timing is particularly important. Reuters had reported the earlier returns approximately six months before Diawara's deportation. The concern was consequently not limited to information discovered after his arrival in Mali. Whether that publicly available evidence was adequately considered by the responsible American authorities remains unresolved.

5.2 Travel Documents Identifying Mali as the Destination

CBS examined documents given to Diawara during the deportation operation that identified Mali rather than Ghana as his destination. A medical document contained the designation SHRC Mali, with SHRC referring to Special High Risk Charter. Both of his DHS-issued baggage tags also identified Mali. Diawara interpreted these records as evidence that American officials anticipated his eventual return to the country where an immigration judge had prohibited his removal.

The documents create a significant evidentiary question because they concern Diawara's individual transportation arrangements. If Mali had been designated as his intended final destination before departure, that fact could bear directly on whether American authorities anticipated or participated in the subsequent transfer. Their significance depends on the administrative processes through which the destination information was entered and used.

DHS disputed that interpretation. Its chief legal officer, James Percival, emphasized that Diawara had been transported by the United States to Ghana, not directly to Mali. A subsequent departmental statement maintained that contractors prepared the baggage tags without determining removal destinations and described the medical document's reference to Mali as a clerical error (Toboni et al., 2026).

Neither explanation can be conclusively accepted or rejected solely from the reported documents. Their evidentiary value depends on the original transportation records, instructions concerning final destinations, and any communications between American and Ghanaian authorities. The records strengthen the case for examining advance knowledge, but do not independently prove that American officials instructed Ghana to deport Diawara to Mali.

5.3 Diplomatic Assurances and the US–Ghana Arrangement

The Department of Homeland Security maintained that Ghana provided diplomatic assurances concerning Diawara's safety. Diplomatic assurances are commitments by a receiving government regarding the treatment of transferred individuals. Their significance depends on their precise wording, credibility, implementation, and the receiving state's record of compliance.

The Committee Against Torture addressed such assurances in General Comment No. 4. Paragraphs 19 and 20 caution against using diplomatic assurances to circumvent Article 3's protection against torture and emphasize the need to assess their reliability. Assurances do not automatically establish compliance where substantial evidence indicates that the promised protection may be ineffective (Committee Against Torture, 2018).

Diawara's circumstances raise a particular concern. An assurance that Ghana would not persecute or torture him within its own territory would not necessarily protect him from deportation to Mali. The relevant safeguards would need to address the risk of onward removal and provide sufficiently reliable protection against the consequences prohibited by the applicable international obligations.

American regulations separately address diplomatic assurances against torture. Under 8 C.F.R. § 1208.18(c), assurances obtained by the Secretary of State may be submitted for a specified assessment of their reliability. That procedure should not automatically be equated with the broader assurances described in DHS guidance concerning third-country deportations. The public account does not establish that the particular regulatory mechanism was applied to Diawara.

Ghana's agreement to receive deportees formed part of a broader diplomatic relationship with the United States. President John Dramani Mahama publicly acknowledged the arrangement in September 2025. Human Rights Watch subsequently examined its terms and the diplomatic circumstances surrounding it. The available reporting does not establish a specific financial payment for Diawara's transfer or demonstrate that the arrangement constituted a binding bilateral treaty.

The distinction between an international treaty and a political or administrative arrangement is relevant. A receiving state's assurances may inform the original transferring state's risk assessment, but they cannot displace obligations arising independently under the Refugee Convention, the Convention Against Torture, or other applicable law. The complete wording and monitoring arrangements of the assurances concerning Diawara remain unclear.

6. International Responsibility of the United States and Ghana

The international law of state responsibility distinguishes conduct attributable to a state from a breach of an international obligation binding on that state. Article 2 of the International Law Commission's 2001 Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts expresses these elements. The Articles are not a treaty, although several provisions reflect customary international law and have been relied upon by international courts (ILC, 2001).

For the United States, the central question concerns its own decision to transfer Diawara to Ghana. ICE officials acted as American state agents when organizing and executing the removal. The disputed element is whether that conduct breached an applicable non-refoulement obligation because onward return to Mali presented a sufficiently established and foreseeable risk.

Ghana's position is different. If its authorities forcibly removed Diawara from Ghana to Mali, the transfer would constitute conduct attributable to Ghana under the ordinary rules governing state organs. Ghana's compliance would then be assessed against its own refugee and human rights obligations. Both countries could potentially incur responsibility for distinct conduct within the same sequence of events.

The distinction is central to state responsibility in international law. The ILC Articles distinguish responsibility for a state's own wrongful act from responsibility arising through participation in another state's internationally wrongful conduct. Their provisions concerning aid or assistance, direction and control, and coercion establish additional requirements that cannot be inferred merely from cooperation between governments.

Article 16 addresses aid or assistance provided with knowledge of the circumstances of another state's internationally wrongful act, where the act would also be wrongful if committed by the assisting state. The ILC commentary further describes assistance given with a view to facilitating the wrongful conduct. The provision requires a sufficient contribution to the other state's act and knowledge of the relevant circumstances. General awareness that a partner government has previously committed violations is not, by itself, enough to establish responsibility under Article 16.

Article 17 concerns direction and control exercised over another state's wrongful conduct. That standard is more demanding than ordinary diplomatic influence or administrative cooperation. No publicly established finding demonstrates that American authorities directed Ghana's specific decision to send Diawara to Mali. The absence of such a finding does not resolve whether the United States independently breached a non-refoulement obligation by exposing him to a foreseeable prohibited return. The two theories require separate legal and evidentiary assessments.

6.1 Ghana's Refugee Protection Obligations

Ghana is a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention, the 1967 Protocol, and the 1969 Organization of African Unity Convention Governing the Specific Aspects of Refugee Problems in Africa. These instruments establish international obligations relevant to the treatment and return of qualifying refugees. Ghana incorporated refugee protections into domestic law through the Refugee Law of 1992, PNDCL 305D.

Article II(3) of the OAU Convention prohibits measures that compel a person to return to or remain in a territory where life, physical integrity, or liberty would be threatened for reasons covered by the Convention. Article V(1) recognizes the essentially voluntary character of refugee repatriation and prohibits repatriation against a refugee's will. These protections are particularly relevant where return occurs through coercion rather than a genuinely voluntary decision (OAU, 1969).

Section 1 of Ghana's Refugee Law prohibits returning qualifying refugees to territories where specified threats exist, subject to the legislation's conditions and exceptions. Its language covers Convention-related threats to life or freedom and additional threats associated with external aggression, occupation, foreign domination, or events seriously disrupting public order. Section 2 also provides protections concerning illegal entry or presence while an application for refugee status is being determined.

These provisions do not establish that every foreign national deported to Ghana automatically acquires refugee status. Their application depends on the statutory definition, the individual's circumstances, and the relevant procedures. Diawara's American withholding order would be significant evidence of a previously recognized risk, but it does not automatically determine his status under Ghanaian law.

His account that Ghanaian authorities forcibly returned him to Mali raises a serious

question about those obligations. The inquiry would include whether the relevant authorities knew of his protection order, whether he had access to an effective opportunity to raise his fears, and whether the return was genuinely voluntary. The available evidence does not establish that Ghana conducted an individualized assessment resolving those questions.

Legal challenges have also arisen within Ghana concerning the detention of American deportees and the legality of the broader transfer arrangement. Human Rights Watch documented proceedings before Ghanaian courts and the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice. Those proceedings provide relevant institutional context, but their existence does not establish a final judicial finding concerning Diawara's individual removal.

7. US Court Proceedings and Possible Legal Remedies

American federal courts have become important institutions in disputes over third-country deportations. The central legal questions involve statutory country-selection requirements, constitutional due process, access to judicial review, and the domestic implementation of international protection obligations. The availability of relief depends on both the underlying allegations and the court's jurisdiction.

A distinction must be maintained between international responsibility and domestic enforceability. The United States has treated the ICCPR and Convention Against Torture as non-self-executing for domestic purposes. Convention Against Torture Article 3 obligations have been implemented through the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998 and immigration regulations. An international obligation does not automatically create an independently enforceable private cause of action in federal court.

That difference becomes especially important after removal. A court may have authority to prevent an unlawful deportation before departure, but a claim seeking relief after the individual has left American territory can encounter different jurisdictional and remedial obstacles. Diawara's litigation demonstrates those difficulties, while other recent proceedings show that removal does not invariably eliminate every possible avenue for relief.

7.1 Diawara's Habeas Corpus Petition

On July 29, 2026, Diawara filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 in the Southern District of Texas. The petition challenged the government's imminent intention to remove him to Ghana. The proceedings were transferred to the Northern District of Texas on July 31, after federal records established that Diawara had already departed the United States.

On September 1, Magistrate Judge David L. Horan recommended dismissing the action as moot. The recommendation relied on government evidence that Diawara was no longer detained in the United States and had been removed on July 30. On October 2, District Judge Karen Gren Scholer adopted the recommendation after finding no plain error. No objections had been filed. The dismissal concerned the court's ability to grant relief in that proceeding, rather than a determination that his removal complied with international law (Diawara v. Warden of Prairieland Detention Center, 2026).

The record also establishes an important distinction concerning legal representation. CBS reported that Diawara had been unable to speak with his lawyer or a judge during detention. The magistrate judge's document confirms that he nevertheless filed his petition with legal assistance. These accounts do not necessarily contradict one another. Assistance in preparing a petition does not establish that a detainee had adequate direct communication or a meaningful opportunity to obtain judicial protection before departure.

The proceedings illustrate how the timing of removal can affect preventive litigation. Diawara sought federal judicial intervention before his deportation, but the challenged transfer occurred before the action was substantively resolved. The available record does not establish that officials intentionally frustrated the litigation. Equally, the jurisdictional dismissal cannot be presented as judicial approval of the third-country deportation.

7.2 DHS v. D.V.D. and Third-Country Removal Procedures

On September 18, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit decided D.V.D. v. Department of Homeland Security, a class-action challenge to DHS guidance governing removals to countries not previously identified as destinations in immigration proceedings. The plaintiffs argued that the policies failed to provide effective notice and a meaningful opportunity to raise fears of persecution or torture before removal.

The First Circuit affirmed substantial portions of a district court judgment finding the challenged guidance unlawful. It upheld the determination that effective notice and opportunities to raise fear-based objections were required under the statutory and regulatory scheme, while vacating two declarations concerning the sequencing of removal destinations because the representative plaintiffs lacked Article III standing on that claim. Its reasoning drew on statutory interpretation and constitutional avoidance rather than independently resolving every constitutional question raised by the litigation (D.V.D. v. Department of Homeland Security, 2026).

The appellate court also addressed the danger of chain refoulement. It referred to allegations involving O.C.G., a person protected from removal to Guatemala who had been transferred by the United States to Mexico and subsequently returned to Guatemala. That example demonstrated the potential consequences of third-country removal where effective protection against onward transfer is absent. The discussion did not determine the facts or legality of Diawara's individual deportation.

On September 29, 2026, the Supreme Court granted review in Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., No. 26-426, and stayed the district court's February 25 judgment pending review. The Court agreed to consider jurisdiction, the availability of classwide declaratory and Administrative Procedure Act relief, and the legality of the guidance under the immigration statute, due process, and domestic implementation of Convention Against Torture requirements. Oral argument was scheduled for December 9, 2026 (US Supreme Court, 2026).

The government's October 23, 2026 merits brief argues that federal jurisdictional restrictions prevent the district court from hearing the claims and that 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1) limits the availability of classwide relief. It also maintains that neither § 1231(b) nor the applicable Convention Against Torture implementing provisions impose the specific procedures required by the lower courts. These are the government's arguments before the Supreme Court, not findings adopted by the justices.

On the merits, the government defends its guidance on the basis that individuals may be removed where credible diplomatic assurances exist or, in the absence of such assurances, after notice and an opportunity to raise fears concerning the destination. It maintains that the Constitution does not require officials to solicit objections affirmatively or provide procedures beyond those authorized by statute and regulation. The opposing position, accepted in substantial part by the First Circuit, emphasizes the need for meaningful procedures capable of identifying risks before removal.

Three justices—Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson—would have denied the government's stay application. The stay suspended the operative effect of the challenged district court judgment while Supreme Court review continued. It did not constitute a final ruling that the DHS policy complied with American or international law.

7.3 Judicial Relief After Third-Country Deportation

The litigation involving Etinosa Osahon provides a relevant comparison. Osahon, a Nigerian national protected from removal to Nigeria, was transferred from the United States to Ghana in May 2026. He subsequently brought proceedings in the Central District of California concerning his removal and the government's obligations following the transfer.

On September 10, 2026, District Judge Michelle Williams Court issued a preliminary injunction requiring government action concerning his return and continuing status reports. Further proceedings produced additional orders governing the arrangements for his arrival in the United States. On October 15, counsel represented to the court that Osahon had returned to Los Angeles. The court's October 19 order recorded that representation and discharged the government's daily reporting obligation (Osahon v. Mullin, 2026).

The comparison shows that completed third-country deportation does not invariably prevent judicial intervention. Osahon's proceedings involved continuing civil claims, specific judicial orders, and continuing supervision of the government's compliance. Diawara's Texas habeas proceeding, by contrast, was dismissed as moot because the court concluded that it could no longer grant the relief sought in that action.

The circumstances do not establish an automatic right of return for every deportee. Jurisdiction, the applicable cause of action, sovereign immunity, statutory restrictions, and the possibility of effective relief remain relevant. A remedy available in one proceeding does not necessarily govern another case involving different claims, parties, or procedural circumstances.

CBS reported that Diawara's lawyer had sought judicial assistance in obtaining his return to the United States. The publicly available record does not establish the complete procedural status or outcome of that effort. No conclusion can be drawn that a court has already ordered his return or finally rejected every possible remedy.

At the international level, established state responsibility may require cessation of wrongful conduct and appropriate reparation. The ILC Articles recognize restitution, compensation, and satisfaction as possible forms of reparation, depending on the violation and resulting injury (ILC, 2001, arts 30–37). Those principles do not themselves establish the jurisdiction of an American court or determine the particular relief available to Diawara.

Conclusion

The United States was not necessarily prohibited from deporting Moussa Diawara to Ghana. His reported 2012 withholding-of-removal order restricted removal to Mali but did not automatically confer immunity from deportation to another legally permissible destination. American immigration law recognizes third-country removal, subject to applicable statutory, constitutional, and international obligations.

The international-law question is more demanding. Under the Refugee Convention, the Convention Against Torture, and relevant human rights obligations, an intermediate transfer may be unlawful if it exposes an individual to a sufficiently established and foreseeable risk of prohibited harm through onward removal. Each legal regime has its own conditions of application. In Diawara's case, the reported 2012 protection decision, Ghana's previously documented returns of protected deportees, and the American travel documents identifying Mali provide substantial reasons to examine whether those conditions were satisfied.

The United States' potential responsibility for its own transfer decision must be distinguished from Ghana's responsibility for the subsequent removal. A breach of non-refoulement does not necessarily require proof that American officials directly instructed Ghana to carry out the final deportation. Deliberate coordination remains a separate allegation requiring evidence of American involvement and, where responsibility for assisting another state's wrongful act is asserted, satisfaction of the additional requirements governing such responsibility.

The available evidence supports a serious legal concern that Diawara's removal may have breached international non-refoulement obligations. It does not justify presenting an international-law violation as judicially established. The precise grounds of his original protection, the information available to American authorities, the substance and reliability of Ghana's diplomatic assurances, and the circumstances of the final transfer remain central to determining responsibility. Diawara's case illustrates a fundamental limit on third-country deportation: transferring a protected individual to another sovereign state does not necessarily end the original state's obligations concerning the foreseeable consequences of its own removal decision.

text:
Here are the morning’s top stories on Monday, October 26, 2026

As immigration sweeps expand the number of detainees filling the nation’s detention centers, the amount of people who manage to be released is also growing. That means a steady stream of people are finding themselves in places they don’t know, including Kern County, which is home to four ICE detention facilities, the highest concentration of any county in California. A grassroots movement there has risen to help people find their way back home.

In a rare Sunday hearing, a panel of the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals questioned the timing and constitutionality of the Department of Justice efforts to intervene in California’s midterm election. The three judge panel seemed skeptical of the DOJ’s demand to hold aside 20,000 ballots, over concerns about the citizenship of voters.

On a Wednesday afternoon in September, the terminal inside the Bakersfield Amtrak and Greyhound station sat mostly empty. It was a regular day on the job for Ismael Larralde, who volunteers at the station to help passengers get to their bus or train.

But since the Trump administration has pushed for mass deportations and Congress approved historic funding for immigration enforcement and detention, Larralde has found himself doing something new: assisting people who have just been released from immigrant detention. “They’re very scared. They don’t know which direction to go, and if sometimes we approach them, they’re hesitant because of all the negativity they’ve been through,” Larralde said.

On this day, Larralde stood next to two men inside the train station who had just been released hours earlier from a nearby detention center. Kern County is home to four Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facilities. It’s the highest concentration of any county in California. People released from the two detention centers in McFarland – Golden State Annex and Central Valley Annex – are sent to Fresno’s ICE field office for processing. Those released from the California City Detention Facility and the Mesa Verde ICE Processing Center are received at the Bakersfield field office.

That field office is located on Truxtun Avenue, just down the street from the train station. It’s where the men released today came from, and it’s where the newly released detainees processed at this office usually end up. Larralde said over the last two years that he has worked at the terminal, he has met people from New York, Maryland, Florida and even as far as Puerto Rico. And he’s learned how to spot someone who just got out. “They come in with red bags. There are documents inside, like onion sacks. A lot of times they just show up with a yellow envelope,”Larralde said.

As the number of detainees filling the nation’s immigration detention centers grows, so does the amount of people who manage to be released, with an increasing number of people filing for petitions of habeas corpus. That’s a legal filing that challenges the government’s reasoning to hold someone in detention. ICE data shows more than 2,500 detainees have come through Kern County just this year. Their average detention was between 25 and 69 days.

Of the two men waiting in the terminal that day, only one man agreed to talk with KVPR. He requested his name not be used. He’s scheduled to appear in immigration court the following month and doesn’t want to jeopardize his case. The man said he’d been living and working in Salt Lake City for nine years with a legal work permit. But over the summer, ICE officers detained him on his way to a grocery store. He spent the past two months in the California City Detention Facility. “In reality, they’re rounding up a lot of people, including those who have [work] permits or who have started the paperwork process – and they’re just taking everyone indiscriminately,” the man said in Spanish.

Jeannie Parent is the founder of Kern Welcoming and Extending Solidarity to Immigrants (KWESI). The organization provides aid to people held in detention centers, and responds when someone is released. “So we’re trying to work together to get him home. That’s the main priority,” she said.

Parent is also in frequent communication with Faith in the Valley, a faith-based organization with presence all over the Central Valley that has picked up its work with immigrants under the heightened enforcement environment. She said it’s unclear how anyone released from detention could ever find their way home without organizations like KWESI, Faith in the Valley and volunteers like Larralde. “They’ve been shuffled around the whole country. They’ve been trafficked, basically, and then left in California, 3,000 miles from home, with no resources, and often their IDs and their work permits and their passports have been taken by ICE as well,” Parent said. KVPR reached out to the Department of Homeland Security about its personal property policy. The agency said all personal property is “removed and secured while a detainee is in custody” and given back “upon arrival to their final destination.” However, DHS did not respond to a request to clarify whether “final destination” refers to their home state or the facility where they were processed for release.

A panel of federal appellate judges on Sunday questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department’s demand that California election officials set aside thousands of mail ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.

During rare weekend arguments, two of the three judges on the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals appeared skeptical of a lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump’s administration in mid-October. The lawsuit accuses California officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review 20,000 names the administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. The administration asked a federal judge to require the state to withhold counting those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The district judge scheduled a hearing for Oct. 27, days after the case was assigned, but the federal government appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, seeking an expedited decision.

Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly told the panel that California is causing irreparable harm “by allowing noncitizens to vote in violation of their own state laws. The damage is irreversible and irrevocable.” The Trump administration has made efforts to identify noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, questioned whether the appellate court even has jurisdiction to hear the case even before a ruling by the lower court. Donnelly argued that the schedule set by the lower court judge was too slow and effectively a denial of the government’s request, as state elections officials process thousands of mail ballots every day.

Judge Gabriel Sanchez, appointed by former President Joe Biden, questioned whether the federal government was violating the Tenth Amendment, essentially commandeering the state to enforce a federal law that makes it a misdemeanor for a noncitizen to vote. The federal government is simply asking California to enforce their own law, which also bans noncitizens from voting, Donnelly said. He argued the state’s refusal to comply with the federal request to set aside the ballots for review was “frustrating the purpose” of the federal law against noncitizen voting. The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections, Bennett said. The executive branch may be “unhappy with what they’re doing, and doesn’t like the manner,” Bennett said, but under the Election Clause the state has the right to determine those issues — including how it sorts out any noncitizen voters.

Attorney Seth Waxman, representing Los Angeles County Clerk Dean Logan, said the federal government’s list was unreliable and that segregating the ballots for a review process would effectively disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters. Waxman cited a review of 200 records from the Trump administration’s list conducted by Los Angeles County staffers. Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, individuals with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States, which the filing notes “is strong evidence of citizenship.”

text:
Policies threatening the safety and stability of refugees in the United states have been a defining feature of the Trump-Vance administration’s xenophobic immigration agenda. Policies hostile to refugees include U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’s (“USCIS”) indefinite hold on all pending green card applications filed by refugees, as well as the re-vetting of those refugees under a November 2025 policy announced by USCIS. Most recently, the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS also published, without notice and comment, an interim final rule (IFR) cutting the time a refugee has to respond to a notice of intent to terminate refugee status from thirty to ten days.

IRAP is counsel in a lawsuit brought by six organizations and four individual refugees seeking to end the Trump-Vance Administration’s illegal policies, which would permit the government to strip refugees across the country of their immigration status and benefits.

Our clients

The individual Plaintiffs are four refugees from various countries who are affected by these policies. Plaintiffs and their families were lawfully admitted to the United States through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program (“USRAP”) after comprehensive security vetting and are not removable under the Immigration and Nationality Act (“INA”). Still, they fear the loss of their immigration status, have already lost essential benefits, and are unable to become legal permanent residents under USCIS’ new policies.

Our organizational plaintiffs include membership organizations Partnership for the Advancement of New Americans (“PANA”), a nonprofit membership organization headquartered in California led by and serving refugees, and African Communities Together (“ACT”), a national nonprofit membership organization of African immigrants fighting for civil rights in the United States. Members of both organizations are subject to these policies.

The organizational plaintiffs also include International Institute of New England and Jewish Family Service of Western Massachusetts, whose core missions include serving resettled refugees in Massachusetts, and HIAS and Refugee Council USA (“RCUSA”), who serve refugee communities across the country. These organizations are increasingly under pressure as their client communities face re-vetting, loss of benefits, and potential termination of their status.

Impact

The Administration estimates that there are over 113,000 unadjusted refugees in the United States who are subject to re-vetting and over 186,000 unadjusted refugees subject to the IFR. Refugees who cannot adjust their status are being deprived of the benefits of lawful permanent residence, including a path to citizenship, eligibility for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (“SNAP”), and, since October 1, 2026, Medicaid coverage. The risk of having their refugee status terminated without a meaningful opportunity to respond places refugees at risk of being separated from their families and removal to countries where they face persecution.

Case status

October 26, 2026: Case is filed in United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts (“Court” or “District Court”). Plaintiffs also file an emergency request for a stay and a stay pending appeal.

Democracy Forward Foundation and A&O Shearman are co-counsel in this lawsuit.

authors: Cindy Galli, Ken Dilanian, Steve Benen

text:
A group of former federal prosecutors and human rights lawyers is coming together to investigate political corruption and law enforcement violence that it says is being ignored by the Justice Department under President Donald Trump.

Organizers said the nonpartisan, nonprofit organization, dubbed the Rule of Law Project, would gather facts and present cases either to state or local prosecutors, or to a future Justice Department it said may operate in a less partisan manner than the current one.

Founder Brad Adams, who spent 20 years with the nongovernmental organization Human Rights Watch overseeing investigations of state violence, said the group was responding to a climate — citing recent stories alleging grift among politicians and incidents like shootings by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers — in which “senior officials openly engage in corruption and federal agents beat and kill innocent people with impunity.”

“The rule of law is on life support, but it’s all of our responsibility to make sure it doesn’t die,” he added.

Adams said the group would be funded by undisclosed private donors, and would operate in a strictly nonpartisan manner, probing corruption among members of both parties.

“The Rule of Law Project’s mission is to bring back the ideal that the law protects and binds everyone, that criminal conduct has consequences and that no one — regardless of office, badge or influence — may escape those consequences.”

The Rule of Law Project will seek to investigate and document instances of official corruption and police violence across the United States that appear to have gone unexamined and unpunished, though without the subpoena power afforded to government investigators. It will gather evidence and witness statements and turn over “prosecution-ready case files” to state and local authorities, or a future Department of Justice the group said may be more willing to take on those cases.

“I do not think we can break the cycle in this country without criminal accountability,” Adams said, adding that he anticipateed working with Congressional investigators where appropriate.

State and local prosecutors have launched investigations into some cases of ICE violence, but have faced obstacles in obtaining evidence.

DOJ officials disputed the idea that they ignore potential criminal activity, saying the department assesses each case on the merits.

The lead investigator will be Mark Blumberg, who spent almost 30 years in the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division investigating and prosecuting acts of official misconduct. For the last 20 years, Blumberg led DOJ efforts to enforce civil rights laws in elections. He also served on the FBI’s Shooting Investigation Review Group and Customs and Border Protection’s National Use of Force Review Board.

The group said he would lead a team of former federal prosecutors and investigators with decades of federal law enforcement experience.

“People need to trust that the game is not rigged against them, that the law applies to everyone,” Blumberg said. “If those in power aren’t held accountable for illegally enriching themselves and using violence against others without cause, that undermines any incentive for the rest of us to follow the law. Our public officials should model the best behavior for our country, not milk it dry for power and riches.”

Organizers said the Rule of Law Project would investigate officials who appear to have used their public office for private gain, including those who solicit or accept something of value in exchange for influencing their official duties, who improperly seek to influence executive and legislative actions, and whose official acts affect their personal financial interest.

A series of news stories over the past 20 months has documented questionable conduct by public officials or FBI corruption investigations that were closed by Trump officials.

More articles

For example, MS NOW was first to report that the FBI recorded Tom Homan accepting $50,000 cash in an undercover sting operation, an allegation Homan has denied. The case did not move forward.

More recently, ProPublica reported that the Trump Justice Department declined to move forward on FBI investigations of potential illegal cash for contract schemes involving Republican Sen. Susan Collins, the late Republican Sen. Lindsay Graham and Democratic Rep. James Clyburn. Collins and Clyburn deny wrongdoing. The FBI told ProPublica that it had found “nothing implicating Senator Collins” and that the stories about the lawmakers were based on “half-baked misleading claims from former FBI personnel and a convicted felon to spin a predetermined narrative.”

Other cases have come to light that typically might have drawn Justice Department scrutiny, including a recent New York Times report that former DOJ official Alina Habba received a $50 million compensation package from the daughter of a Venezuelan billionaire who sought and got a pardon from Trump. Habba denies wrongdoing and the DOJ has not indicated whether it will — or will not — investigate the matter.

The Rule of Law Project will also investigate excessive-force cases and improper conditions of confinement, with a specific focus on unlawful conduct by ICE and CBP, the group says. Investigators will also look into federal interference with protected liberties, including the right to vote.

After an ICE officer shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine in July, officials said the FBI was not conducting a civil rights investigation.

The DOJ also declined to open a civil rights investigation into the January ICE shooting of Renée Good in Minneapolis.

“We only take cases that an independent Justice Department would have pursued in ordinary times,” Blumberg said. “That’s the standard I held myself to as a prosecutor. We’re not here to seek retribution or to settle scores. We’re here to ensure the law applies to the powerful the same way it applies to the rest of us.”

Since Watergate, the Department of Justice has operated independently of the White House in choosing which cases to investigate and prosecute. Days after he was sworn in, Attorney General Todd Blanche said he would not pledge to run the department independent of Trump and the White House.

“No, I’m not going to pledge that. And no attorney general should ever pledge that,” he told NBC in August.

Among the board members of the new group is Kenneth Roth, former executive director at Human Rights Watch.

“Since the current U.S. government won’t investigate allegations of ICE violence or official corruption, we will,” he said. “To lay the foundation for prosecutions when they become possible.”

text:
U.S. Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, a five-term Democrat who defeated Republicans in all five general elections, faces his toughest campaign yet after his South Texas district was redrawn to favor the GOP.

President Donald Trump won the new district by 10 points, giving Republican Eric Flores an edge heading toward the Nov. 3 election — provided his party can retain recent gains made with Latino voters. Both campaigns are focused on immigration issues, primarily by tying their opponent to unpopular policies from their party’s president.

Texas’ 34th Congressional District, which stretches from Brownsville to Corpus Christi, is one of five redrawn last year by Republicans in the Texas Legislature who wanted to protect the GOP majority in the U.S. House. As those races have become more competitive than Republicans anticipated, the party is banking on Flores to flip the Democratic seat.

The GOP’s Congressional Leadership Fund is shifting part of $3 million it had reserved for Rep. Henry Cuellar, the Laredo Democrat whose reelection chances have improved, to boost Flores’ campaign. In addition, a Trump-led campaign rally originally planned for Waco will be held Tuesday in Corpus Christi.

Flores has been endorsed by Trump, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson and Majority Leader Steve Scalise, both R-Louisiana. The federal prosecutor and National Guardsman who served on the border is also backed by several county constables and sheriffs, as well as the National Border Patrol Council.

“I’ve been in the trench with them,” Flores said of the Border Patrol, pointing to his service during Operation Guardian Support, when Trump ordered National Guardsmen to the border during his first term. “I don’t know if [Gonzalez] has a single law enforcement endorsement because he doesn’t know what he’s talking about.”

With Joe Biden in the White House, migrant encounters at the border peaked at a historic high of 2.5 million in 2023, according to the Migration Policy Institute — a situation Flores is happy to point out on the campaign.

“Border security is still on a lot of peoples’ minds. We lived through it,” he said. “We don’t want that back. I mean, your homes and your ranches and your farmlands getting ravaged.”

“Meanwhile, my opponent was saying Biden was on the right track,” Flores added.

Gonzalez, who in a 2021 NPR interview called Biden’s approach “a good immigration plan,” that same month also predicted that loosening Trump’s first-term border restrictions would lead to a “catastrophic” surge of migrants.

This election cycle, Gonzalez has focused on the latter message.

“I was one of the most critical Democrats in the country on President Biden on the way they handled the border,” Gonzalez said. “We should have a very secure border that people can’t just show up and ask for asylum under antiquated laws and get in and let loose. I think we never should have done that.”

Gonzalez also said that, looking back, he understands why many of his constituents voted Republican in 2024. “I think if I had not been a member of Congress and I had been an independent voter that cycle, I probably would not have voted for Democrats that year,” he said.

In turn, Gonzalez hopes frustration over inflation, combined with the Trump administration’s “hyperaggressive ICE raids devastating our economy,” will turn any advantage Republicans gained from redistricting on its head.

“I think a lot of Latinos in this country feel offended by the policies that have come out of this administration, and you know, obviously, I think there’s going to be repercussions at the ballot box,” he said.

The Gonzalez campaign hammered this theme when it paid for a Brownsville billboard showing Flores posing with Trump — both flashing a thumbs-up — under the words “Trump endorsed.” The billboard, presented in the style of a Flores campaign ad, also read: “Support ICE!”

The Flores campaign responded with a cease-and-desist letter demanding the billboard owner take down the ad, saying it illegally misappropriated Flores’ image and likeness.

Gonzalez criticized the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement as excessive and inhumane.

“We don’t want to go grab somebody with a weedeater in their hand and slam them against a concrete wall, and bloody them up, and beat them up, and handcuff them and throw them in a wagon,” Gonzalez said. “That’s not who we are in South Texas.”

“The president told us he was going to deport criminals, and he didn’t just go after criminals,” Gonzalez said. “He went after the vast majority of the immigrant population.”

According to a report by the Migration Policy Institute released this month, one-fifth of deportations during the first 18 months of Trump’s current term involved people with a criminal conviction.

Flores said context is important when looking at immigration enforcement because “closer to 10 million illegal aliens were allowed in this country.”

“When [Gonzalez] talks about ICE, the first question he should ask himself is why is ICE doing what they’re doing?” he said.

“From the get-go I have said we need to prioritize the criminals. Your drug traffickers, your child predators, those creating production of child pornography, your gun traffickers, your money launderers. There’s plenty. That’s who we should be prioritizing first,” Flores said.

If Gonzalez “wants to talk about a balance with ICE, the first thing he should ask himself is what legislation he’s put forth to fix any of it,” Flores added. “He’s not done anything other than complain on Facebook.”

Gonzalez defended his productivity in Congress, saying he helped bring about $8 billion in federal resources to his district, including to public schools and the healthcare system.

He also said voters this year are far less concerned about illegal border crossings that are down significantly in recent years.

“It’s not an issue because right now, it’s not a problem,” Gonzalez said.

Instead, Gonzalez said South Texas voters are more concerned about affording groceries, gas, housing and healthcare. “That is the common denominator across the country,” he said.

He blamed inflation on Trump’s tariffs and his war in Iran — policies Gonzalez hopes to reel back if his party wins majority control of the U.S. House. Among his other priorities are protecting Social Security as well as grants for low-income schools.

Flores defended military action in Iran.

“Forty years of presidents, not one has done anything about Iran. Kamala said it, Biden said it, Obama said it. Finally, President Trump does something about it,” he said, calling Gonzalez’s criticism a “let’s just blame Trump” charade.

Flores also stood by the administration’s tariffs, pointing to the high U.S. trade deficit, which according to the U.S. Department of Commerce, totaled $918 billion in 2024.

“It was time for America to be treated fairly when it comes to that. Now, it has brought back manufacturing, it has brought back jobs. Has the consumer paid for that? Yes, and that’s the portion that I wish that we could fix,” he said. “That’s something that I want to focus on day one to try to help that.”

Flores also said he’ll forge his own path in Congress.

“I was not that traditional Republican because I was pushing, from the get-go, a solution for a work visa program,” Flores said. “I think a lot of people are just completely opposed to that, and that’s not me. I’m going to do the best thing that’s right for the district.”

Implementing a work visa program is a policy both candidates share, pointing to a workforce shortage in the district.

Another shared priority is securing water for Corpus Christi and the Coastal Bend, where years of drought have strained households, businesses and industry.

“I believe the federal government, who collects billions of dollars of taxes from the energy that’s being exported out of that port, has an obligation to step in and do what’s right and help pay for desalination operation or whatever it takes to assure that we have permanent water sustainability,” Gonzalez said.

Both candidates have been robust fundraisers this cycle, with Gonzalez collecting $5.2 million and Flores raising $3.9 million, according to Federal Election Commission filings updated Thursday. Gonzalez also had more available cash with $1.4 million on hand as of Oct. 14, compared to Flores’ $246,000.

text:
Dennys Alcivar loves to travel outside his native Ecuador. But the flight he boarded in September, leaving Salt Lake City, was nothing like those vacations.

Alcivar boarded what the ICE Flight Monitor at the nonprofit Human Rights First calls a shuffle flight. Unlike deportation flights that take people out of the country, shuffle flights move detainees between U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centers and jails.

He was chained for the flight, which to him was excessive, but he recalled joking that he felt as important as the drug lord El Chapo.

“Entiendo que son protocolos de seguridad, lo tengo claro, pero es absurdo porque te revisan en cada movimiento y estás encerrado en todos los pasos que vas,” he said in Spanish.

“I understand they’re security protocols, that I understand, but it’s absurd because they check you at every move and you’re locked up for every step of the way.”

The morning of his departure started at the Weber County Jail, where he was detained after his arrest in Ogden. ICE took him to the Salt Lake City International Airport, and he recalled being told he was heading to California. Unlike everyday travelers, there was no security line, gift shop or gate. He and the other detainees were taken to the tarmac where they walked up a set of stairs onto a plane, away from commercial aircraft.

This flight network has increased dramatically during President Donald Trump’s second term, said Fetaine Seddighzadeh, reporting and monitoring analyst with the flight monitor.

“We've seen at least 50 new cities come into the domestic shuffle network,” she said, including three in Utah: Salt Lake City, St. George and Cedar City.

The latter airport only had one ICE flight since tracking began in 2020, and Seddighzadeh doesn’t know if there will be more. But flights through Salt Lake City and St. George have been consistent. With 19 through Salt Lake and nine through St. George, September was Utah’s busiest month for ICE flights since they began passing through the state in March 2025, according to internal ICE Flight Monitor data.

Through September, the data shows that top destinations for flights from Salt Lake City this year are El Paso, Texas, and Bakersfield and Victorville, California. Routes through St. George have mostly gone to Twin Falls, Idaho. These are just the first stops after Utah. The planes continue afterward to other stops, and detainees could be taken off at any of them.

Except for two women who stayed on until a later stop, the flight was mostly men, Alcivar said. Shuffle flights typically make two to four stops before returning to their starting point, Seddighzadeh said.

In some ways, the ICE flights are a distorted funhouse mirror of normal domestic flights.

There was a safety briefing, Alcivar said, but he couldn’t hear it very well. He was a volunteer firefighter in his native Ecuador, so he worried about what he’d do in an emergency.

“Ya había visto la salida de emergencia, pero digo, pero al final del día estoy esposado, y ¿cómo ayudo a los demás?”

“I’d already seen the emergency exit, but I mean, but at the end of the day I’m handcuffed, and how do I help others?”

ICE policy is to restrain detainees with handcuffs, waist chains and leg irons on flights. That worries Human Rights First, Seddighzadeh said. Plus, safety isn’t their only concern.

“Moving people around farther from their communities, their families, their legal counsel just puts really, like, additional barriers on people who are in the system,” she said.

On Alcivar’s flight, there was also a snack. After a long day of delays, he said detainees each received a sandwich, a bottle of water and some cookies.

During the experience, Alcivar saw the United States in a new light.

He entered the country legally with a tourist visa, then applied to change it to a student visa to learn English. The request was still pending when he was arrested, leaving him in limbo, according to his attorney. He believed he’d been in the country legally. He said he’d always thought of the United States as a country where rights are respected, with a justice system different from Latin America.

“Siempre he tenido ese concepto y yo decía en cada momento, pero ¿Qué está pasando? ¿Por qué no me escuchan?”

“I’ve always had that understanding, and I kept saying, ‘But what is happening? Why won’t they listen to me?’”

There were lighter moments with fellow detainees on the flight, like with young Venezuelan men singing. The detainees wore the clothes they were arrested in. One man joked about Alcivar’s long-sleeve white button-down and jeans. He was very white-collar, while everyone else was blue-collar — dressed to work in construction or painting, and the group laughed.

From the California City detention center, Alcivar filed a habeas petition, and a judge ordered his release. He’d been in detention for more than a month. A community organization helped him get a bus ticket back to Utah.

Back in the state where he’d been living, Alcivar spoke before the Ogden City Council to tell people about his arrest, which the Ogden Police Department is investigating. His family wants him to return to Ecuador, he said.

“O sea mi vida está allá, pero yo les digo no, está bien, pero yo quiero ejercer la ley. No puedo irme del país con todos estos temas sueltos.”

“I mean, my life is there, but I tell them no, it’s fine, but I want to uphold the law. I can’t leave the country with all these loose ends.”
