text:
A longtime youth baseball coach known throughout the D.C. region as “Coach A” is being held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody in Louisiana, according to his family.

Amaury Monsalve, a husband and father of two, has coached baseball in D.C. and Virginia for more than 25 years, including at Alice Deal Middle School, Jackson-Reed High School and Woodson High School. His family said Monsalve, who is originally from Venezuela, is a lawful permanent resident living in Virginia with no criminal record.

On Oct. 19, Monsalve was taken into ICE custody after a judge denied his citizenship case.

“Amaury’s difficulties stem, according to our examination, from serious errors made by a former immigration attorney more than 20 years ago, when Amaury had limited command of English,” Robert Carmona-Borjas, CEO and co-founder of the Arcadia Foundation, told WTOP. He said Monsalve is a lawful permanent resident who was seeking U.S. citizenship.

‘Mom, ICE took him.’

Monsalve’s family said he had a previously-scheduled hearing Oct. 19 related to his citizenship case. A day before that hearing, Monsalve was stopped by D.C. police while working as a chauffeur, according to his wife of 16 years, Aniushka.

According to a police report, Monslave was pulled over in a Chevy SUV for allegedly running a red light on the morning of Oct. 18. Police said they found a handgun, a fifth of tequila and a clear bag with a white powder — reportedly determined to be cocaine.

The decision of whether to file formal charges falls on U.S. Attorney for the D.C. Jeanine Pirro. Her office confirmed to WTOP on Monday that it did not file any charges against Monsalve or any of the passengers in the SUV.

The passengers were released, but Monsalve was held overnight until his immigration hearing.

The next day, Aniushka and one of the couple’s sons waited outside the immigration courthouse, but she said her husband never emerged.

“My son was coming out telling me, ‘Mom, ICE took him,’ and I screamed, and I went inside to look for the staff. They were turning the lights off, and I went and asked them ‘Why? What do you mean?’ And then they told me ICE took him,” Aniushka said. “We only found out because they were closing.”

Monsalve has since been transferred among multiple detention facilities and is now being held in Louisiana. A bond hearing is scheduled for Nov. 3.

An appeal filed the same day he was taken into custody remains pending before the Board of Immigration Appeals, according to Carmona-Borjas. It was not immediately clear what effect, if any, the appeal may have on Monsalve’s detention status or potential removal proceedings.

8 arrests during traffic stop

A police report obtained by WTOP listed a handful of offenses associated with the traffic stop on Oct. 18, including possession of an unregistered gun, ammunition, an open container of alcohol and a controlled substance.

Monsalve and all 7 of his passengers were arrested by D.C. police but it does not appear any of them were formally charged. Following the arrests, all 8 people were taken to the D.C. Department of Corrections but none were charged, according to Pirro’s office and police.

It isn’t clear exactly what happened between their arrival and the moment Monsalve was taken into ICE custody. Aniushka said her husband told her officers brought a warrant for his arrest to court.

Online court records show a search warrant was executed on Monsalve and list the case as closed.

Concerns about conditions in ICE detention

Aniushka said she is “very concerned” about her husband’s well-being in detention. She said Monsalve has told her by phone that he and other detainees are ill and have had difficulty obtaining medical care. She also said she has been unable to create a commissary account to send him money for food and hygiene products.

“He was desperate. He said, ‘What have you done? Have you done something for me?’ And I said, ‘Yes, of course. I told you we did the appeal’. And he said, ‘They’re telling me I have nothing, and they keep bringing me papers to sign,’” Aniushka said.

Aniushka said she and Carmona-Borjas advised Monsalve not to sign documents he did not understand. However, Monsalve later told them detention facility staff returned and had him provide a fingerprint.

Carmona-Borjas questioned whether Monsalve fully understood the documents involved.

“That’s not right. You know, regularly you put a fingerprint when you don’t know how to sign,” Carmona-Borjas said. “We don’t like that kind of trick … to put the fingerprint in any document that he didn’t want to sign. That’s not right.”

WTOP has reached out to ICE for comment regarding Monsalve’s detention, the family’s account of his case, and allegations concerning conditions at the facility.

Mark, 14, who was coached by Monsalve for three years at Alice Deal Middle School, said the detention has been difficult for him and his teammates.

“When he coached me, he was always trying to uplift everyone, and he was trying to make sure everyone had an opportunity to play, no matter how much money they had or how good they were,” Mark said.

Monsalve’s family has created a GoFundMe campaign to help cover legal costs and offset the loss of its main source of income.

title: Trump administration can hold immigrants in ICE custody without bond, court rules
authors: Uriel García, Uriel J. García, Texas Tribune, www.houstonpublicmedia.org
description:
The troopers turned the men over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who held them in detention without allowing them to see a judge.
The Trump administration appealed, arguing that federal immigration law says undocumented immigrants should be held until deportation without bond hearings — a policy it put in place in July 2025.
Friday's ruling is welcome news for the Trump administration, which has prioritized immigration enforcement as part of its mass deportation efforts.
A policy change by the Trump administration Under federal immigration laws, the government can quickly deport undocumented immigrants who recently crossed the U.S.-Mexico border without giving them a chance for a bond hearing.
Since January 2025, immigrants have filed more than 89,000 petitions against the Trump administration, seeking their release.
text:
This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

Immigrants who entered the country illegally don't have a right to seek bond while they’re in custody and going through deportation proceedings, even if they've set roots in the U.S., a federal appeals court ruled Friday.

In a 10-7 ruling, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans ruled that current immigration laws allow the federal government to hold detained immigrants until they’re deported — regardless of whether they have made a life in the U.S. and lack a criminal history.

Trump-appointed Judge Cory Wilson wrote in the court's ruling that if undocumented immigrants have not been legally admitted to the U.S., they are only entitled to whatever rights Congress has spelled out in immigration laws. He added that if undocumented immigrants in custody want to be free from detention, "they can do so at any moment by agreeing to leave the country."

In a concurring opinion, Judge Andrew Oldham agreed.

"Because such aliens remain legally unadmitted, they receive exactly the same due process rights that they would have if they had come through a legal port of entry — which are whatever rights Congress chooses to give them," Oldham wrote.

Judge Leslie Southwick, a George W. Bush appointee, wrote in his dissent that the ruling has created an "impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents."

Rebecca Cassler, senior litigation attorney at the American Immigration Council, who argued the case before the 5th Circuit, said the court's ruling is an attack on constitutional due process rights, which have been guaranteed to anyone living in the U.S., regardless of immigration status.

"The right to due process is a fundamental constitutional protection, and it is meant to protect every person in this country. Because of today's decision, that right is hollow for immigrants in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi," she said. "But the logic of the 5th Circuit's decision threatens everyone in this country: When courts degrade the meaning of liberty for some, we all suffer the consequences."

Mass deportation efforts

The case stems from the arrest of three men in Texas by state troopers between November 2025 and February 2026 during routine traffic stops. All three have lived in the country for at least 14 years, worked during that time and have children who are American citizens. The troopers turned the men over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who held them in detention without allowing them to see a judge.

Ignacio Sosnava Rodriguez, Miguel Angel Gomez Alvarado and Alejandro Villegas Angel were eventually released from ICE custody after federal judges found that holding them without a chance for a bond hearing violated the men's due process rights. The Trump administration appealed, arguing that federal immigration law says undocumented immigrants should be held until deportation without bond hearings — a policy it put in place in July 2025.

Friday's ruling is welcome news for the Trump administration, which has prioritized immigration enforcement as part of its mass deportation efforts.

"Big win in the Fifth Circuit on mandatory detention for illegal aliens, a principle codified in 1996 legislation but ignored by the deep state for decades," James Percival, a lawyer in the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, said on social media, referring to Clinton administration immigration law that expanded the list of immigrants who can be more easily deported.

"Rejecting due process"

Gracie Willis, an attorney with the National Immigration Project, which is representing the three Texas men, said the general public should be concerned that a federal court believes the government can hold people indefinitely without justification.

"We look at this case as an affront to due process, as the 5th Circuit rejecting due process," Willis said. "It’s really a shocking extension of this attempt to criminalize immigrants and to hold immigrants in detention without any opportunity for them to be released, thereby creating an environment of fear."

Willis said her organization is still assessing what legal action to take and has not decided if it plans to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

She said immigration lawyers are anticipating how district courts are going to react to this ruling. Many district judges have ruled that immigrants being held in detention centers have a right to bond as long as they are not a flight risk or a danger to the community.

Even though Friday's ruling is limited to the 5th Circuit, which includes Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, the Trump administration has transferred many immigrants from other states to detention centers in Texas.

A policy change by the Trump administration

Under federal immigration laws, the government can quickly deport undocumented immigrants who recently crossed the U.S.-Mexico border without giving them a chance for a bond hearing. But for those who have lived in the U.S. for months or years before being detained, the law gave them the right to challenge their detention.

In July 2025, the Trump administration announced a policy change, saying that anyone who has been arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents — regardless of how long they've been in the country — doesn't have a right to bond.

Earlier this month, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear a separate but similar case that directly challenges the Trump administration's mandatory detention policy.

According to ProPublica, immigrants filed more habeas corpus petitions — a legal procedure that allows a person detained by the government to challenge their imprisonment — in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration than in the past three administrations combined.

Since January 2025, immigrants have filed more than 89,000 petitions against the Trump administration, seeking their release.

Friday’s ruling doesn’t prohibit other detainees from filing habeas corpus petitions if they entered the country legally.

Politico found that more than 400 federal judges — appointed by presidents of both major political parties — have ruled in favor of immigrants' right to due process in more than 5,000 cases since the Trump administration's policy change last year.

In comparison, 41 judges have sided with the administration's interpretation of the law in 250 cases, according to a Politico analysis of federal government data.

title: Court ruling fails to end wait for thousands of immigrants stuck abroad without visas | WGLT
description:
That's because this January the Trump administration banned the processing of immigrant visas for citizens of 75 countries.
On its website, the State Department acknowledges the visa ban is no longer in effect due to the court ruling.
This means even immigrants with visas approved would have to go through additional screening.
"I've never seen a substantial pause on visa processing … I really haven't," the former consular officer said.
But the battle over visa processing has affected many immigrants who fall into the high-performing category.
text:
Late last year, Dustin Hoffman and his wife Gloria started the paperwork to secure a visa for her to live in the U.S.

The couple, along with their 5-year-old daughter Chaya and Hoffman's 12-year-old step son Israel, lived together in Argentina, where Hoffman had moved in 2013 after doing a deployment with the U.S. Army in Iraq.

"My daughter is growing up and she's very smart and my stepson he's very smart," Hoffman said. "But the resources in Argentina for an autistic child and the school system in Argentina … I don't know. I just feel like I needed to give my daughter the same opportunities that I had growing up."

But nearly a year later, the kids and Gloria are stuck in Argentina in bureaucratic limbo due to continuing delays in the processing of their visa.

That's because this January the Trump administration banned the processing of immigrant visas for citizens of 75 countries. Many of the migrants were already in the process of getting a visa. Some already had the visa approved; they were just waiting to get the physical visa delivered to them.

Hoffman's wife is from Colombia, one of the countries on the list.

A federal judge this August ordered the ban to be lifted, but Hoffman's family still has not gotten their visa, and the State Department continues to ask them to provide additional evidence to prove they have the financial means to live in the U.S. without becoming a public charge.

Attorneys representing migrants say the Hoffman family's case is emblematic of a wider problem: They say the Trump administration is not complying with the federal court order and is instead slow-walking the processing of the visas.

"So while technically the ban doesn't exist, it doesn't matter practically if people are still not being able to get their green card interviews or have their interviews not be finished and not get their immigrant visa stamps foils and be able to come into the United States," said Alexis Axelrad, the president elect of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

A new training creates additional delays

The visa ban affected more than 280,000 immigrants who had applied for visas by the time the policy went into effect in January.

According to an analysis by the libertarian think-tank Cato Institute, the ban targeted thousands of close family members of U.S. citizens and permanent residents, including spouses and minor children. The Cato report called it "one of the most extreme legal immigration policies in U.S. history."

Now stuck in their countries unable to come to the U.S., many are rethinking what to do.

The State Department declined to comment for this story, telling NPR "the matter referenced is subject to pending litigation." On its website, the State Department acknowledges the visa ban is no longer in effect due to the court ruling.

The agency told NPR in August it had paused the processing of visas as it launched an in-depth "training program" for embassies and consulates on identifying immigrants who could become a burden on taxpayers — a public charge.

This means even immigrants with visas approved would have to go through additional screening.

This pause is uncommon, a former State Department consular officer told NPR. She asked not to be identified because she fears it could affect her job prospects.

"I've never seen a substantial pause on visa processing … I really haven't," the former consular officer said. "The department is doing this because this is what the policy is from the president … to reduce illegal immigration, remigrate people and only accept refugees from South Africa."

But families such as the Hoffmans are stuck in limbo. He says he misses his daughter, stepson, and wife every day. He said his daughter cries "all the time" and asks for her father. His wife is overwhelmed.

"Let me put it this way: Our family is a family. We need to be there for each other," Hoffman said. "Just like any family, it's not functioning very well while we're separated."

The brightest is left behind

During his first term, President Trump said he wanted to attract the brightest immigrants to come to the U.S.

Right-wing organizations, including the America First Policy Institute, have also endorsed a "merit-based" immigration system.

"America's immigration system should prioritize immigrants with education, skills, and well-paying jobs waiting for them in the U.S. because these individuals are most likely to contribute to America's society and economy, benefitting all Americans," the organization wrote in March 2026.

But the battle over visa processing has affected many immigrants who fall into the high-performing category.

One of them is Dr. Fernando Lizcano, a Colombian national whose research focuses on major cardiovascular health challenges in the U.S., including obesity.

He applied for an EB-1A visa, which is reserved for immigrants "of extraordinary ability," including "an outstanding professor or researcher," according to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

"My intention is to continue with my academic biomedical research in the United States," Lizcano told NPR from his office in Bogotá. "(I) have been exploring opportunities also where I could combine all my experience in endocrinology with molecular biology, translational research."

Because USCIS deemed him qualified for an EB-1A, all that was left for him was to apply for the visa itself and get it stamped in his passport.

But he is still in Colombia, awaiting for the State Department's final approval.

"This is not fair," Lizcano said.

The waiting game is taking an emotional toll on many of the immigrants — and their loved ones — whose visas are now up in the air.

Hoffman, the U.S. veteran awaiting his wife's visa to be approved, is worried about his own mental health. He told NPR his doctors have increased his psychiatric medicines.

"I was OK before all this started happening," he said.

He works as an Uber driver, and with Trump's war in Iran, gas prices have skyrocketed, cutting into his income.

He's struggling to pay both his mortgage in the U.S., and rent in Argentina for his family.

"We're living on a dream and a prayer right now," Hoffman said.

☀️ Good morning from The Legal File! Here is the rundown of today's top legal news:

🎓 Lawyers gird for congressional probes if Democrats take control

A Democratic takeover of at least one chamber of Congress following next month's midterm elections could be a boon to law firms angling for roles in a potential surge of congressional investigations.

Several lawyers and lobbyists in Washington said they're communicating with current and potential clients in anticipation of a spate of new probes on Capitol Hill if Democrats tip the balance. Reuters has reported that Democrats are widely expected to win control of the House, though the Senate is too close to call.

Anyone ignoring inquiries from Democratic lawmakers risks the chance they could have subpoena power in the next Congress, said Brian Pomper, who co-leads Akin Gump's lobbying and public policy practice.

"They should really be preparing now," Pomper said.

After two years in the minority during Republican President Donald Trump's first term, newly-empowered Democrats could scrutinize a range of targets, from administration figures to corporate donors and participants in business deals brokered by the Trump family. Unlike the White House, private companies cannot claim that their activities are protected by executive privilege.

US law firm Brownstein Hyatt launched a website to track investigative activity, said Will Moschella, who co-chairs the firm's government relations department, and posted hundreds of letters Democratic lawmakers in the US House and Senate have sent since last year that could augur future probes.

Lawyers at several firms said they expanded their congressional investigations practices over the past year, while others are still hiring

Read more.

🏛️ US Supreme Court rulings reshape midterm election battlefield

The November 3 midterm elections are quickly approaching after an electoral cycle shaped to an unusual degree by decisions of the US Supreme Court, a development that prompted Justice Elena Kagan to voice alarm this week. Here’s what to know:

In April, the court's 6-3 conservative majority gutted a key Voting Rights Act provision. That made it harder to challenge maps as racially discriminatory, and several Southern states quickly dismantled districts with large Black populations. The court has also allowed starkly partisan maps, including Texas's. Justice Kagan warned that the court's 2019 ban on federal gerrymandering challenges is making the country "even more" polarized.

"It is making what I think is unfortunately a too-polarized country even more so," Kagan told an audience at Catholic University's law school in Washington, expressing concern over implications for American democracy.

In June, the court struck down caps on party spending coordinated with candidates. Republican committees have since far outspent the old limits. This month, the court also allowed discounted TV and radio ad rates for parties.

Last month, the court rebuffed a Trump-backed effort to restrict mail voting, which Democrats use more often. Only US Supreme Court Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito publicly dissented. The court also declined to let the USPS enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots. That followed a June decision endorsing grace periods for mail ballots over Republican objections.

The court barred Missouri from using its redrawn pro-GOP map. It also allowed California's pro-Democratic map after letting Texas's pro-GOP map stand.

Read more.

🚨 Detained migrants have no constitutional right to bond hearings, US court rules

A US appeals court ruled on October 23 that President Trump's administration is not required under the US Constitution to give detained immigrants a chance to seek release on bond.

In a 10-7 ruling, powered by its conservative majority, the New Orleans-based 5th Circuit decided that the Constitution's Fifth Amendment due process protections do not require that immigration detainees receive bond hearings.

"To the extent petitioners seek to vindicate a liberty interest to be free from physical restraint in the most abstract sense, they can do so at any moment by agreeing to leave the country," US Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote in the decision.

The ruling, if left to stand, would eliminate a key avenue for detained migrants in the three states under the 5th Circuit's jurisdiction — Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi — to argue for release, especially if the US Supreme Court decides the administration's detention practice complies with immigration law.

The Supreme Court this month agreed to consider the issue, which has divided lower courts. Numerous lawsuits by migrants arguing they were being unlawfully detained have flooded the courts as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, implemented Trump's mass deportation agenda.

The Supreme Court is considering only whether such hearings are required by statute, not by the Constitution, the issue the 5th Circuit addressed with the October 23 decision.

While the 5th Circuit in February had adopted the administration's reading of immigration law as requiring mandatory detention, a 2-1 panel of the court in July held that ICE could not constitutionally detain people for more than 90 days without providing hearings to argue for release on bond.

The decision, which came in lawsuits by two Mexican citizens and one Honduran, carried particular importance because Texas and Louisiana, within the 5th Circuit's jurisdiction, house the nation's largest numbers of immigration detainees.

But the full 5th Circuit agreed to rehear the case, and on October 23 reversed course, concluding that detained immigrants are not constitutionally entitled to proceedings in immigration court beyond what Congress provided by statute.

Read more.

🗳️ US appeals court appears skeptical of Trump DOJ's lawsuit over California voter rolls

A federal appeals court appeared skeptical on October 25 of a lawsuit filed by President Trump's administration that seeks to force California officials to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots the administration says were sent to noncitizens ahead of midterm elections.

During a rare weekend oral argument, two judges on a three-judge panel of the 9th Circuit sharply questioned a Justice Department lawyer about the lawsuit, a high-profile effort by the Trump administration to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the November 3 midterms.

The Department of Justice's lawsuit signals the willingness of Trump's administration to contest midterm results that will decide control of the US Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.

At the end of the two-hour oral argument, Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said the three-judge panel would try to rule as quickly as possible.

Trump's Justice Department has warned election officials across California that they could be targets of federal scrutiny if they refuse to help identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls. It has distributed to California officials a list of 20,000 people it says are likely aliens registered to vote in the state, a Democratic stronghold.

California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and, in a court filing, stated that the Justice Department's assertions relied on suspect data.

All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation this year found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.

Read more.

text:
A federal appeals court has ruled in favor of the Trump administration’s policy allowing the indefinite detention of thousands of immigrants without the right to be released on bond. The decision by the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals would mean even immigrants who’ve lived in the United States for decades and have no criminal record could be detained for months — even years — while their cases are reviewed. Other U.S. courts have overwhelmingly opposed Trump’s indefinite detention policy, saying it violates immigrants’ constitutional and due process rights. The ruling centers on Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, with advocates warning the impacts will be felt nationwide. The American Immigration Council said in a statement, “When courts degrade the meaning of liberty for some, we all suffer the consequences.” The Supreme Court is set to hear a case challenging the policy during this term.

This comes as deaths in ICE custody continue to skyrocket under Trump’s second term. Over the weekend, it was confirmed a 48-year-old immigrant from El Salvador has died while jailed at the D. Ray James ICE Processing Center in Folkston, Georgia. Luis Sandoval was reportedly found on Friday morning with a “ligature around his neck.” He was pronounced dead about an hour later. He’s at least the 60th immigrant to have died in ICE custody since Trump returned to office. Sandoval’s death came amid an ongoing hunger strike inside the Folkston facility denouncing inhumane conditions. Immigrants there have been reportedly threatened with force-feeding and other retaliatory actions. The ICE facility is run by the for-profit prison company GEO Group.

In more related news, a 79-year-old pastor from Uganda has been released from a for-profit ICE jail in Colorado after 13 months in custody. The Rev. Edward Nalwamba reportedly lost 35 pounds and the strength to walk after his confinement at the Aurora ICE Processing Center, which is operated by the GEO Group. He also suffered from pneumonia for three weeks and did not receive any medical treatment. On the day of his release, Nalwamba had to be carried out by three other detainees, as ICE provided no wheelchair.

During his first term, President Trump said he wanted to attract the brightest immigrants to come to the U.S.

authors: via Scripps News Group, www.scrippsnews.com, via-scripps-news
description:
Circuit Court of Appeals appeared skeptical of a lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump's administration in mid-October.
The lawsuit accuses California officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review 20,000 names the administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls.
The administration asked a federal judge to require the state to withhold counting those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, questioned whether the appellate court even has jurisdiction to hear the case even before a ruling by the lower court.
The federal government is simply asking California to enforce their own law, which also bans noncitizens from voting, Donnelly said.
text:
A panel of federal appellate judges on Sunday questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department's demand that California election officials set aside thousands of mail ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.

During rare weekend arguments, two of the three judges on the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals appeared skeptical of a lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump's administration in mid-October. The lawsuit accuses California officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review 20,000 names the administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls.

The administration asked a federal judge to require the state to withhold counting those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The district judge scheduled a hearing for Oct. 27, days after the case was assigned, but the federal government appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, seeking an expedited decision.

Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly told the panel that California is causing irreparable harm “by allowing noncitizens to vote in violation of their own state laws. The damage is irreversible and irrevocable.”

RELATED STORY | DOJ threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rolls

The Trump administration has made efforts to identify noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare.

Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, questioned whether the appellate court even has jurisdiction to hear the case even before a ruling by the lower court.

Donnelly argued that the schedule set by the lower court judge was too slow and effectively a denial of the government's request, as state elections officials process thousands of mail ballots every day.

Judge Gabriel Sanchez, appointed by former President Joe Biden, questioned whether the federal government was violating the Tenth Amendment, essentially commandeering the state to enforce a federal law that makes it a misdemeanor for a noncitizen to vote.

The federal government is simply asking California to enforce their own law, which also bans noncitizens from voting, Donnelly said. He argued the state's refusal to comply with the federal request to set aside the ballots for review was “frustrating the purpose” of the federal law against noncitizen voting.

The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections, Bennett said. The executive branch may be “unhappy with what they’re doing, and doesn’t like the manner,” Bennett said, but under the Election Clause the state has the right to determine those issues — including how it sorts out any noncitizen voters.

Attorney Seth Waxman, representing Los Angeles County Clerk Dean Logan, said the federal government's list was unreliable and that segregating the ballots for a review process would effectively disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.

Even if election staffers spent just three minutes checking each of the expected 2.75 million mail ballots against the government's list, the process would take 140,000 man-hours, Waxman said — or about 16 years of working time.

Waxman cited a review of 200 records from the Trump administration's list conducted by Los Angeles County staffers. Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, individuals with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States, which the filing notes “is strong evidence of citizenship.”

If the administration disagrees with how California runs its elections, it can ask Congress to change that process, said attorney Sam Siegel, representing California Secretary of State Shirley Weber.

The federal government has provided no credible evidence to support its suspicions, said Siegal.

“It has no basis in law or in fact,” he told the panel. “We just dispute the premise that noncitizens are voting."

But Judge Patrick Bumatay, who was appointed by Trump, said everyone has an interest in ensuring that only eligible citizens vote. He suggested that granting the administration's request for an emergency order could provide clarity.

“Without an injunction, you will never know” if that is happening, Bumatay told Seigel.

Bennett said the panel would try to issue a ruling as quickly as possible.

title: Todd Blanche Crashes Out Over Pressure Against Trump's Alaska Lawsuit
description:
Donald Trump has already admitted that he was the one who ordered the lawsuit, but Blanche refused to provide any details.
(The Supreme Court only ruled on Lula’s petition, though the requests were the same.)

Polls show that he and Lahn are currently trailing Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand by about 11 points—in a state Trump won by 13 points two years ago.

text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche crashed and burned over the weekend while trying to defend the Justice Department’s lawsuit to block Alaska from certifying its Senate election results in the event that Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses due to voter “confusion.”

The lawsuit alleges that the Senate election should be nullified if Sullivan loses because there’s another “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” on the ballot also running as a Republican, and the Trump administration thinks voters will be too confused. Alaska’s Supreme Court in June upheld lower court rulings that found the two Sullivans could run in the same election—but the Trump administration has waited until just days before the election to intervene.

Appearing on CBS News’s Face the Nation Sunday, Blanche threw a tantrum as host Margaret Brennan showed that Sullivan was clearly listed as the “(Registered Republican) Incumbent” on Alaska’s ballot.

“I mean you’re not telling the truth, you’re not being honest with the voters!” Blanche whined.

Donald Trump has already admitted that he was the one who ordered the lawsuit, but Blanche refused to provide any details. “Who did he tell to do it?” Brennan pressed.

“So, I don’t—I will never, ever, ever talk about communications that I have with the president of the United States. I never have and I never will,” Blanche said.

Brennan read from the lawsuit that the DOJ had asked that Alaska’s state elections board and ballot counting review board “not certify an election result that may be impacted by voter confusion.”

“The confusion is defined as ‘Senator Sullivan not winning,’ and ‘had all votes cast for Daniel J Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan then he would’ve won,’” she said, leaving a lengthy pause for Blanche to respond.

“Well, that’s not what it says,” Blanche said.

“I’m quoting from it,” she said. “You are telling them not to certify it. What right does the federal government have telling a state not to certify or how to certify?”

“You know if you talk the whole time, you’re not going to get answers out of me!” he fumed.

Blanche didn’t fare much better during an appearance on CNN’s State of the Union Saturday. Host Dana Bash quoted Trump’s claim that “the Democrats are trying to steal this important Republican seat.”

“He’s admitting it’s political. Do you see your job as helping Republicans keep this seat?” Bash asked.

“He’s not admitting it’s political!” Blanche cried. “Wait, you’re saying that a president saying that there’s something improper happening at the ballots is necessarily political? He’s the executive, he’s supposed to make sure that everything in this country is running right!”

Blanche raged that Democrats were “cheating” and Bash had “cherry-picked” that quote.

He finally exploded after Bash suggested that there were concerns that Trump was laying the groundwork to overturn the election, like “what we saw after January 6.”

“I mean oh, stop it!” Blanche shrieked. “Oh you gotta stop it with that. You’re not being a real person! Come on, man! That is crazy!”

Surely, when your arguments become that the other side is simply crazy, that’s how you know you’ve got a winning lawsuit. Clearly, Blanche has veered into unknown territory: It is extremely abnormal for the Justice Department to be involved in election certification. But that won’t stop the Trump administration’s most blatant effort so far to swing ballots in Republicans’ favor.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s decisive victory in Brazil’s presidential election Sunday was already being disputed by his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, as results were coming in.

Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, said that the results of the runoff election should be annulled because of a Brazilian Supreme Court ruling extending voting by two hours. However, both Lula and Bolsonaro’s parties had called for that extension, making his point moot. (The Supreme Court only ruled on Lula’s petition, though the requests were the same.)

Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party supported the extension because voters in urban São Paulo and Bahia, where it has a strong support base, had trouble getting to the polls due to trouble with bus services. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party, meanwhile, cited heavy rains in the southern parts of Brazil, where its supporters are more numerous.

Bolsonaro’s complaint is not likely to sway the Supreme Court. The high court’s president, Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed by the elder Bolsonaro, confirmed the election result, noting that extending times did not affect the electoral process or the vote count. Lula won 51.79 percent to Bolsonaro’s 48.21 percent, a difference of 4.4 million votes.

U.S. President Donald Trump had pushed for Bolsonaro’s party to win, having supported Jair Bolsonaro during his tenure and disputed his prison sentence over attempting to overturn Brazil’s elections in an attempted coup d’état in 2022. Trump has not yet commented on the result, but his son Donald Trump Jr. did on X Sunday night.

Complaining about Brazil’s Supreme Court, Trump Jr. posted that “if a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause.” Perhaps he’s just mad that Brazilians have done what Americans failed to do: lock up a corrupt far-right leader and keep him from returning to power.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and his wife, state Senator Angela Paxton, invested $600,000 into a business run by a man convicted of fraud.

The Texas Tribune reports that the Paxtons gave the cash to a construction materials business run by Scott Sherman, a home builder who pleaded guilty to mortgage fraud in 2014, through what was presented to the public as a blind trust. In reality, the Paxtons’ business activities were not shielded, as should be the case in a blind trust.

According to the Tribune, which cited previously unreleased records from Ken Paxton’s 2023 impeachment investigation, Sherman’s companies sent the Paxtons thousands of dollars while they were facing mounting tax debts. Ken Paxton was investigated by the Texas state legislature and was eventually acquitted. Now he’s Texas’s Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate in a tight race with Democratic challenger James Talarico.

Paxton’s business dealings fly in the face of his public statements. He said in a news release last year that “in Texas, we fight fraud head-on and will not rest until every last corrupt actor is brought to justice.” Ethics experts told the Tribune that his activities undermine his position as Texas’s top law enforcement official.

Richard Painter, a former chief ethics lawyer to President George W. Bush, said he thought Paxton would be smarter than this. Referring to people like Sherman, Painter said, “They’ll pay out their friends while they’re not paying their taxes, run up debt. But the question is, why is the attorney general of Texas dealing with those kinds of people?”

Painter added that he thought “the attorney general of Texas would have the good sense not to be dealing with a convicted felon.”

Angela Paxton filed for divorce from Ken last year on “biblical grounds,” referring to her husband’s infidelity. Ken Paxton has continued to deal with shady characters since his investment in Sherman, spending New Year’s Eve 2024 partying with his mistress and two campaign donors who both fled the U.S. from health care fraud charges.

A 45-year-old Republican candidate in Iowa is being sued by his parents for $275,000 in unpaid rent.

The Des Moines Register reported that the parents of lieutenant governor nominee Derek Wulf allege that he stopped paying rent two years ago on the farmland he rented out from them. A court petition filed Tuesday demands repayment and also accuses him of lying about his assets in financial documents to a lender.

While Wulf has yet to comment, his Trump–endorsed running mate, gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn, denied that Wulf owes his parents any money at all—and insinuated that the conflict was spurred by the poor health of Wulf’s father. Wulf’s parents rejected that, calling the claim “categorically false.”

Duane and Jackie Wulf, 83 and 82 years old respectively, join a long list of creditors demanding repayment from the Republican candidate. Eight people and companies have sued Wulf and his company, Shallow Creek Land & Livestock, since 2023 for payments owed to them. All but one of the lawsuits have been settled. That one is from the WCF Financial Bank, which claims that Wulf is over a year behind on credit payments.

Wulf is a 45-year-old man with a wife and two children running for lieutenant governor. These financial issues are not only embarrassing but raise alarming questions about how he might abuse a position in office. Hopefully, Iowa will never have to find out. Polls show that he and Lahn are currently trailing Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand by about 11 points—in a state Trump won by 13 points two years ago.

A federal appeals court on Friday stripped due process rights from hundreds of immigrants held by Immigration and Custom Enforcement.

In a 10–7 en banc decision, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that ICE detainees with pending immigration hearings are not entitled to receive a bond hearing, where a judge could assess their dangerousness and flight risk, regardless of how long they have been in detention.

The decision blocks efforts by federal judges who have been ordering the release of hundreds of immigrants—many of whom have no criminal record and have deep ties to the United States—held without bond by ICE’s mass deportation policy.

After the Fifth Circuit upheld ICE’s policy in February, other federal judges discovered that they were able to argue that detention violated immigrants’ constitutional due process rights. In the past year, judges have ruled against detentions without bond more than 21,150 times. The Fifth Circuit has now choked off that legal argument.

The case will likely head to the Supreme Court, which is set to decide on a number of immigration reform cases in the coming term.

text:
Rodney Taylor was just two years old when he arrived in the US from Liberia on a medical visa. By the age of 10, both his legs had been amputated. Georgia became his home, where he raised a family and worked as a barber. But his immigration status remained unresolved.

In early 2025, Rodney was arrested by officers from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The arrest was based on a burglary conviction from his youth. The state of Georgia had already pardoned him for that offence in 2010.

Rodney spent 15 months behind bars at the Stewart Detention Center in southern Georgia. Today, he's back with his family. But he faces deportation. And his future in the country he has called home for almost his entire life hangs in the balance.

Meanwhile, some 200 kilometers (125 miles) north, the Trump administration was planning a massive new ICE detention center to hold up to 10,000 people. But in Social Circle, a small town in the heart of Trump country, the plans sparked an unexpected backlash. A progressive activist and a Trump supporter found themselves on the same side of a political battle, united by one goal: to stop the detention center from being built.

text:
What is the administration doing?

In a first in U.S. history, the government has separated tens of thousands of children from parents who were arrested on immigration violations, often deporting them without their kids. Many such parents entered the U.S. legally as asylum seekers and have been working and raising families while pursuing citizenship. This spring, the Brookings Institution counted more than 146,000 children who are U.S. citizens and have had a parent deported; more than 22,000 have had both parents deported. Sometimes deportees are given the option to take their children with them—but not always. When Physicians for Human Rights interviewed women deported to Honduras this year, they found that many had not been asked if they had children, while others simply had their kids taken. One was parted from her 2-month-old breastfeeding baby. Migrant advocates say the crisis mirrors 2018, when the first Trump administration’s policy of separating families at the southern border sparked an uproar. “It’s leading to all the same forms of trauma,” said Kelly Kribs, an attorney for immigrant children. “But the speed and the scale of the separations now is at a level we’ve never seen before.”

What happens to children left in the U.S.?

Many go to relatives or friends, but because deportees have little or no time to arrange for care, some end up in foster care. When Marlyn, a Venezuelan with a pending asylum application, landed in ICE detention after a traffic stop in Alabama, her two young children, including a 2-year-old just weaned, were left with her co- worker. When she chose to accept deportation rather than endure prolonged detention in a case likely to fail, she said she begged to have her children sent with her. “I told them, ‘I have no one to take care of them.’ But they never did anything.” Nearly a year later, Marlyn has been unable to arrange extradition for her toddler, who doesn’t recognize her in video calls. Some parents choose to leave their kids behind because they are returning to countries roiled by violence. One Haitian woman, identified by The Guardian only as L.T., made the wrenching decision to leave her sick baby with a grandmother, knowing that there wouldn’t be medical care in gang-plagued Haiti. Now she’s racked by fear that her daughter could wind up with strangers. “I’m terrified of losing my baby,” she said.

What does the law say?

The law allows for parents to be deported without their children, but until recently there were protections. ICE policy held that federal agents should avoid separating families and either deport them together or confirm a caregiver is in place. The Trump administration revised the policy to say agents should do that “when operationally feasible,” which advocates say gives ICE leeway to ignore it. The administration insists it doesn’t intentionally separate families, and that this only occurs when parents make the choice to self- deport. But critics say otherwise. ICE is intent on meeting its deportation quotas, said Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), even “if that means tearing families apart and traumatizing children.” Migrant advocates also cite a growing trend of children being taken from parents and put into federal custody.

Why is this happening?

Children of detainees are being reclassified as unaccompanied minors and sent to the Office of Refugee Resettlement. When Luis, a construction worker from Venezuela, was detained with his 11-year-old son, Andrés, after being arrested in El Paso, he said agents removed Andrés and transferred him to ORR instead of sending him to his grandfather. Case workers said Andrés couldn’t sleep in foster care and screamed for his parents at night. It’s not clear how common such reclassifications are, but Mother Jones spoke to a dozen lawyers who confirmed the trend. “They’re kidnapping people’s kids and keeping them in government custody,” said Jen Smyers, who was a Biden-era ORR official. There’s a process for applying to get them out, but the administration has made it arduous—to protect children from predators, it says—and ICE has arrested undocumented people who apply.

Are minors ever deported alone?

Frequently. An analysis by Pro Publica found that judges have issued over 10,000 removal and voluntary departure orders for unaccompanied minors every month, a rate four times higher than in Trump’s first term. Most of these children came from Central American countries riven by violence and economic upheaval, have no criminal record, and are pursuing legal residence. Minors with Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, granted to those who’ve suffered parental abuse or neglect, used to be protected from deportation, but the Trump administration ended that policy. It also ended $200 million in annual funding for the Acacia Center for Justice, a nonprofit that provides legal services to migrant children.

Has there been pushback?

Not much. Migrant advocates say there’s been a notable shift from 2018, when blowback over family separations led to legal challenges, bipartisan opposition, and an eventual climbdown. This time, there’s no explicit policy to challenge in court, and the separations are happening outside public view—no media images of children in cages. Advocates also cite less resistance within the administration, as staffers who might have objected have left or been laid off. The fallout in human trauma will be vast, experts say, especially for the youngest children. “They are left with a sense of abandonment that’s kind of imprinted,” said Michele Heisler, a doctor with Physicians for Human Rights. Her organization also documented signs of trauma among separated mothers, including panic attacks and uncontrollable crying. The “gratuitous level of cruelty,” she said, “is hard for all of us to understand.

text:
Dozens of activists joined the Sisters of St. Joseph of Orange and two other social justice groups Oct. 7 for an interfaith prayer vigil outside an ICE detention center where four detainees have died since January 2025 and organizers say inhumane conditions continue.

The vigil outside the Adelanto ICE Processing Center, in the California desert about two hours northeast of Los Angeles, was a collaborative effort between the sisters, Clergy and Laity United for Economic Justice, and the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights.

In July, in response to a lawsuit by detainees alleging inhumane conditions, including failure to provide clean drinking water, proper nutrition and adequate medical care, a federal judge ordered changes at the center. In addition to ordering access to clean drinking water, adequate food, free soap and hygiene products, the order mandated the facility be cleaned daily, and that detainees are provided blankets and temperature-appropriate clothing, Cal Matters reported.

The order came in a preliminary injunction after detainees sued over conditions and the judge found they are "likely to prevail" in their case that their Fifth Amendment rights against inhumane conditions are being violated, the nonprofit news outlet said.

"We believe that every human life is sacred, regardless of immigration status. Families deserve to remain together, and no person in government custody should suffer or die because of neglect, inadequate care, or institutional irresponsibility," the sisters said in a press release announcing the vigil.

"We stand in solidarity with families harmed by cruel policies that have led to detention, deportation, and family separation. We affirm their God-given dignity and call for their freedom from detention as they process their immigration case."

Novenas ahead of US midterms

The mid-term elections in the United States are approaching fast, and several groups are preparing for the event with prayer.

Network Catholic social justice lobby is joining Catholics in Communion for a virtual election novena, which will be held every evening starting Nov. 1. The novena begins at 7:30 p.m. Eastern time and will not be recorded, but will have live Spanish interpretation.

Those who register will receive a Zoom link that is good for all nine sessions; participants can attend as many sessions as they are able. In addition to the prayer, which will utilize the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' "Novena for Faithful Citizenship," there will be election-related updates, opportunities to help ensure all votes are counted, and check-ins with local communities holding vigil across the country.

That novena comes on the heels of another one, hosted by the Leadership Conference of Women Religious, that begins Oct. 26 and continues through Election Day, Nov. 3.

Each day, LCWR will post a 10-minute video prayer, which will include excerpts from the LCWR Declaration of Commitment, petitions, and prayers for the safety of candidates, voters, and election officials.

The prayer will be posted daily on the LCWR website and be available for use at any time.

text:
Why It Matters

The Trump administration's policy of removing noncitizens to third countries remains in effect after the Supreme Court granted review, stayed a lower-court ruling that had vacated the policy, and scheduled oral argument for Dec. 9. ​

According to a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report, advocacy groups Refugees International and Human Rights First estimate that more than 25,000 individuals have been removed to third countries as of September 2026, under agreements with more than 30 countries, while the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has not made public any data on the total number of agreements or transfers.

The CRS report notes that current use of this authority "substantially outpaces past practices."

The Big Picture

President Trump's January 2025 executive order "Securing Our Borders" directed the Secretary of State to coordinate with the Attorney General and DHS Secretary to pursue additional international cooperation, including safe-third-country agreements.

In February 2025, DHS issued internal guidance identifying categories of noncitizens with final removal orders to consider for third-country removal, including those who qualified for withholding of removal or Convention Against Torture (CAT) protection and those previously released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.

The July 2025 ICE memorandum specifies that when the State Department finds diplomatic assurances credible, a noncitizen may be removed without further procedures; when assurances are absent or not credible, ICE must issue a Notice of Removal and generally wait 24 hours before proceeding. A noncitizen must affirmatively express fear to trigger a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services screening for withholding of removal and CAT protection.

Advertisement

A federal district court issued a preliminary injunction in March 2025 requiring written notice and a meaningful opportunity to raise CAT claims, but the Supreme Court stayed that injunction in June 2025, enabling DHS to resume removals. In February, the district court dissolved the injunction and vacated DHS's policy, and the First Circuit stayed that decision pending appeal before largely affirming the judgment.

The Trump administration has justified third-country removals as a national security and enforcement tool, particularly for noncitizens with criminal records who cannot be removed to their home countries. Critics say noncitizens receive inadequate notice and have faced human rights abuses in destination countries.

The Bottom Line

The Supreme Court's grant of review and stay in Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., No. 26-426, allows third-country removals to continue while the justices consider the underlying legal questions. The respondents' brief is due Nov. 16 and the reply Dec. 1, ahead of the Dec. 9 oral argument.

Congress may wish to consider options ranging from codifying the July 2025 ICE memorandum to requiring additional procedural protections or mandating congressional reporting on third-country agreements.

text:
NEW BEDFORD — More than 100 people gathered in Riverside Park Sunday afternoon to call for the release of those detained during a recent immigration enforcement surge on the South Coast.

The demonstrators came from across Massachusetts at the behest of LUCE, a statewide network of advocates that monitors U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity throughout the commonwealth.

“We pray for the men, women, and children detained by ICE,” said Brother Brave Fung, an Episcopal monk with the Community of Francis and Clare. “We pray for the broken families torn apart suddenly by the disappearance of their loved ones.”

The protest was a reaction to ICE’s mass arrests on the South Coast last month, concentrating on New Bedford on Sept. 21 and 22.

Demands put forward by LUCE included that ICE “release everyone” detained during the surge; that Gov. Maura Healey “provide substantial support to affected families and communities”; that elected officials including the governor and Mayor Jon Mitchell advocate on immigrants’ behalf; and that the U.S. Congress institute comprehensive immigration reform.

Healey said about 40 people were detained during the September ICE arrests in New Bedford. On Oct. 21, ICE issued a news release that said its agents had detained 82 people in a three-day operation in southeastern Massachusetts. The agency identified only seven of those detained, all of whom allegedly had criminal charges. Only one of those, João Ferreira, had been previously identified by The Light.

A statewide analysis of state and federal court documents by The Light shortly after the surge ended found that only four of 23 men, including Ferreira, had criminal charges on their records in Massachusetts.

The surge left Acushnet Avenue nearly deserted for a week, as immigrants and their families stayed home out of fear, skipping work and leaving their homes only when necessary.

“I’ve never seen anything like it,” Petronila Morales, the owner of Restaurante y Tortillería Guatemalteco, told The Light a day after it recorded the arrests of two men by federal agents outside. “This restaurant always has at least two or three people here at tables eating.

“Everyone is so scared,” she added. “No one is coming out.”

In a September interview with The Light, Mayor Mitchell said there was little the City could do.

“The unfortunate part is, as frustrating as it has been, there’s not a lot that the local government or state government, frankly, can be doing,” he said. “But we want people to know that if they need to understand their legal rights, that we’re going to help them understand them.”

Protest

During Sunday’s event, demonstrators cheered as Ricardo Rosa, a Cabo Verdean community advocate, criticized municipal leaders for a lack of reaction to the raids.

“In extraordinary times, we don’t need ordinary municipal leaders,” Rosa said. “Refuse to cooperate with ICE and actively obstruct [ICE’s] lawlessness.”

State Rep. Christopher Hendricks, of the Bristol 11th District, attended the event to show his support to the demonstrators.

“It’s incumbent on us and incumbent on us as a community that we all stick together like this,” he said, “so when we see those injustices, we not only know what to do, but we can be there for one another.”

New Bedford Public Schools Supt. Andrew O’Leary also attended. O’Leary has repeatedly voiced support for immigrant communities since the mass deportation agenda of President Donald Trump’s second term hit New Bedford. On Oct. 5, in reaction to the surge, the School Committee voted almost unanimously to enact guidelines in line with the PROTECT Act for interactions with ICE at schools.

Also present was At-Large City Councilor James Roy. The progressive said at an Oct. 21 meeting of the New Bedford Human Rights Commission that he would bring forward to the full City Council the commission’s idea to put forward an ordinance prohibiting the use of city property for civil immigration enforcement.

The September raids brought the total count to well over 100 detained in the New Bedford area since early 2025.

Contact Kevin G. Andrade at kandrade@newbedfordlight.org

title: Connecting the Dots: From Research to Legal Practice and Policy - Electronic Immigration Network

text:
Climate change and natural disasters are increasingly relevant to asylum and human rights cases. However, recognising their legal significance is not always straightforward. One of the main challenges is understanding how academic research and international jurisprudence can be translated into practical legal arguments that national courts and tribunals can consider.

The new UK Practice Toolkit: Climate, Disasters & Protection Claims, is an important step towards addressing this challenge [1]. It brings together academic research, legal experience and policy expertise to help UK practitioners identify and develop claims involving climate change and natural disasters within existing legal frameworks.

Why academia and legal practice need each other

I have always believed that academic research and legal practice should not operate separately. Both are essential, but each brings a different perspective.

Academic research gives us the space to explore new ideas, question established approaches and identify gaps in the law. It allows us to consider how existing legal principles might respond to emerging challenges, including climate-related displacement.

Legal practice, on the other hand, brings these ideas into contact with the realities of individual cases. Practitioners understand the difficulties of gathering evidence, preparing legal arguments and meeting the legal tests applied by judges. An argument may be persuasive in academic writing, but its practical value depends on whether it can be supported by evidence and applied within the relevant legal framework.

This is why bringing the two together is so valuable. Academic research can encourage lawyers to look at familiar legal questions differently, while practical experience can help researchers understand which arguments need further development and which difficulties arise in real proceedings. The relationship should work in both directions. Research informs practice, but practice also raises new questions for research.

A connected chain: research, practice and policy

I see this process as a connected chain with three important links: academic research, legal practice and policy. The first link is research. It helps us understand emerging challenges, explore new ideas and consider how the law might respond to situations that existing legal frameworks may not have fully anticipated. The second link is legal practice. Lawyers draw on this research to identify relevant issues, gather evidence and develop arguments that can be presented before courts and tribunals. Through this process, academic ideas are tested against the realities of individual cases and the requirements of existing law. As more cases are brought, judicial decisions may gradually help clarify how legal principles apply to climate-related harm. The third link is policy. Over time, developments in case law, supported by academic research and practical experience, may contribute to wider discussions about whether existing legal frameworks and policies adequately address the challenges arising from climate-related displacement. These discussions may, in turn, encourage the further development of existing legal protections and greater recognition of the particular difficulties faced by people seeking protection in the context of climate change and disasters.

However, this is not simply a one-way process. Court decisions can raise new questions for academic research. Challenges encountered by practitioners can reveal gaps in legal guidance or areas where further research is needed. Policy developments can also create new questions for both researchers and lawyers. Each part of the chain informs and strengthens the others. Research can inform legal practice, legal practice can contribute to the development of case law, and judicial developments may eventually influence policy. At the same time, the experience gained through litigation and the decisions reached by courts can encourage further research, fresh legal thinking and new approaches.

For me, this is what connecting the dots really means: recognising that meaningful legal development does not happen in isolation, but through continued dialogue between those who research the law, those who practise it and those who shape policy

The Toolkit as a connecting point

What makes this Toolkit particularly valuable is that it brings these different perspectives together in one practical resource. It draws on international research and guidance while addressing the specific requirements of UK immigration and human rights law. It offers practical assistance with identifying climate-related issues during client interviews, gathering country evidence, working with experts and developing legal arguments. Its case studies also demonstrate how climate-related factors may arise in real proceedings, even where a claim is not initially understood as a climate case.

In this sense, the Toolkit is more than a collection of legal information. It provides a meeting point between academic knowledge and the everyday work of legal practitioners. It also creates opportunities for further learning. As practitioners begin to use the Toolkit, their experiences may help identify new questions, improve legal arguments and contribute to future editions of the resource.

A Starting Point, Not the End

A single decision does not necessarily change the law or lead to a change in policy. Much will depend on the facts of future cases, the available evidence and how courts interpret existing legal principles. Nevertheless, I believe the Toolkit can help open a new chapter in UK legal practice. By making research and international guidance more accessible to practitioners, it may encourage the identification of climate-related issues that have previously been overlooked and support the development of carefully evidenced legal arguments.

My hope is that this will encourage more practitioners to explore the climate dimensions of their cases and, where appropriate, bring well-supported arguments before courts and tribunals. More decisions addressing these issues could, over time, contribute to changes in legal understanding and policy. For me, that is the real value of this project. Research, legal practice and policy are not separate worlds. They are connected parts of a continuing process, and the Toolkit can help strengthen the links between them.

The Power of Collaboration

I would also like to express my sincere thanks to all the wonderful colleagues who contributed to the development of this Toolkit, and particularly to Earth Refuge and Refugee Legal Support for bringing us together. It has been a real pleasure to work alongside people with different backgrounds, experiences and expertise, all sharing the same commitment to improving protection for people affected by climate change and natural disasters.

For me, this collaboration is itself an example of what the Toolkit represents: the value of bringing academic research, legal practice and policy perspectives together to achieve something meaningful.

text:
This post is the first in a series of reflections about Latino Heritage Month, the disenfranchisement of immigrants and people of color in the United States, and how systemic racism and oppression damage our democracy and worsen the impacts of climate change and other environmental harms.

Over the past month, we celebrated the culture and many contributions of Latinos in the United States, which have touched every facet of American society. However, one month is not enough to truly honor the presence, full history, diversity, and intersectional identity of Latinos (or any other group, for that matter) in the United States.

It’s perhaps more important than ever to continue to reflect and learn from similar moments throughout U.S. history in which U.S. government policies have disenfranchised, criminalized, and called for the detention of Indigenous people and immigrants of many different backgrounds and countries of origin. As early as 1790, U.S. policy denied citizenship to any non-white person, including Native Americans, slaves, and freed slaves. Throughout different times in its history, U.S. policy has also targeted and excluded immigrants from Southeast Asia, China and Japan, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, Africa, the Middle East, and Southern and Eastern Europe from human rights and citizenship.

In more recent history, on day one of his second administration, President Donald Trump issued an executive order that called for excluding from birthright citizenship children born to certain categories of noncitizens, even when those children are born in the United States. A second order issued in 2026 seeks to prevent non-citizens from giving birth in the U.S. at all. Thus far, the U.S. Supreme Court has defended birthright citizenship as written in the Fourteenth Amendment, but the administration continues to press ahead in seeking exclusions.

Especially during a time when the culture, history, and safety of all immigrant communities and individuals with marginalized identities in the United States are under attack by the Trump administration — most immediately through immigration enforcement and detention and also directly through an agenda of deregulation — we should not look away or ignore the fact that we are living through a very dark chapter in America’s story. Especially for Latinos and anyone with an immigrant background, a nightmare continues to unfold.

As a direct result of the expansion of violent, illegal immigration enforcement actions by the Trump administration, many lives have been lost, countless families have been destroyed, justice has been delayed, and millions of American dreams have been deferred. To date, at least 61 people have been killed in our country at the hands of the Trump administration and federal officers as a direct result of the expansion of immigration enforcement and detention that are being carried out in violation of legal pathways to immigration and revocation of humanitarian and asylum programs. Countless others have also lost their lives as a direct result of being separated from their families by either suicide, being separated from their primary caretaker, being denied medical care, and other unknown reasons.

As of August 2026, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has arrested at least 500,000 immigrants, including 8,952 children, elderly people, disabled people, and pregnant women. An overwhelming majority of those detained had no criminal record and were following immigration laws and court procedures. Over 500 U.S. citizens have also been detained, and more than 23,000 undocumented immigrants have been deported to a country other than their country of origin. At least 60,000 remain detained in inhumane conditions, including children, across 400 active for-profit detention centers that are funneling billions of taxpayer dollars to private prison contractors, facility owners, and operators who are carrying out horrific acts for maximum profit — without transparency and accountability.

What these numbers mean is that thousands of valued members of our communities have been violently removed and disappeared. Countless more remain locked down at home and unable to work, attend school, or take their children to parks, and they’re unable participate in public or civic life out of fear. Many continue to rely on their children, friends, and the kindness of neighbors, volunteers, and advocates for mutual aid and access to basic necessities, legal services, and a lifeline to society.

The sense of fear and psychological terror that the presence and aggression of federal officers in schools and public places like parks have instilled in communities all over this country —especially among children — has been chilling and should never be normalized. By attempting to condition access to federal funding and resources with agreements and cooperation of local and law enforcement, the Trump administration is also attempting to further erode and undermine public trust and participation at all levels of not only federal, but also state and local government, even causing many to question our sense of belonging in our own communities.

These violent and inhumane actions will leave a permanent mark and trauma among immigrant families and communities as a whole. These actions are also a central pillar in the Trump administration’s implementation of Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation’s blueprint for weaponizing the federal government to advance an authoritarian and white supremacist agenda, and further extract and consolidate public resources into the hands of a small few. The Trump administration continues to implement many actions and policy changes outlined in Project 2025 on immigration, education, healthcare, employment, and civil rights, and it’s doing so through Congress, administrative procedures, regulation and deregulation, the courts, and executive control of federal agencies. All of these actions are designed to harm and have immediate effect on all immigrants, especially Latinos.

In the next two parts of this series, we will further explore and expand on how racism, federal disinvestment, deregulation, and attacks on voting rights will have far-reaching, generational effects, not only on Latinos and immigrants, but also U.S. citizens, including naturalized citizens, mixed status families, Americans whose primary language is one other than English, and all citizens, families, workers, and communities in the U.S. and beyond.
