title: Congress is freeing Trump of the limited legal requirements left on him by the Supreme Court
description:
In July 2024, the Supreme Court provided presidents sweeping protection from criminal prosecution for actions taken in office under the “core constitutional powers” of the position.
The ruling only addressed criminal liability and did not curtail Congress’ constitutional authority to investigate presidential conduct, control federal spending, enact statutory restrictions and, in serious cases, pursue impeachment.
The Government Accountability Office – an independent agency that examines how taxpayer dollars are spent – said tactics like these violate federal law.
When one party controls Congress and the presidency, legislators may become more invested in advancing their party’s agenda than they are in defending their institution’s constitutional authority.
The result is a political system in which a president can act in ways that may violate federal law, undermine democratic norms and encroach on Congress’ constitutional authority.
text:
On the evening of Oct. 11, just weeks before the 2026 midterm elections, a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to stop airing taxpayer-funded television advertisements praising President Donald Trump.

Yet two of the ads continued running past the court’s deadline, including during broadcasts of “60 Minutes” and “ABC World News Tonight.”

The commercials in question aired in violation of a decades-old congressional prohibition against using federal money for unauthorized publicity and propaganda. Yet Republican congressional leaders did little to stop the president’s ad spending. That left outside organizations and a political candidate to challenge them in federal court.

The episode illustrates a larger development in Trump’s second presidency. Across disputes involving federal spending, government agencies and military operations, the administration has asserted authority that is either restricted by law or that the legislative branch has reserved for itself.

But responsibility for enforcing those limits is increasingly falling to organizations, institutions and individuals outside of the legislative branch.

As a scholar of the American presidency and deliberative democracy, I pay close attention to how the nation’s chief executive exercises power and communicates with the public.

When presidents are allowed to break rules and disregard democratic norms without consequence, I worry that citizens will grow cynical and lose faith in the idea of self-government.

As this happens, citizens may come to see the law as something that applies selectively, depending on who holds power, and lose confidence in the institutions responsible for holding their leaders accountable.

They may also begin to accept the absence of accountability as a normal feature of political life, weakening the public expectations on which democratic government depends.

Practical immunity

Congress is not the only branch of government demurring from holding the president accountable.

In July 2024, the Supreme Court provided presidents sweeping protection from criminal prosecution for actions taken in office under the “core constitutional powers” of the position.

In “Trump v. United States,” the court held that former presidents cannot be criminally prosecuted for actions taken under powers the Constitution gives exclusively to the president. Along with this “absolute immunity,” the justices also granted “at least presumptive immunity” for other official acts.

In their decision, the court’s conservative majority extended the meaning of official conduct to the “outer perimeter” of presidential responsibilities and prohibited courts from examining a president’s motives when determining whether an act was official.

The ruling only addressed criminal liability and did not curtail Congress’ constitutional authority to investigate presidential conduct, control federal spending, enact statutory restrictions and, in serious cases, pursue impeachment.

Yet the Republican majority in Congress has largely declined to exercise these powers against Trump, in areas ranging from declaring war to spending money.

Their acquiescence is helping create a new form of official protection, which I call “practical immunity.” In using this term, I am borrowing from the work of scholars who study abuse in the American penal system.

Those thinkers argue that legal obstacles, institutional hesitation and political incentives sometimes make it difficult to hold public officials accountable, even when the law suggests there has been illegal conduct.

That is what appears to be increasingly happening now with Congress, the courts and the president.

When Congress stops defending its laws

The television ads case illustrates the conundrum of practical immunity.

In opposing the temporary restraining order, the Trump administration’s attorneys did not contest the argument asserted by the plaintiffs – Common Cause and two unions – that the expenditures violated federal appropriations law. Instead, they said the plaintiffs lacked standing to sue. They also argued that the case was moot because the advertising campaign was ending.

Those arguments failed in court. Yet the administration’s defense demonstrated how elusive enforcing a law can be when Congress fails to assert its constitutionally granted role, even when the underlying legal restriction is clear. To win, a plaintiff must establish a concrete injury and persuade a judge to intervene. While this happens, the disputed conduct often continues.

In this case, the president went on spending public money in violation of the law. The GOP-led Congress, meanwhile, remained silent, even though its own role was being usurped.

Another boundary that Trump has repeatedly tested is the so-called “power of the purse”, which is among the legislative branch’s most important constitutional responsibilities. Presidents may spend federal money only for purposes Congress has authorized. The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 protects lawmakers’ decisions against presidential efforts to ignore congressional appropriations.

In September 2026, Trump’s administration canceled more than US$800 million in congressionally approved spending for immigrant services, climate change and civil rights for minority groups. The cancellation was done through a maneuver known as a pocket rescission. The administration timed its action to make it difficult for Congress to consider or stop the rescission. The Government Accountability Office – an independent agency that examines how taxpayer dollars are spent – said tactics like these violate federal law.

When this happened, a few members of Congress tried to intervene and stop the rescission, but the Republican majority blocked their efforts.

The collapse of institutional rivalry

The separation of powers divides authority among the legislative, executive and judicial branches of government to prevent too much power from becoming concentrated in any one place.

The architects of the Constitution anticipated that officials in different branches would compete to preserve their authority. In Federalist No. 51, James Madison argued that maintaining the balance established by the separation of powers depended on the ambitions of public officials coming into conflict. Members of Congress could be expected to resist presidential encroachments because those encroachments diminished their own power.

Fierce partisanship has complicated this arrangement.

Legal scholars Daryl Levinson and Richard Pildes have shown how political competition mostly now happens inside and between parties, rather than among branches of government. When one party controls Congress and the presidency, legislators may become more invested in advancing their party’s agenda than they are in defending their institution’s constitutional authority.

Trump’s influence over Republican voters intensifies these incentives. Lawmakers who oppose him risk public ridicule, primary challenges and diminished political support. Defending congressional authority may therefore carry greater immediate – and personal – political costs than allowing presidential power to expand.

The result is a political system in which a president can act in ways that may violate federal law, undermine democratic norms and encroach on Congress’ constitutional authority.

Madison’s constitutional design assumed that public officials would defend the powers entrusted to them. The danger to the American constitutional system emerging in Trump’s second term is that congressional leaders have begun to regard those powers as expendable, allowing the president to exercise authority under conditions of practical immunity. He faces little fear of meaningful institutional consequences.

title: American Foreign Policy Horror Story - by Daniel W. Drezner
description:
This focus has come at a cost, as I have not written a ton about American foreign policy during that time.
After all, I have been pretty clear in thinking the midterms would even have much an effect on American foreign policy.
Over the past week and a half, Mr. Trump has set aside years of U.S. foreign policy by openly embracing Mr. Putin and easing the economic pressure on the Kremlin.
On Oct. 9, Mr. Trump announced that the United States would buy Russian diesel, asking for no concessions from Mr. Putin in return.
Yeah, that is the perfect story to encapsulate just how much Trump and his team have beclowned American foreign policy.
text:
Discerning readers might have noticed that the hard-working staff here at Drezner’s World has focused on the 2026 midterms in recent weeks, offering exposure therapy for Democrats. This focus has come at a cost, as I have not written a ton about American foreign policy during that time. Subscribers might wonder about this allocation of effort. After all, I have been pretty clear in thinking the midterms would even have much an effect on American foreign policy.

So why am I not writing about the Trump administration’s recent approach towards the Russo-Ukrainian war or the ongoing operations in the Persian Gulf or even the continued trade war with Canada?

To be honest, this is mostly about preserving my sanity.

You see, to write posts on Drezner’s World, I need a theme or a narrative that can be explained in a relatively pithy manner. Chaos in the State Department? That’s an easy one to explain. Sanctioning the International Criminal Court? That requires either too much verbiage (“The history of international law begins with Grotius….") or too little (“What a dumbass move”).

Unfortunately, U.S. foreign policy right now is a complete shitshow. The only success this past month was the administration’s successful coercion of European allies to release diesel fuel reserves — which pissed off said allies while not affecting diesel prices all that much.

Meanwhile, the situation in Iran is, um, not great. In fat the situation remains basically unchanged since the summer, which means that Iran continues to exert a chokehold over commerce that crosses the Strat of Hormuz. The U.S. has continued it's Year of Retreat as a result of Operation Epic Fury, as reports of unconventional Iranian attacks have triggered rapid withdrawals from overseas military bases as well as various Gulf embassies and military posts. Multiple U.S. allies in the region are learning that they cannot count on this administration to have their back. Even Peter Thiel is privately admitting that it was a bad idea.

I am not even going to bother recounting the administration’s ill-fated push to rekindle bilateral relations with Russia despite its ongoing attacks on Ukraine. Instead I’ll just quote from the New York Times’ Valerie Hopkins on how recent U.S. actions obviously advance the interests of Russia’s Vladimir Putin:

Mr. Putin has never been so close to his goal of normalizing relations with Washington without having to make any compromises on Ukraine.

Over the past week and a half, Mr. Trump has set aside years of U.S. foreign policy by openly embracing Mr. Putin and easing the economic pressure on the Kremlin. At the same time, Mr. Trump has vilified President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, the putative American ally trying to defend his nation against a Russian invasion.

On Oct. 9, Mr. Trump announced that the United States would buy Russian diesel, asking for no concessions from Mr. Putin in return. The Trump administration went on to pressure Ukraine to stop striking oil refineries — Kyiv’s most powerful lever — and suspended Russia sanctions that Mr. Trump had just signed into law. Mr. Trump declared that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine.”….

Ever since Mr. Trump returned to office, Russia has sought to separate the conflict in Ukraine from potential business agreements and closer diplomatic ties with the United States. The Trump administration held back, even as it slashed aid to Ukraine, largely continuing a Biden administration policy of refraining from economic deals with Russia until Mr. Putin stopped the war.

The White House now says such deals will help Russia see the benefits of peace.

Look, I’m something of an expert on economic statecraft and I am pretty confident that constructive engagement with Vladimir Putin will work about as well as it did with the apartheid regime in South Africa in the early 1980s.

Then there is the trade war with Canada, which is going so poorly that the U.S. Ambassador to Canada is acting like a little bitch criticizing Canada’s government while denying that a trade war exists between the two countries. Meanwhile the administration is lowering tariffs on Canadian imports critical to Maine in a desperate bid to help Susan Collins keep her job as U.S. Senator.

All of this is horrible. It will take years to clean up this mess. Furthermore, even a strong midterm performance from Democrats will not necessarily constrain a determined Donald Trump from wreaking even more carnage.

Trying to straightforwardly assess just how much damage is being done is an exercise designed to induce depression. Instead, searching for examples that serve as the perfect metaphor for Trump administration fuckwittery is the saner path.

So the hard-working staff here at Drezner’s World would like to thank the Washington Post’s Alex Horton and Dan Lamothe for reporting out this Pete Hegseth and staff story that so perfectly captures this administration’s incompetence:

It was early this year when Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wanted to move the world. A replica of it, anyway.

Two floor globes said to be used by Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower during World War II are housed in the Pentagon, where subsequent generations of Army leaders became custodians of the artifacts, according to people familiar with their lineage and an accompanying plaque dating them to the 1930s.

The historical significance was attractive to Hegseth, these people said, and his staff requested that the secretary’s office become the new home to one of the 30-inch globes.

Ordinarily, moving historical items within the building is a deliberate process overseen by trained curators. Instead, Hegseth’s staff dispatched its own team to relocate an Eisenhower globe. They lost control of the artifact and dropped it, sending the globe crashing onto its base and impaling the fragile shell near Antarctica, according to those familiar with the incident. The resulting gash appears to be several inches wide….

After publication Thursday, a Defense Department official provided The Post with a brief, unattributed statement acknowledging the mishap. “Accidents happen,” it says, “we are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired.” The statement does not say how much the repairs are expected to cost and when they would be complete.

The Army office in possession of the globe had expected to consult with experts at the U.S. Army Center of Military History on how to ensure its safe transport and properly document its relocation to Hegseth’s office, according to two people familiar with the matter. Like others, they spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a previously undisclosed incident that is viewed as an embarrassment within the Defense Department.

The history staffers were furloughed due to a partial government shutdown stemming from a dispute in Congress over aspects of the Trump administration’s immigration policy. When the experts could not be reached, Hegseth’s staff decided to move the globe themselves, these people said.

Yeah, that is the perfect story to encapsulate just how much Trump and his team have beclowned American foreign policy.

text:
On one hand, state election officials say the likelihood of federal immigration officers stalking polling places on Election Day, scaring away voters in an attempt to influence the election is remote. On the other, some have been preparing for that possibility.

In Denver, which has gone to court to try to block U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers from voting locations, election workers are being trained to watch out for immigration officers, document their presence and de-escalate any interactions with them.

Boulder County’s clerk is asking voters who see ICE officers at voting places to alert her office or call 911 if they feel unsafe.

“Our approach is to de-escalate and redirect the situation to ensure that voting continues to happen in a manner that supports voters and reduces harm and the risk of violence,” Clerk Molly Fitzpatrick, a Democrat, said in a social media video, joined by Boulder County Sheriff Curtis Johnson and District Attorney Michael Dougherty.

In Eagle County, officials have been addressing questions about ICE as part of the overall training for election workers that includes how to respond to emergencies, delays and complications like blizzards or wildfires.

Election officials, particularly Democratic ones, say they want to be prepared for anything and respond to community fears and speculation.

They are also operating knowing that the Trump administration’s heavy involvement in immigration enforcement and in elections is unprecedented in recent American history, culminating with the attack on the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, an attempt to stop Congress from certifying election results.

“Our judges are civically minded and pay attention to current headlines, so addressing these topics is necessary. Our goal is simply to ensure they are fully prepared to keep voting smooth, neutral, and secure,” Eagle County Clerk Becky Close, who is unaffiliated, said in an email.

Colorado is unique in that the vast majority of voters — about 90% — don’t actually vote in person. Every registered voter gets a ballot in the mail, and most return it through the Postal Service or turn it in at a drop box.

That means even if federal immigration officers were to show up at polling places, only a small share of the electorate would interact with them.

Last month, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE officers have the authority to go to polling places if there’s a threat to the location or if they’re serving a warrant on someone they have been actively tracking. He accused Democrats of “fearmongering” by expressing concern over ICE going to polling places.

After Denver joined with civil rights and voting groups to sue to make sure ICE officers didn’t show up at voting locations, the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that ICE isn’t planning operations targeting polling locations. But it still left the door open to arrests happening at polling places if there was “an active public safety threat.”

Denver’s clerk, Democrat Paul Lopez, thinks it’s unlikely immigration officers will be at the polls in Colorado, since it’s not a swing state. Colorado has consistently voted blue in statewide races for more than a decade. But he does think ICE’s suggestion that arrests could happen is a “scare tactic” meant to discourage people from voting.

For any voter worried about ICE being at polling locations, Lopez suggests that they cast their mail ballot at one of the city’s many 24-hour ballot drop boxes. If there happens to be anyone hanging out around one, they can visit another one another time, he said.

“We have an intimidation-proof way of voting — it’s a ballot box,” he said.

Department of Justice gets involved

But while getting ready for the possibility of ICE showing up, election officials learned last week that the Department of Justice planned to send election observers to Adams County on Election Day.

The Department of Justice has said the monitoring is consistent with longstanding practice. Adams County was singled out because it is covered by a section of the federal Voting Rights Act that requires states, counties and cities to provide election materials, including ballots, in other languages if they meet certain criteria, such as having at least 5% of voting-age citizens who speak another language, department spokesperson Kiersten Pels,said.

Adams County has had to provide election materials in Spanish since it was added to the program in 2022, Adams County Clerk Josh Zygielbaum, a Democrat, said. Five other Colorado counties are currently required to provide materials in Spanish under the law — Alamosa, Conejos, Costilla, Denver and Saguache. Two are required to provide them in Ute — La Plata and Montezuma.

Back in 2022, under Democratic President Joe Biden, Zygielbaum said the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division reached out to the county to help it comply with the Voting Rights Act, calling it a “wonderful partner” then.

But now he is suspicious of the DOJ is coming to the Democratic-leaning county amid a tight race in the 8th Congressional District between Republican U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans and Democrat Manny Rutinel. The district includes part of Adams and neighboring Weld County, as well as a sliver of Larimer County. The race could help determine which party controls Congress.

Zygielbaum said making voting accessible to Spanish-speaking voters, as the Voting Rights Act requires, hasn’t been an issue there.

“The difference now is that they are not coming in a support capacity and the attorneys being sent are prosecutors,” he said Friday.

The DOJ notice to Adams County was sent by Jake Bachard, a trial lawyer with the Civil Rights Division’s Voting Rights Section, who offered to set up a virtual meeting with Zygielbaum to discuss their monitoring plans. He said the monitors would only observe.

“They do not intrude or interfere in any way with the voting process,” he wrote.

The Secretary of State’s Office has asked the Department of Justice to provide more details about what part of the voting process it wants to observe. In a letter to Bachard on Thursday, Deputy Secretary of State Andrew Kline said department observers would need the office’s permission to get access to secure parts of the process, like counting mail ballots.

ICE lawsuits

The lawsuit brought by Denver, the League of United Latin American Citizens, UnidosUS and Common Cause proactively asks a federal judge in Washington, D.C., to block ICE from being at voting locations after reports immigration officers made arrests in parking lots of polling locations in San Antonio, Texas and Ventura County, California, in May and June. Minnesota’s Hennepin County, home to Minneapolis, has also joined the lawsuit.

It claims that the Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE, has established a policy allowing its officers to conduct enforcement operations at polling places. Allowing ICE officers at polling places, the lawsuit says, would violate a Civil War-era law that bans federal officials from sending troops or “armed men” to polling places. It was passed at the end of the war in response to the Lincoln administration’s practice of sending troops to border states to suppress votes for pro-Confederate or anti-war candidates. The only exception to the law is if the troops or armed men are needed to “repel armed enemies of the United States.”

Two other similar lawsuits have also been filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., one by the NAACP and other civil rights groups and another by Democratic Congressional leaders Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, committees aimed at electing Democrats to Congress and the Democratic Governors’ Association. Besides violating the Civil War law, these suits argue that allowing ICE officers at voting locations would violate the Voting Rights Act’s ban on voter intimidation. A federal judge ruled Friday that the three cases should be consolidated and considered together.

Denver has not reported any ICE agents at its polling places, but is hoping to avoid any confrontations by getting a ruling from a judge.

If there was an instance where ICE officers were intimidating voters at the polls, the city would go to court to seek an emergency injunction to stop it, Jon Ewing, a spokesperson for Mayor Mike Johnston, said.

Under an executive order signed by Johnston earlier this year, the city’s police officers would have a duty to intervene to stop any “violent and unlawful behavior by ICE”, he said.

In a statement, the Denver Police Department said it would respond to any reported law violations at voting places, including those involving ICE, “with a focus on de-escalation” while relying on legal advice from the city’s attorney’s office.

Poll monitors

Just Vote Colorado, a coalition that recruits and trains people to serve as nonpartisan poll monitors, has seen an increase in people looking to help monitor voting because of concerns about whether there would be federal interference in the election, said Aly Belknap, the executive director of Colorado Common Cause, which is part of the coalition.

About 800 people have signed up to get training this year, she said. In 2024, the group had 300 volunteers.

Because of the fear of ICE being at the polls and the increase in immigration enforcement generally, the coalition is teaming up with the Colorado Rapid Response Network, which provides updates on ICE sightings and whether or not they were confirmed on its Facebook page, for this year’s election, she said. It’s telling poll monitors to report any ICE officers at the polls to the network. She said the network will let the coalition know about immigration enforcement near voting places.

In person voting centers in Colorado for the Nov. 3 election began opening Oct. 19 and so far no ICE agents have been reported anywhere in the state.

At a training for about 50 poll monitors in Denver earlier this month, Belknap said there was no credible evidence that ICE will be at the polls in Colorado. But she said monitors, wearing yellow T-shirts announcing their role, could still help anyone who was afraid of voting this year.

“Fear is the point to get people to not vote so we’re there to be the antidote to fear,” she told the group, which included many first time volunteers.

They included Rudy Garcia, a retired teacher from Denver who said he wanted to defend the voting process for both immigrants and people of color largely because of the surge in immigration enforcement.

He said he wonders whether people of Mexican descent who are citizens in his neighborhood might be hesitant to vote after months of immigration officers pulling people over doing everyday errands. He said people shouldn’t have to be afraid to do ordinary things, including voting.

“This is a crisis. It’s a political electoral crisis of everyday life in America now and we got to rise up. We got to defend each other,” Garcia said.

Vita Lantz-Brown, a retired nurse from Arapahoe County who has served as a poll monitor for over 20 years, plans to be stationed at a polling location on Election Day once again from 7 a.m. until polls close at 7 p.m. If there are still people in line when the polls close, she’ll be ready to order them pizza, as she has in the past.

Lantz-Brown, 60, thinks this is the most important election in her lifetime because, she said, democracy is at stake. She believes the Trump administration will use every tool it can to scare people not to vote, including ICE or Department of Justice monitors.

“I’m just going to be very alert,” she said.

title: After decades of partnership, Trump's policies have pushed U.S. allies away | Opinion
description:
For generations of Germans, the United States had always felt like the slightly cooler cousin from overseas.
Politically, the U.S. helped West Germany get back on its feet after World War II had left it in rubble.
For decades, Germany and the rest of Europe knew they could count on the United States, and America was guaranteed devoted partners across the pond.
After Trump’s defeat in 2020, Europeans thought that America had come to its senses.
Seeing Trump being not only reelected, but cheered on as he berated partners, allies, and friends across the globe, had an impact.
text:
Wim Orth is a journalist with WELT in Berlin and an Arthur F. Burns fellow at The Inquirer.

For generations of Germans, the United States had always felt like the slightly cooler cousin from overseas. In culture, there were icons like Coca-Cola, denim jeans, fast food chains, rock and roll — and, of course, Hollywood — that shaped culture not only in America but across the Atlantic as well.

Politically, the U.S. helped West Germany get back on its feet after World War II had left it in rubble. The Marshall Plan, signed by President Harry S. Truman, helped Germany and other European governments rebuild, and the trust shown by America toward the German people would frequently overrule the doubts that British and French forces had toward their former enemy.

That trust went so far that just a few years after the war, the U.S. stationed nuclear warheads in bases in Germany and encouraged the Adenauer government to set up its own army again. To guarantee a contained German military, the Bundeswehr became part of NATO right after its founding. Additionally, government and military leaders worked closely together with the U.S. to prove that the days of aggressive German militarism were a thing of the past.

From then on, Germans and Americans in particular — and Western Europe and Americans in general — would work in unison to counter aggression by the Soviet Union and its proxies, defend West Germany against the constant threat of Soviet invasion, and eventually bring down the Berlin Wall and shred the Iron Curtain.

For decades, Germany and the rest of Europe knew they could count on the United States, and America was guaranteed devoted partners across the pond. In case there was any doubt, this partnership and its steadfastness was proved when Article 5 of the NATO treaty was invoked for the first and only time so far on Sept. 12, 2001.

After the terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington, it was America’s NATO partners who helped patrol the American skies and were part of the war on terror, commanding several missions in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Now, take all that shared history and goodwill and put it in the trash.

Today, not even two years since Donald Trump returned to the White House, there is painfully little trust left between the United States and its NATO partners — only plenty of doubt that if the situation were reversed, and Europe were attacked, that America and its NATO allies would step side by side into the breach.

After months of being battered and bruised by Trump and his administration, most Germans aren’t even mad about the situation anymore. Some are disappointed, others have simply moved on from the cooler cousin who grew up and grew distant. In the regions formerly under Soviet control, people may even turn to a bit of “I told you so” thinking.

When Trump was first elected in 2016, his presidency was regarded by many Europeans as an “accident” of the country’s curious electoral system, where having the most votes does not automatically equal victory. After all, how could the same voters who made history when they sent Barack Obama to the White House (twice!) now support a bigoted charlatan?

» READ MORE: Trump’s open alliance with Putin betrays the United States and helps Russia kill Ukrainians | Trudy Rubin

Europeans were convinced that it was over for Trump after he lost the 2020 presidential contest against Joe Biden and lied about the election being stolen, with his falsehoods culminating in the assault by Trump supporters on the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. Trump then went on trial several times and was found liable for sexual abuse and was convicted of 34 felony counts.

And yet … when Americans went to the polls in 2024, Trump defeated Kamala Harris. There were no Electoral College excuses as he won the popular vote by more than two million votes. That Election Day result was the moment when many Europeans shifted from hope to utter disbelief.

Unlike the eye rolls that greeted much of Trump’s ridiculous rhetoric during his first term, the president’s words and deeds the second time around have seriously damaged the relationship between Europe and America.

Incidents like Vice President JD Vance supporting far-right extremists under the guise of lecturing Germans on free speech at the Munich Security Conference, the scandalous treatment of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and Trump’s apparently unwavering support of Vladimir Putin, even as Russia continues to target Ukrainian civilians and play with provocations toward NATO — including a failed drone attack on a German airport.

Europe was used to having a bad partner in the White House during Trump’s first term. Now, we wonder if the term partner can even be applied anymore.

Threats of annexing Greenland or Canada, withdrawing the U.S. from NATO altogether, and even the thought that Trump is considering a three-way summit with China and Russia to determine Ukraine’s fate have only added to the estrangement.

(And that’s not even considering the Trump administration’s assault on human rights as it deploys immigration enforcement agents — who have so far killed nine people and shot at least a dozen more — and detains people indefinitely in substandard conditions over civil immigration offenses.)

» READ MORE: I saw firsthand how Ukraine could win the war — if Trump weren’t determined to hand the country over to Putin | Trudy Rubin

While some podcasters and journalists in Europe seem to embrace the president’s sillier shenanigans — think renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario — many people I’ve spoken with in Europe have lost faith in the United States.

A recent study conducted across Europe found 73% of respondents agreeing to the question whether they “think it’s time for Europe to go its own way.” In Germany, just 27% see the U.S. as a “trustworthy partner” anymore.

Polling in the U.S. finds that Americans themselves are repudiating Trump’s policies and there is hope that the midterm elections will provide a critical check on the president’s rampant abuses and ill-advised positions.

But it may be too little, too late.

After Trump’s defeat in 2020, Europeans thought that America had come to its senses. Seeing Trump being not only reelected, but cheered on as he berated partners, allies, and friends across the globe, had an impact.

The damage has been done, and one or two elections won’t be able to erase the doubt that lingers.

title: Court ruling fails to end wait for thousands of immigrants stuck abroad without visas - NPR
description:
That's because this January the Trump administration banned the processing of immigrant visas for citizens of 75 countries.
On its website, the State Department acknowledges the visa ban is no longer in effect due to the court ruling.
This means even immigrants with visas approved would have to go through additional screening.
"I've never seen a substantial pause on visa processing … I really haven't," the former consular officer said.
But the battle over visa processing has affected many immigrants who fall into the high-performing category.
text:
Late last year, Dustin Hoffman and his wife Gloria started the paperwork to secure a visa for her to live in the U.S.

The couple, along with their 5-year-old daughter Chaya and Hoffman's 12-year-old step son Israel, lived together in Argentina, where Hoffman had moved in 2013 after doing a deployment with the U.S. Army in Iraq.

"My daughter is growing up and she's very smart and my stepson he's very smart," Hoffman said. "But the resources in Argentina for an autistic child and the school system in Argentina … I don't know. I just feel like I needed to give my daughter the same opportunities that I had growing up."

But nearly a year later, the kids and Gloria are stuck in Argentina in bureaucratic limbo due to continuing delays in the processing of their visa.

That's because this January the Trump administration banned the processing of immigrant visas for citizens of 75 countries. Many of the migrants were already in the process of getting a visa. Some already had the visa approved; they were just waiting to get the physical visa delivered to them.

Hoffman's wife is from Colombia, one of the countries on the list.

A federal judge this August ordered the ban to be lifted, but Hoffman's family still has not gotten their visa, and the State Department continues to ask them to provide additional evidence to prove they have the financial means to live in the U.S. without becoming a public charge.

Attorneys representing migrants say the Hoffman family's case is emblematic of a wider problem: They say the Trump administration is not complying with the federal court order and is instead slow-walking the processing of the visas.

"So while technically the ban doesn't exist, it doesn't matter practically if people are still not being able to get their green card interviews or have their interviews not be finished and not get their immigrant visa stamps foils and be able to come into the United States," said Alexis Axelrad, the president elect of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

A new training creates additional delays

The visa ban affected more than 280,000 immigrants who had applied for visas by the time the policy went into effect in January.

According to an analysis by the libertarian think-tank Cato Institute, the ban targeted thousands of close family members of U.S. citizens and permanent residents, including spouses and minor children. The Cato report called it "one of the most extreme legal immigration policies in U.S. history."

Now stuck in their countries unable to come to the U.S., many are rethinking what to do.

The State Department declined to comment for this story, telling NPR "the matter referenced is subject to pending litigation." On its website, the State Department acknowledges the visa ban is no longer in effect due to the court ruling.

The agency told NPR in August it had paused the processing of visas as it launched an in-depth "training program" for embassies and consulates on identifying immigrants who could become a burden on taxpayers — a public charge.

This means even immigrants with visas approved would have to go through additional screening.

This pause is uncommon, a former State Department consular officer told NPR. She asked not to be identified because she fears it could affect her job prospects.

"I've never seen a substantial pause on visa processing … I really haven't," the former consular officer said. "The department is doing this because this is what the policy is from the president … to reduce illegal immigration, remigrate people and only accept refugees from South Africa."

But families such as the Hoffmans are stuck in limbo. He says he misses his daughter, stepson, and wife every day. He said his daughter cries "all the time" and asks for her father. His wife is overwhelmed.

"Let me put it this way: Our family is a family. We need to be there for each other," Hoffman said. "Just like any family, it's not functioning very well while we're separated."

The brightest is left behind

During his first term, President Trump said he wanted to attract the brightest immigrants to come to the U.S.

Right-wing organizations, including the America First Policy Institute, have also endorsed a "merit-based" immigration system.

"America's immigration system should prioritize immigrants with education, skills, and well-paying jobs waiting for them in the U.S. because these individuals are most likely to contribute to America's society and economy, benefitting all Americans," the organization wrote in March 2026.

But the battle over visa processing has affected many immigrants who fall into the high-performing category.

One of them is Dr. Fernando Lizcano, a Colombian national whose research focuses on major cardiovascular health challenges in the U.S., including obesity.

He applied for an EB-1A visa, which is reserved for immigrants "of extraordinary ability," including "an outstanding professor or researcher," according to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

"My intention is to continue with my academic biomedical research in the United States," Lizcano told NPR from his office in Bogotá. "(I) have been exploring opportunities also where I could combine all my experience in endocrinology with molecular biology, translational research."

Because USCIS deemed him qualified for an EB-1A, all that was left for him was to apply for the visa itself and get it stamped in his passport.

But he is still in Colombia, awaiting for the State Department's final approval.

"This is not fair," Lizcano said.

The waiting game is taking an emotional toll on many of the immigrants — and their loved ones — whose visas are now up in the air.

Hoffman, the U.S. veteran awaiting his wife's visa to be approved, is worried about his own mental health. He told NPR his doctors have increased his psychiatric medicines.

"I was OK before all this started happening," he said.

He works as an Uber driver, and with Trump's war in Iran, gas prices have skyrocketed, cutting into his income.

He's struggling to pay both his mortgage in the U.S., and rent in Argentina for his family.

"We're living on a dream and a prayer right now," Hoffman said.

title: The country where anti-migrant anger is spiralling into murder - i Newspaper
description:
Violence has been a recurring feature of anti-migrant protests that have swept the country this year, including cases of looting, arson, and murder.
Following the protests, South Africa launched a major crackdown on undocumented migrants.
Amnesty South Africa said the killing last week “represents the latest wave in a rising tide of violence against migrants in South Africa.
Official government figures show 2.4 million foreign nationals among the population of 62 million.
The country’s high unemployment rate – at 33.6 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, according to Statistics South Africa – is also driving anger.
text:
A grisly video showing a foreign national being murdered on camera has highlighted the escalating violence of South Africa’s anti-migrant movement, following months of protests.

A mob of around 50 people beat a foreign national to death during protests against immigration in Durban on the country’s east coast last week, police said. The man is believed to have been in his late thirties or early forties.

Footage published on social media purported to show the attack, with protesters breaking off from a crowd to chase and assault a man attempting to flee. Police did not give the victim’s nationality ⁠and said the motive for the killing was unknown.

Five men aged 19 to 46 were being held for questioning over the killing on Friday.

Violence has been a recurring feature of anti-migrant protests that have swept the country this year, including cases of looting, arson, and murder. Nigeria, Mozambique and Malawi have all reported deaths of their nationals, and at least four people were killed during protests in Durban, a hotspot for anti-immigration sentiment, earlier this year.

This month, ‌anti-migrant protests in ⁠Durban and Johannesburg’s Soweto township turned violent after a court ruling made it easier for foreign citizens to claim asylum. Foreign-owned businesses were looted and cars set on fire.

Protesters in South Africa have been demanding tighter border controls and more deportations, claiming that migrants are contributing to high unemployment and crime rates, and crumbling public services.

Following the protests, South Africa launched a major crackdown on undocumented migrants. African governments have moved to repatriate their nationals in recent months, with about 60,000 Malawians returning, according to official statistics, and thousands more returning to Zimbabwe, Nigeria, Mozambique and elsewhere.

However, violence and protests have continued to escalate. Human rights groups have condemned such attacks and called on authorities to do more to prevent them. Amnesty South Africa said the killing last week “represents the latest wave in a rising tide of violence against migrants in South Africa. The justice system must start acting as a deterrent to these attacks and killings. The government has a legal obligation to protect everyone within its borders, regardless of nationality or immigration status.”

The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights urged South Africa to declare the attacks on foreign nationals a crisis, and to “conduct prompt, impartial, thorough and transparent investigation into this heinous mob killing”.

South Africa’s President, Cyril Ramaphosa, has condemned acts of violence while promising to reform the immigration system and crack down on illegal crossings.

Anti-migrant movements have flared sporadically in post-apartheid South Africa. In 2008, at least 62 people were killed during anti-migrant riots.

But this bout of unrest is curious because immigration has fallen sharply, says Ivor Chipkin, head of the New South Institute think-tank in Johannesburg.

“Migration to South Africa has fallen off dramatically since 2015 so it’s not as if these protests arise as a response to some new wave,” he said. Official statistics show immigrants make up 4 to 5 per cent of the country’s population.

Official government figures show 2.4 million foreign nationals among the population of 62 million. Protesters claim there are many more in the country without documentation.

The country’s high unemployment rate – at 33.6 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, according to Statistics South Africa – is also driving anger. A report this year found that 83 per cent of South Africans wanted the government to reduce or entirely eliminate the entry of foreign job seekers.

Chipkin suggests the recent protests were partly driven by political parties seeking to exploit them ahead of local government elections next month.

Former president Jacob Zuma, who was jailed on corruption charges after leaving office in 2018 and is now leading the new MK Party – an offshoot of the ruling African National Congress – has backed the movement.

Action South Africa, a political party led by former mayor of Johannesburg Herman Mashaba, has been at the forefront of protests. Mashaba has called for “war against the invaders” and said South Africa cannot import “Ebolas.”

The protests also highlight the breakdown of government, Chipkin believes, citing blackouts and water shortages in Johannesburg, and a chronically under-resourced police force.

“It’s a real crisis of services,” he said. “I think people are feeling tremendous economic and social pressures, which are real, and political mobilisation is directing those grievances against migrants.”

Police leadership is corrupt and “largely captured by criminal networks”, said Chipkin, arguing that this had resulted in a lack of officers on the street and allowed incidents such as the mob killing this week. In a violent country with one of the world’s highest homicide rates, the force is ill equipped to tackle crime.

“Even public service-minded police are going into circumstances where they’re outgunned and they don’t have vehicles,” he said.

Chipkin suggests that authorities should be pushing back against the lawlessness rather than indulging it, and that reforms to a chaotic immigration system were also necessary.

But many South Africans are also counting down to municipal elections on 4 November, he believes, after which parties and candidates will no longer have an incentive to fuel the fire.

text:
A rare Sunday federal appeals court hearing for the Justice Department's voting lawsuit against California closed without a ruling.

The department requested that the court issue one by Tuesday prior to the scheduled 1 p.m. PDT hearing before the district court.

The arguments followed a surprise appeal by the Trump administration, which claims a district judge did not act quickly enough to address the administration's allegations of roughly 20,000 potential noncitizen voters on the state's voter rolls.

A three-judge panel that includes two appointees of President Donald Trump and one appointee of former President Joe Biden heard arguments on DOJ's efforts to segregate ballots from the alleged noncitizens.

California officials have countered that the list is unverified and includes the names of lawful voters, despite recent charges announced by DOJ of roughly 28 individuals from the list accused of voting and immigration-related crimes.

Earlier the DOJ sent letters last week to every county in California asking local elections officials to help identify potential voters who may be in the U.S. illegally, according to a letter described to ABC News.

"Within 48 hours, we ask that you commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not," according to a letter sent by Justice Department officials to every county in California and described to ABC News. "The Department strongly urges you and your agency to work with the Department of Justice to ensure the integrity of California's federal elections before taking actions that risk significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure."

Earlier this month, the DOJ filed suit against California accusing the state of failing to review a list of alleged noncitizens that the Trump administration claimed were sent mail-in ballots for next month's midterm election.

In court papers filed earlier this week, Los Angeles officials said a preliminary analysis of 200 of the names on the 20,000-person list, included a "high percentage" of individuals who say they were born in the U.S. and many more who have no voting history at all.

Of those 200 individuals, officials said, nearly 40% "indicate that they were born in the United States, which is strong evidence of citizenship; and 71.2% of the records have no voting history," according to a filing.

The Justice Department's rushed efforts to have an appeals court quickly rule on its lawsuit faced considerable skepticism from the three-judge panel in Sunday's emergency hearing.

Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, repeatedly questioned whether the appeals court had jurisdiction to step in at this stage in the litigation, and expressed considerable constitutional concerns over the lawsuit itself.

"I don't see how we have jurisdiction," Bennett said to DOJ attorney Matthew Donnelly after pressing him over the timeline of the government's decision to seeking emergency appeal when a hearing before the district judge is already set for this Tuesday.

Donnelly claimed that the DOJ's decision to seek relief from the appeals court came after disclosures by the state of the numbers of mail-in ballots already being processed in advance of the election -- which number in the hundreds of thousands.

But Bennett's most significant concerns appeared to be the nature of the lawsuit and it appearing to directly contradict the Constitution's Elections Clause -- which mandates that states have jurisdictions over the manner their elections are run.

"How can it preempt something that is expressly authorized by a provision of the Constitution?" Bennett asked. "How can the legislature making laws with regard to the manner of holding elections be preempted by a criminal statute passed by the Congress, especially when both the Congress and the California Legislature have made it illegal for non-citizens to vote?"

Donnelly repeatedly pointed to DOJ's position that the way California is administering its elections -- and not acting on the hard drive of potential 20,000 likely non-citizens -- infringes on the federal government's ability to enforce the federal statute barring voting by illegal immigrants.

That explanation didn't appear to sit well with Bennett, however, who pointed out that the Constitution specifically tasks Congress with jurisdiction over how states administer their elections and not the Judiciary.

"How can we, a federal court, do what is reserved to Congress, which Congress, in my view, hasn't done?" Bennett asked.

"Your Honor, I would just simply -- unfortunately -- disagree with you that 18 USC 611 is not an election law that fits in the power of Congress," Donnelly replied.

The judges also appeared to express concern about last-minute intervention to force California to segregate certain mail-in ballots given the state has provided a declaration saying if such an order was implemented it could have a "catastrophic" impact on tabulating the upcoming election.

Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, repeatedly pressed California's attorney Samuel Siegel over why an injunction wouldn't be appropriate to ensure non-citizens votes are being actively cast in the ongoing election.

"Without an injunction, you will never know, correct?" Bumatay asked. "Because if -- if the ballots are cast and separated, then they're going to be tabulated, and there's no way of knowing."

"Your Honor, we would respectfully disagree with that because of the number of steps that people have to take to attest to their citizenship, to declare consistent with what is required by both federal and state law that they are citizens when they register to vote," Siegel responded.

Even as Bumatay's questioning suggested he had more sympathy to granting the government some kind of relief, both Bennett and Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden appointee, appeared unified that the extraordinary relief being sought by DOJ was not appropriate at this juncture.

"That's why I have a problem with the relief that's being sought here because I just don't see -- Congress and the California legislature have said non-citizens can't vote, and this lawsuit is about 'we don't like the way you're sorting citizens from non-citizens, and I just don't see 611 as telling California how to do the sorting," Bennett said.

"That's absolutely right, Your Honor, and to reiterate my earlier point, if the federal government, if the Executive Branch wants that authority in the first instance, they need to go ask Congress for it, they haven't done that," Siegel said. "They ask this court to short circuit the democratic process and issue an order, not just on the eve of an election, but as an election is underway."

In closing remarks, Bennett said the panel "will try to decide this case as quickly as possible."

MAGA personality Samuel Sey, who describes himself as a "blogger, a teacher, a pro-life advocate, and a public speaker," was taken by ICE agents and is currently being held in an Ohio jail. The jail's website states he was booked on Oct. 21 and is still being held in custody for ICE.

A donation page made on behalf of Sey confirmed he was detained by ICE while traveling.

"He is a husband, father, school teacher, married to Annie with three beautiful children, and has been living here as a legal resident of the United States from Canada," the page stated.

The page also stated that his wife is working to get him released on bail "so he can fix any clerical issues that need to be addressed for his legal residence."

Sey previously announced on social media in 2022 that he had obtained a marriage license to wed his wife, Annie.

A DHS spokesperson told the Daily Beast, "On October 21, ICE arrested Samuel Sey, an illegal alien from Ghana, at the Columbus International Airport. Sey entered the United States legally in 2022 but overstayed his length of admission by over four years, in violation of our nation's laws. Sey has no pending applications and accepted voluntary departure. He will remain in ICE custody until removed from the United States.

"We do not pick and choose which laws to enforce or where to enforce them.

"We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return."

Sey, 39, is the author of the blog SlowToWrite. He has been vocal about his support for ICE agents, writing in one social media post, "If you love America, you should support ICE."

He's even gone as far as to say that God would actually be against people who protest ICE agents.

"God isn't just against anti-ICE protestors who persecute Christians while they are worshipping at church. He is also against the idealogy [sic] of anti-ICE protestors," he wrote in one post. "Christians who condemn the "protestors" but refuse to condemn their ideology should know that."

In another post, he proclaimed that " anti-ICE protestors are influenced by Satan."

After Minnesota mother Renee Good was shot and killed in her car in January, he echoed popular talking points on the right claiming that she was attempting to ram agents with her car, despite video evidence suggesting otherwise.

"The woman would still be alive if she didn't try to run the ICE agent over. You can be saddened by her death and admit that it was self-defense," he wrote.

While he has been largely pro-ICE, Sey is oftentimes critical of President Donald Trump, especially on the president's ever-changing views on abortion.

One post from 2024 reads: "It's a sobering sign of God's judgment on America that although thousands of babies could die because of Trump—he is a significantly better option than Kamala Harris."

text:
OAKLAND, Calif. (KGO) -- Community activists are calling on Eastmont Mall owners to stop allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to stage operations on the property, alleging the site has been used to transfer detainees for more than a year.

Dozens of advocates gathered Sunday in Parking Lot 'C' at Eastmont Mall in Oakland, staging a symbolic "die-in" to honor people who have died while in ICE custody. Organizers say the demonstration was intended to draw attention to what they describe as ongoing ICE activity at the shopping center.

"We are here today because we want ICE out of Eastmont Mall and all health care facilities," said Gabriela Galicia, executive director of the Street Level Health Project.

Galicia said legal observers have documented ICE agents using the parking lot since December 2025.

"In June 2026, a community member was picked up at their house and taken to this parking lot, where they were transferred to another ICE vehicle," Galicia said.

MORE: Investigation underway after pedestrian allegedly struck by ICE vehicle in Northern California

Advocates say the alleged enforcement activity is particularly concerning because the parking lot is adjacent to an Alameda County community health clinic. They argue the presence of federal immigration agents has created fear among immigrant families seeking medical care.

"People are afraid to come here. You become afraid to go to the clinic, you get sick and others get sick around you," said Francisco Herrera of the Nuevo Sol Day Labor and Domestic Worker Center.

A county sign posted in a portion of the lot under Alameda County control states that the area may not be used for immigration enforcement activities.

Activists are also directing their concerns toward Tidewater Capital, the private owner of the Eastmont Mall property.

"We want the owners of the property to put safety first and say to ICE, 'Do not come here,'" Herrera said.

MORE: Video of masked ICE arrest in San Francisco's SoMa neighborhood sparks outrage

The issue has drawn attention from Alameda County leaders. Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas attended Sunday's event and pledged to continue monitoring ICE activity in the area.

"I'm going to remain vigilant in protecting our communities against ICE," Bas said.

The controversy follows a recent incident involving ICE agents and a detainee who was taken to Highland Hospital for treatment. Advocates allege the man suffered fractured ribs after being tackled by an agent.

In response to questions about activity at Eastmont Mall, the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement: "ICE's presence in public parking lots is fully authorized under federal law and is a standard practice for law enforcement agencies nationwide."

MORE: ICE agents accused of breaking man's arm in dramatic arrest caught on video in Long Beach

Activists dispute that characterization, noting that Eastmont Mall is privately owned.

"This is not a public parking lot. It's a private parking lot," Herrera said.

ABC7 Eyewitness News reached out to Eastmont Mall property owners for comment but had not received a response as of Sunday evening.

Organizers say they plan to send an open letter to Oakland city leaders and mall ownership this week, asking that all ICE-related activity be barred from the property.
