For the first time since plainclothes federal immigration agents had held her to the ground at the airport, choking and screaming for help, the Ukrainian immigrant encountered a kind face. Her new cellmate, Blanca, swept her into a hug.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Tranquilo,” she soothed. Don’t worry.

Outside, the violent video had made Gorb a symbol of Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s airport arrest strategy, which has targeted travelers over visa overstays, including some with pending asylum cases and no criminal record. But her experience inside detention also reveals how women tangled in the Trump administration’s deportation crackdown — including many who were also arrested at airports — have relied on one another as they search for the legal help they needed to get out.

Blanca removed bedsheets from a yellow tote packed with items issued to each detainee at California’s largest immigration detention center. She made the top bunk and set out Gorb’s tiny tubes of shampoo and toothpaste.

“Agua?” Blanca asked.

She led Gorb to a fountain in the common room, where a parade of women in slate-blue uniforms and orange plastic clogs brought her plastic cups, plates and packaged noodles. It was Thursday, they explained. The commissary wouldn’t open until the weekend. Take these, they told her. You’ll need them.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Gorb had cuff-shaped bruises on her wrists and purpled knees from her arrest. Surrounded by women living through the same nightmare — and so willing to help — she began to feel less alone.

“I need to adapt to this for now,” she told herself. “Who knows how long I’ll be here?”

Gorb quickly picked up the rhythms of detention: chow time and detainee counts, or “cuenta.” But it took about a week for her to learn that the video of her arrest had spread beyond San Francisco newspapers and TV stations. Friends in Ohio and Europe saw it before she had the chance to explain where she was. New girls who joined the unit recognized her.

The Department of Homeland Security said Gorb was arrested because her visa expired in 2011. Gorb said she maintained legal status beyond that point as a college student, but when Russia first invaded Ukraine in 2014, she said it wasn’t safe for her to go back.

Gorb, 39, had spent a decade building her community in San Francisco. Friends rallied around her and raised $70,000 to help her find a lawyer. After seven weeks in detention, she was released on bond.

Her immigration case is still moving through court. She wears an ankle monitor wrapped in a bandanna, and goes to the ICE office in downtown San Francisco for regular check-ins. But she’s always thinking about the women inside California City. They need someone who isn’t afraid to speak up, she said, and she’s already been thrust in the spotlight.

Chronicle investigations and state reports have found the detention center’s medical care is insufficient and conditions are dire. The state’s attorney general has called them “cruel” and “inhumane.”

Now, just over five weeks since she left detention, Gorb estimates she has already sent more than $5,000 to her friends’ commissary accounts and phone cards. She’s launched a fundraising campaign for their attorney fees and bonds, promoting it by showcasing portraits she drew in detention of the women in her unit.

“The longer I wait,” Gorb said, “the longer they stay in there.”

Gorb works from a notebook that fits in the palm of her hand. She made it inside California City, using what she could: a photocopied coloring book page of a cheetah as the cover, protected by cellophane from two slices of bread, with binding stitched from threads of her underwear. The pages are filled with more than a dozen phone numbers and “A-numbers” — the nine-digit ID assigned to each detainee at California City.

Gorb still messages regularly with five women in detention through an app they can access on 10 tablets spread across the unit. Every minute on the tablet costs 5 cents. Outsiders have to pay 30 cents per message they send. Phone calls are even more expensive. Commissary orders are made on the tablets — like online shopping without photos. Freeze-dried coffee, Oreos, extra socks.

“Many families are afraid to even start any fundraisers — maybe they’re not all documented,” Gorb said. “Some are just ashamed, even though they should not be.”

A good attorney is the biggest barrier for most of those still at California City, she said. Sometimes they’re ineffective — other times, they’re not even actual attorneys, detainees said.

In text messages obtained by the Chronicle, one firm pressured a detainee’s family for payments over Zelle. The attorney’s name had circulated in the unit, but his name doesn’t appear in the California Bar Association’s lawyer lookup, and the firm’s website no longer exists.

“There’s a real dearth of services,” said Shira Levine, the deputy legal director of the Immigration Institute of the Bay Area. “There’s phenomenal attorneys in private practices and nonprofits, but often they’re at capacity or there are long waitlists.”

Gorb struggled to find an attorney who was reliable and knowledgeable. She described her first attorney as inexperienced, a waste of thousands of dollars.

Then, there are fees. Levine said the market rate for an attorney to petition to get someone out of detention is about $10,000. The rest of their immigration case could rack up a lot more billable hours.

“You’re looking at thousands of dollars, and there is a really big range,” Levine said.

Bonds can also range from $1,500 to $35,000 or more — Gorb’s was $8,000, which she paid from the fundraiser her friends launched for her.

Time inside doesn’t move the same. It didn’t help that the only clock in Gorb’s unit was an hour off — it was never changed after daylight saving time.

Gorb remembers the waiting. Waiting to talk to a doctor via video call. Waiting to get her bruises examined and recorded in her medical records. Waiting for pay phones to open. For an attorney call. To go outside.

Yard time isn’t guaranteed. At one point, it was moved from 9 a.m. to 5 a.m. But watching a sunrise, Gorb decided, was better than not going outside at all.

Isabelle Bueno, 28, came to California City after Gorb had been in detention for more than a month. She’s from Brazil and has lived in San Francisco for eight years. She, too, was picked up by ICE at SFO, as she headed out on a getaway to Yellowstone National Park.

“It would have been a beautiful trip,” she said.

Gorb tried to welcome Bueno the way Blanca had greeted her. She gave her snacks and commissary essentials. Bueno learned the basics quickly — like that the line for the microwave could take an hour, and heating up anything in the pitiful machine might take more than six minutes.

Gorb welcomed Bueno to her common area table, where women did puzzles and chatted. Gorb sketched with commissary-purchased colored pencils and paper. The sketches became a lifeline and a way to document the facility, where detainees and visitors’ cameras aren’t allowed. Gorb drew her friends. She drew her cell. She drew a TV playing CNN as it reported that ICE planned to spend $20 million on electrical shock gloves.

Some, she gave out as gifts. Others she kept, titled and time-stamped.

Bueno saw women try to work out their own legal defenses on scrap paper next to women coloring. Women unable to afford attorneys helped one another write petitions to challenge their detention.

“It goes from chill time, talking,” Bueno said, “to some really serious things like a habeas petition. You hear a lot of calls with lawyers. A lot of cries from court hearings.”

But from Gorb, she felt instant kindness. Their overlap together was short, about 12 days.

“But it was enough time for us to create the bond,” Bueno said. “She’s so special.”

After her release, Gorb picked up odd jobs. A photography gig; a catering event. She tried to keep her mind busy, but sometimes it is called back to her detention. Working a coffee cart during San Francisco’s Tech Week, the water fountains at the Metreon mall reminded her of being back at SFO.

She’s never watched the video of her arrest, but the panic is still visceral. She remembered she had headphones on and didn’t hear officers calling for her to stop. She felt them put pressure on her neck. She remembers screaming, “Why are you doing this?”

Still clutching her phone, she managed to tap out a string of text messages to a neighbor:

“I’ve got me”

“Help”

“ICE”

On a recent Saturday, Gorb carried stacks of her artwork, freshly printed on thick paper, to Abacus Row, a jewelry store and gallery on Nob Hill, for her first exhibit about her time at California City.

The drawings capture the women, but also the tablet checkout, pay phones, trays of food and dingy showers.

Ana Carreño, 32, originally from Mexico, drove an hour to the art show from Santa Rosa. She, too, was picked up at the San Francisco airport by ICE agents, held in California City and was released on the same day as Gorb.

“We ‘trauma bonded,’” Carreño said, repeating the English phrase she learned from Gorb.

She pointed to Gorb’s illustration of the sun setting above the prison yard, her favorite of the display.

“For an hour, we can be free,” she said.

Bueno, who had been released a week earlier, also came to the show.

“My heart is still there with them,” Bueno said, glassy-eyed, looking at the familiar faces lining the walls.

Attendees sipped on what Gorb called “prison coffee,” the exact freeze-dried brand she had inside. She wore the gray gym shorts she purchased from the commissary and a pair of orange clogs. She had a rosary around her neck, blue and yellow. She’s not religious, but Blanca gave it to her because it matches the colors of the Ukrainian flag.

Stacks of flyers displayed scannable codes so people could donate directly to fundraisers for legal aid. She hopes that the exhibit, titled “Don’t forget about us,” can travel around San Francisco and continue to raise money.

“All of this,” she said while standing in front of more than two dozen of her drawings, “is for my girls.”

text:
Oregon is dropping its lawsuit to halt construction of an immigrant detention center in Newport, after the U.S. Department of Homeland Security confirmed it’s no longer pursuing the project.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials’ effort to build a detention center at the Newport Airport first came to light a year ago, after the agency relocated a Coast Guard rescue helicopter that had been based there since 1987. That prompted a series of lawsuits from the city, the state and community members — some aimed at preserving rescue helicopter access for coastal tourists and the local fishing fleet, others at keeping ICE from setting up a jail.

On Friday, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, confirmed in federal court filings that it has abandoned plans to build a detention center in Newport and that it presently has no plans to build anywhere in Oregon. DHS also agreed to give Newport leaders at least 30 days’ notice if it resumes efforts to build a detention center there, through Aug. 1 of next year.

Officials in Newport, which joined Oregon in the lawsuit to keep ICE out, applauded the news.

“Our responsibility is to stand up for our residents, protect our community’s future and ensure that decisions affecting Newport are made with the transparency and accountability our community deserves,” Mayor Jan Kapla said.

DHS officials did not respond to an emailed request for a comment. In earlier court disclosures, the agency revealed that it had started working to bring a detention center to Newport by fall 2025, moving the Coast Guard helicopter to make room for that project, and originally expected to house detainees there as early as the start of 2026.

The helicopter has been back since December, after a judge ordered its return in a separate lawsuit that is still under way.

State Attorney General Dan Rayfield said Oregon will continue to fight to keep the rescue helicopter in Newport, and celebrated the end of the lawsuit over the planned detention center.

text:
Live updates: President Donald Trump holds rally in Perry ahead of Election Day

President Donald Trump is visiting Perry Saturday night.

PERRY, Georgia (41NBC/WMGT) – President Donald Trump is visiting Perry on Saturday, October 24, for a rally ahead of the November midterm elections.

The rally is scheduled to take place at Guardian Centers, located at 600 Perry Parkway. Doors are scheduled to open at 3:30 p.m., with the event beginning at 5:30 p.m. Trump is expected to deliver remarks at 7 p.m.

The rally was originally scheduled to take place in Macon before being moved to Perry.

41NBC is on the ground in Perry, covering the event as supporters gather ahead of the president’s arrival.

Check back here throughout the day for live updates from 41NBC.

8:57 p.m. President Donald Trump left the stage at Guardian Centers in Perry at 8:57 p.m., bringing Saturday night’s rally to a close.

Trump concluded his remarks by encouraging attendees to vote Republican in the November midterm elections before ending the night with his signature dance.

8:54 p.m. President Donald Trump told supporters the country’s “golden age” is underway as he began wrapping up his remarks in Perry.

Trump welcomed Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson and U.S. Senate nominee Mike Collins to speak during the closing portion of the rally.

He encouraged attendees to vote Republican in the November elections.

“We love you and everybody in this room,” Trump told supporters.

Trump concluded his remarks at approximately 8:56 p.m.

8:30 p.m. President Donald Trump told supporters in Perry that he would provide $5,000 payments to adult American citizens if Republicans maintain control of both the U.S. House and Senate in November.

Trump described the proposed payments as a “Trump dividend,” saying the money would come from tariff revenue.

He said the payments would be available to adult U.S. citizens, with the condition that recipients spend the money in the United States.

Trump also warned of economic consequences if Democrats win control of Congress, comparing the potential impact to the Great Depression.

The proposed payments are not currently guaranteed and would require congressional approval.

Trump also discussed his support among Hispanic voters, praising the community and claiming that border security is a major priority for Hispanic Americans.

8:22 p.m. President Donald Trump continued discussing his administration’s economic and national security priorities during Saturday’s rally.

Trump emphasized the importance of manufacturing vehicles in the United States.

He also highlighted military spending, claiming his administration invested $1 trillion in the armed forces.

“We have the greatest military in the world,” Trump told supporters.

Trump referenced U.S. military operations involving Venezuela and Iran while praising the strength of the armed forces.

He also discussed oil production, claiming the United States is receiving millions of barrels of oil.

8:15 p.m. President Donald Trump continued his remarks in Perry by praising his administration’s economic policies.

Trump claimed more Americans are working than ever before and said poverty rates among several demographic groups, including Hispanic, Native American, Asian American and African American populations, have reached historic lows.

He also credited tariffs with encouraging Audi to bring a manufacturing facility to Middle Georgia.

Trump claimed $22.2 trillion in investments have been committed to the United States because of his administration’s policies and said exports have reached record levels.

The president also discussed the growth of data centers, encouraging communities to welcome development while seeking financial benefits from companies building the facilities.

“You should be cool on data centers because you can make a fortune on them,” Trump said.

He argued that rejecting data center development could result in companies moving investments to China.

8:10 p.m. An Audi North America executive joined President Donald Trump on stage at Guardian Centers in Perry following the announcement of a new manufacturing facility planned for Peach County.

The announcement marks a proposed major investment in Middle Georgia’s manufacturing industry.

8:09 p.m. President Donald Trump announced during his rally in Perry that German automaker Audi plans to invest approximately $4 billion in a new manufacturing facility in Peach County.

According to the Mid-Georgia Gateway Joint Development Authority, the project is expected to create approximately 4,500 jobs.

The manufacturing facility is planned for the Middle Georgia Megasite in Peach County.

The announcement follows a regional partnership involving Peach, Macon-Bibb and Houston counties through the Mid-Georgia Gateway Joint Development Authority.

The proposed facility represents a major economic development announcement for Middle Georgia.

8:06 p.m. President Donald Trump turned his attention to the news media during Saturday night’s rally, criticizing reporters covering the event.

“The press is against me. They’re crooked. They’re false. Everything is fake,” Trump said.

As Trump referenced the media, attendees turned toward the designated press area and began booing journalists, including members of the 41NBC news team.

Trump continued criticizing news organizations during his remarks.

8:02 p.m. President Donald Trump praised his administration’s tariff policies during Saturday night’s rally in Perry.

Trump claimed tariffs have generated revenue for the United States and encouraged companies to keep operations and investments in the country.

He described tariffs as a major component of his administration’s economic strategy.

7:59 p.m. President Donald Trump told supporters that his administration has strengthened border security and reduced illegal immigration.

Trump claimed no immigrants had been admitted into the country illegally under his administration and said the nation’s murder rate was at its lowest level in 125 years.

He also praised Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Border Patrol agents.

Trump discussed inflation and energy costs, predicting oil prices would decline.

7:49 p.m. President Donald Trump told supporters in Perry that he believes he won three presidential elections rather than two.

“We won like nobody has ever seen,” Trump said.

Trump also discussed military investments made during his first term in office.

He praised support from evangelical and Christian voters, emphasizing the importance of religion in the United States.

“To be great, we need our religion back and much stronger,” Trump said.

The president also told supporters that he and first lady Melania Trump voted early in Florida.

7:22 p.m. President Donald Trump continued addressing supporters at Guardian Centers in Perry as attendees stood throughout the venue.

Trump criticized Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, calling him a disgrace to Georgia and accusing him of supporting policies that would weaken border security and Second Amendment protections.

Trump praised Republican Senate nominee Mike Collins, saying he believes Collins would better represent Georgia.

The president also discussed immigration, making disparaging remarks about immigrants from Somalia and other countries.

Trump claimed his administration had secured the southern border, prompting attendees to chant “USA! USA!”

He also discussed Greenland, claiming Denmark had signed an agreement concerning the territory.

Trump shifted to public safety, criticizing crime in cities led by Democrats, including Atlanta.

He claimed his administration’s intervention in cities such as Memphis, Tennessee, and New Orleans, Louisiana, had resulted in major reductions in crime.

Trump said crime had declined by 83% in Louisiana over six months and 84% in Memphis over eight months.

The president also discussed deploying National Guard troops in Washington, D.C., praising their work on public safety and describing efforts to address crime, homelessness and graffiti.

Trump claimed his administration had removed approximately 500 career criminals from Washington and said crime in the nation’s capital had significantly decreased.

He again criticized Ossoff’s immigration policies and praised Collins as a candidate who would protect American culture, religion and national security.

7:15 p.m. President Donald Trump took the stage at Guardian Centers in Perry shortly after 7:15 p.m., telling supporters he was glad to be back in Georgia.

“We’re going to send Mike Collins to the Senate,” Trump said.

Trump also criticized Democrats, telling supporters, “We’re going to crush the radical left Democrats.”

The president’s appearance comes ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, with Georgia’s U.S. Senate and governor’s races among the contests receiving national attention.

7:14 p.m. Country music star Jason Aldean took the stage at Guardian Centers in Perry to introduce President Donald Trump.

Trump appeared moments later to address supporters gathered for Saturday night’s rally.

6:18 p.m. Former U.S. Sen. Kelly Loeffler took the stage at Guardian Centers in Perry, encouraging attendees to vote in the November midterm elections.

Loeffler began her remarks by criticizing the news media, asking attendees to cheer for what she called the “fake news” outlets covering the event.

She encouraged supporters to take 20 minutes to vote, framing the upcoming election as a choice between “America first or America forgotten.”

Loeffler also praised President Donald Trump’s policies on manufacturing, immigration and election security.

“President Trump is replacing made in China with made in America,” Loeffler said.

She urged attendees to support Republican candidate Rick Jackson and described the election as a choice between “commonsense or crazy.”

Loeffler concluded by declaring that Georgia was “Trump country.”

6:08 p.m. Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Collins took the stage at Guardian Centers, criticizing Democratic incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff ahead of their November election matchup.

“I’m just an old blue collar trucker from Georgia,” Collins told the crowd.

Collins criticized Ossoff’s background, describing him as “a guy that wants to talk like Obama, look like a Kennedy, lie like Pinocchio.”

He also accused Ossoff of contributing to government shutdowns over disagreements involving immigration, health care and funding for immigration enforcement agencies.

Collins emphasized his working-class background and support for Trump’s “America First” agenda.

As he spoke, more supporters continued entering the venue, with some standing as seating areas filled.

The crowd broke into chants of “USA! USA!” during his remarks.

Collins encouraged attendees to vote in the upcoming election, prompting the crowd to chant, “Vote! Vote! Vote!”

5:57 p.m. U.S. Rep. Austin Scott, a Republican representing Georgia’s 8th Congressional District, addressed supporters at President Donald Trump’s rally in Perry.

Scott criticized immigration policies under former President Joe Biden, claiming millions of people entered the country illegally during his administration.

He also criticized diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, calling them “exclusion, not inclusion.”

Scott discussed federal spending overseas, prompting boos from some attendees.

“America is better than that,” Scott said.

He praised Trump’s handling of border security, tax policies and the military while also criticizing Democrats.

Supporters continued entering Guardian Centers during Scott’s remarks, with some standing inside the venue.

5:53 p.m. Houston Gaines, the Republican nominee for Georgia’s 10th Congressional District, took the stage at Guardian Centers in Perry.

Gaines referenced the University of Georgia’s football game against Florida, comparing the possibility of a football victory to a Republican victory in the November elections.

He also mentioned Democratic political figure Keisha Lance Bottoms, prompting boos from the crowd.

Gaines encouraged supporters to participate in early voting and bring others to the polls.

“We need everyone we know to get out and vote,” Gaines said.

5:49 p.m. Jim Kingston, the Republican nominee for Georgia’s 1st Congressional District, addressed attendees at President Donald Trump’s rally in Perry.

Kingston criticized Democrats and their efforts to gain political support in Georgia.

“The national left are obsessed with turning Georgia socialist blue. And I’m here to tell you that’s not happening,” Kingston said.

“The right leads to prosperity the left leads to hell,” he added.

Kingston also encouraged attendees not to apologize for loving their country.

5:43 p.m. John Cowan, the Republican nominee for Georgia’s 11th Congressional District, took the stage at Guardian Centers in Perry.

Cowan encouraged attendees to support Republican candidates Rick Jackson and Mike Collins in the upcoming November elections.

He also discussed his “America Patients First” health care proposal, calling for greater patient protections and competitive insurance markets that focus on patients’ overall health rather than only treating illness.

“I’ve got solutions, president trump has solutions, rick Jackson has solutions, mike collins has solutions,” Cowan said.

Cowan urged supporters to vote early and encourage friends, family members, church members and neighbors to participate in the election.

He also encouraged attendees to “invest in the conservative movement” by voting Republican.

Supporters continued entering the building and finding seats throughout his remarks.

5:30 p.m. Brandon Beach, the 46th treasurer of the United States, addressed the crowd at Guardian Centers in Perry ahead of President Donald Trump’s scheduled remarks.

Beach, who was appointed by Trump in 2025, oversees the U.S. Mint, Fort Knox and the Bureau of Engraving and Printing.

During his remarks, Beach discussed a new dollar coin featuring Trump, saying the coins would be available at banks next month.

“I want to challenge you and go to your favorite liberal coffee shop, use it and watch their heads explode,” Beach told attendees.

Beach also praised Trump’s economic policies, saying the administration is working to bring manufacturing jobs back to the United States.

He discussed the Republican-backed tax and spending legislation known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” highlighting provisions involving working families, tips and Social Security benefits.

5:27 p.m. The national anthem began at Guardian Centers in Perry as attendees gathered for President Donald Trump’s scheduled remarks.

5:26 p.m. Attendees recited the Pledge of Allegiance before breaking into chants of “USA! USA!”

The crowd cheered as the event continued.

5:21 p.m. President Donald Trump’s rally in Perry began with remarks about the importance of the nuclear family, followed by an opening prayer.

“Lord we ask you watch over these participants,” the speaker said during the prayer.

“Lord we are thankful we can assemble,” the speaker added.

4:55 p.m. Supporters continue making their way into Guardian Centers in Perry ahead of President Donald Trump’s scheduled remarks.

Attendees have been steadily entering the venue throughout the afternoon after passing through security checkpoints.

Music is playing inside the venue, and vendors are selling Trump merchandise as the crowd continues to gather.

2:54 p.m. 41NBC entered Guardian Centers in Perry on Saturday afternoon to prepare for President Donald Trump’s visit.

Supporters began making their way inside the venue after passing through security screenings conducted by the Secret Service and other security personnel.

1:20 p.m. Vendors were selling barbecue and grilling food while a man played an instrument nearby. Some attendees could also be heard chanting, “USA! USA!”

1:13 p.m. Blake Marnell told 41NBC he wants to see President Donald Trump bring more manufacturing jobs to the United States.

Marnell also expressed concerns about immigration, saying he believes many of the country’s problems are connected to the issue.

“We’d be in better shape if we had fewer illegal aliens in the country,” Marnell said.

1:06 p.m. Paulina and Blair Kendall spoke with 41NBC about Paulina’s 14-year journey to obtain U.S. citizenship.

Paulina, who came to the United States from the Philippines on a visa to marry her husband, said the process involved numerous challenges.

The couple said they support legal immigration but believe the process needs improvement, describing it as costly and difficult to navigate.

They said they hope President Donald Trump will address those challenges while continuing to enforce immigration laws.

1 p.m. April Carmichael told 41NBC she wants to see improvements in health care, particularly for people with limited financial resources.

Carmichael described President Donald Trump as “really good to people. And he helps a lot of people.”

She also said she hopes Trump will take another look at the death penalty and review cases more closely.

12:58 p.m. Dorothy Harp told 41NBC she wants to see improvements in overall affordability, including lower gas prices.

Harp also expressed support for stronger border security, saying she believes President Donald Trump has done a good job securing the nation’s borders.

She added that she would like Trump to eliminate property taxes for senior citizens.

12:55 p.m. Raven Armstrong told 41NBC she is strongly opposed to abortion and wants to see it eliminated.

“We’re christians so we are very for Israel and want to see it be a better place,” Armstrong said.

She also expressed concerns about gas prices and said she hopes they will decline.

“Trump is amazing. I love trump,” Armstrong said.

“He makes people happy. He knows how to make people happy,” she added.

12:53 p.m. Debbie Armstrong told 41NBC she wants to see improvements in the economy, lower gas prices and changes to immigration policies.

“I would like to see things go so much easier in Israel and the economy. Gas prices have got to come down but there everything’s got to be better in our country. I don’t like illegal people coming in. I just really wish that could stop,” Armstrong said.

12:42 p.m. Fred Proctor, 87, told 41NBC he wants President Donald Trump to continue military action against Iran.

Proctor said he wants Trump to “continue the war with Iran and turn that place into a glass factory.”

He also said he believes the country would be in a difficult position if Trump had not become president.

Proctor added that he wants the president to do more for older Americans, particularly when it comes to Social Security benefits.

“Social Security really isn’t that much money,” Proctor said.

12:40 p.m. Dianna Baker and James Smith told 41NBC they came to the United States as refugees from South Africa and are grateful to President Donald Trump.

“We are refugees and we came here legally so we want to thank Donald trump,” Smith said.

Baker said she would like to tell the president, “thank you for saving us.”

12:37 p.m. Rose Poole told 41NBC she wants President Donald Trump to focus on lowering gas prices and the overall cost of goods.

Poole said affordability is among her concerns as she attended Saturday’s rally in Perry.

12:33 p.m. Kevin McCain, 21, told 41NBC he arrived at Guardian Centers around 9:30 a.m. for President Donald Trump’s rally.

McCain, who said he is a first-time voter, identified gas prices and the economy as some of his top concerns.

He also said he wants to see Trump continue working toward his goal of “making America great again.”

41NBC is on the scene as preparations continue for the event.

The earliest attendee 41NBC spoke with said they arrived at approximately 6:30 a.m., hours before doors are scheduled to open.

Trump is expected to speak at 7 p.m.

title: Community members protest ICE detention of La Galette owner | News | kake.com
description: Supporters gathered outside La Galette French Bakery in Wichita’s Delano district Saturday, calling for owner Rob Attar to come home after he was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KAKE) — Supporters gathered outside La Galette French Bakery in Wichita’s Delano district Saturday, calling for owner Rob Attar to come home after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained him during an annual immigration check-in Thursday.
Rob’s wife, Krista Attar, wears her husband’s wedding rings while she waits for answers.
“I have his diamonds, and these are my diamonds,” she said. “So, he’s with me.”
Outside the bakery, supporters held signs, chanted “Bring Rob home!” and a band played music to show their support.
“I’m hoping that he just comes home and he just gets back in the kitchen and provides all the wonderful food here,” said Megan, a Wichita protester.
Attar has owned and worked at the French bakery for decades. Krista said he handled most of the cooking, baking and preparation.
“He is worth it. And I haven’t met anybody that didn’t like Rob in some way,” she said.
Krista described her husband as someone who was always willing to help others.
“He's incredibly talented; he's got a memory like a steel trap, so I am flapping without wings,” she said.
Attar has lived in the United States since 1993. According to reporting on court records, he pleaded guilty to 10 charges in a 2000 federal case involving drug and weapons offenses.
The charges included distributing marijuana, aiding and abetting marijuana and crack cocaine possession, possessing cocaine with intent to manufacture crack cocaine, and firearm offenses related to drug trafficking.
He was sentenced to six years in federal prison in January 2001. His attorney says Attar lost his green card in 2004 and has not had any further trouble with the law since.
The Department of Homeland Security says Attar lost his legal status because of his convictions.
Krista said her husband attended his regular immigration check-ins every year, and she expected Thursday’s appointment to be like the others.
“I thought this is going to be like every other year,” she said. “And then he called me moments later, just before I drifted off, and he said, ‘Krista, they got me. I have cuffs on.’”
The detention comes as immigration enforcement continues in Kansas and across the country.
In September, ICE reported 104 arrests during a three-day enforcement operation in southwest Kansas from Sept. 22-24.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office
said the operation targeted noncitizens with criminal histories.
Nationally, an analysis by
the Migration Policy Institute published Oct. 22
estimated about 660,000 deportations during the previous fiscal year. That was about 26% above the annual average under the Biden administration, according to the analysis. It also found that many people deported from inside the country had lived in the United States for years.
Megan said she believes Attar was doing his part in the community.
“You know, we’re all Americans and everything. We’re just doing our jobs, and that’s what he was doing. And he did everything by the book,” she said.
Attar is not the only Wichita business owner whose detention has raised concerns. Yessica Pena, the owner of Lady Burritos LLC, is currently being held at the ICE Detention Center in Chase County, along with her mother, sister, and brother.
Wichita City Council member Joseph Shepard said business owners such as Attar and Yessica are non-violent and contribute to the community.
“So long as they’re contributing to the vitality and the fabric of our community, and they’re not causing harm to others,” Shepard said, “Yessica and Rob are two individuals who are doing that, but ultimately, I think that our City Council, including the mayor, has a responsibility to affirm that.”
Shepard said he wants the City Council to discuss a resolution addressing the local immigration enforcement presence.
Krista said she wants leaders to review her husband’s case.

text:
An advocacy group says it wants Coeur d’Alene to take a stance against Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity.

Members of North-Idaho-based nonprofit Idaho for All told City Council members on Tuesday that an official resolution should locally restrict ICE’s “heavy-handed and intimidating” nationwide conduct.

“I understand that I may be young, but I can tell right from wrong,” said public commenter Kylon Keon.

Local partnerships with ICE first emerged earlier this year.

In July, the Post Falls Police Department became the first police department in Idaho to join the 287(g) task force program, which deputizes state and local officers to perform federal immigration enforcement. The partnership has so far led to multiple joint immigration arrests between ICE and Post Falls Police, with additional immigration arrests being made solely by Post Falls Police.

The Spirit Lake Police Department officially entered the task force program earlier this month.

Idaho for All members argued on Tuesday that ICE activity has led to more than 50,000 monthly arrests being made and that municipal partnerships with the federal agency divert local resources from normal tasks.

“The way that ICE has been able to run free and do things that clearly violate human rights does not make me feel safe when they come inside this community,” Keon said.

The Coeur d’Alene Police Department does not intend to join the 287(g) task force program or partner with ICE, Chief Greg Yeager said.

“It’s a tool that some agencies use,” he told the Coeur d'Alene Press in an email last month. “But not one we’ve had need of.”

Mayor Dan Gookin confirmed with the Coeur d’Alene Press that “our police department isn’t interested in the program for various reasons.”

Council member Christie Wood, a former Coeur d’Alene Police officer, told The Press on Wednesday that she would support passing a resolution but that the city’s police department would comply with federal laws.

“In Coeur d’Alene, we’ve always been a leader when it comes to human rights issues or issues that we think negatively affect our community,” she said. “Sometimes, we end up on an island.”

She also expressed concerns about the local police department working with ICE agents, questioning whether they’re “well-trained” and whether the city would be left “cleaning up the mess.”

Wood’s advocacy for the resolution, however, would need majority support to get on the city’s agenda.

“Whether it will end up on our agenda, I really don’t have a feel for,” she said. “Because that would take the mayor and the majority of council to get that on the agenda, but I don't know if that will happen.”

Idaho for All says it fights racism and civil injustice.

text:
Alejandro Mayorkas is the former U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security, serving under the Biden administration from 2021-2025. Prior to this role, Mayorkas worked in private law practice and as the U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California from 1998-2001 after being nominated by President Bill Clinton. From 2013-2016, Mayorkas then held the position of Deputy Secretary of Homeland Security under the Obama administration. As a 2026 Harvard Institute of Politics resident fellow, Mayorkas sat down with the HPR to discuss his career journey, immigration policy achievements, and criticisms of them.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Harvard Political Review: Please introduce yourself, your background growing up, and how you got into your career in public service.

Alejandro Mayorkas: I was born in Havana, Cuba, as was my sister and father. My mother was born in Romania and fled World War II and could only travel safely with her parents to Cuba. My father was educated in college and graduate school in the states, but returned to his home country to start a business there when the Cuban Revolution occurred. My father and mother did not want to raise their children under a communist regime, so we left Cuba and came to the United States. We lived in Miami for a few years, and my father, who really had to start all over again, found better work in Los Angeles. I grew up most of my life in Los Angeles. I always had a desire to enter government service, because this country gave everything to my family and created opportunities we would never have had in the country of my birth, and I wanted to give back.

HPR: That’s a great reason to go into public service. Coming from an immigrant family, you probably have a unique perspective on the issue of immigration and immigration policy. How do you think your personal and family experience influence the way you think about these issues?

AM: I certainly have a deep appreciation for this country’s identity as a place of refuge for those fleeing persecution. I understand the trauma that is involved when someone leaves the country of one’s birth, where one lives not necessarily by pure choice, but by compulsion, and I understand the fragility of life and the difficulties sometimes of the journey, and I also carry with me a deep and profound patriotism.

HPR: Following up on how you got into public service, one of the first roles you had in immigration was at the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). Can you discuss that role a little bit?

AM: My public service actually began in 1989 in the administration of George Bush, Sr. I started as a career government servant, as a federal prosecutor. I was a prosecutor trying criminal cases for about eight and a half years, and then I was promoted to the position of United States Attorney, which was a political appointment in the administration of President Clinton.

HPR: In that part of your life where you worked as a prosecutor and then got appointed by Clinton into that position, what work do you feel like you did in that capacity [that] shaped your thinking in the later part of your career?

AM: I did not focus on immigration law and policy. Before, I was focused on law enforcement and criminal justice, and subsequently, as the deputy secretary and the secretary. My portfolio was far broader than immigration exclusively, but I developed a reverence for the men and women in law enforcement, their mission of public safety, and their courage in sacrificing their own well-being to keep others safe.

HPR: What is your most proud accomplishment in your role at USCIS?

AM: Let me take a step back first. I had wanted to enter the Obama administration, continuing my work in criminal justice, but I had the good fortune of meeting Secretary Janet Napolitano, the Homeland Security Secretary in the first term of President Obama’s administration. She was very intrigued by my identity as an immigrant, but also my background in law enforcement. The premier responsibility in the Department of Homeland Security is the counterterrorism mission, and so my background in law enforcement, she felt, would facilitate the advancement of that mission. At USCIS, I created the Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate to better accomplish that mission. The creation and building of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program (DACA), was something I’m deeply proud of.

HPR: Regarding counterterrorism, what challenges did you feel navigating the landscape of that specific area, especially in a post-911 era?

AM: The gravity of the challenges cannot be overstated. I don’t think that the American public appreciates the extraordinary capacity in a post-9/11 world, the maturity of the counterterrorism architecture in the federal government, and the threats that were thwarted by not just DHS, but by the FBI, by the law enforcement and intelligence community — on the federal level, but also on the state and local level, working collaboratively. The threat streams are diverse, they are grave, and I have everlasting respect for the people who dedicate themselves to that mission, to fighting it.

HPR: I was curious to hear your thoughts on public concerns that arose during the initial counterterrorism efforts in the Bush administration, especially regarding privacy rights concerns and racial profiling of certain ethnic groups in the crackdown on protecting national security.

AM: In the Department of Homeland Security, we have a statutorily created Office of Civil Rights and Civil Liberties and an Office of Privacy. It is absolutely critical that we accomplish our national security mission, our national security imperative, while respecting individuals’ constitutional rights. Racial profiling is not acceptable. It is important that we do have to make certain sacrifices, not in terms of our constitutional rights, but certain sacrifices in our daily lives, in the service of our security mission. For example, we have to go through screening at airports. You don’t know a world when there weren’t magnetometers, the metal detectors at the airport.

HPR: I want to shift back to DACA for a moment, since you mentioned that was one of the biggest immigration policies in the Obama administration. How would you describe the policy?

AM: The policy is very clear in writing that individuals who were of a certain age and were brought to this country at a certain age, met certain requirements — such as no criminal history, etc — were eligible. People who met a certain criteria, because they really knew no other country other than the United States. Those of us in positions of leadership felt it would be unjust to return them by reason of their unlawful presence in the United States to a country that was completely foreign to them. The idea was to provide them with lawful presence. They didn’t necessarily have a path to citizenship, for example, but they had a lawful presence so that they could continue in their education and continue to work and contribute to society.

HPR: I want to hear your responses to some criticisms of DACA. Firstly, if people entered unlawfully in the first place — granted we’re talking about minors brought across the border — what incentives does it create if the system allows unlawful individuals, though minors, into the country? Secondly, from the direction of a lot of pro-immigration advocates, why not give these people a potential pathway to citizenship?

AM: With the second, Congress is the only body that can provide a path to citizenship for the DACA recipients, unless there is another path already existent in immigration law. That cannot be accomplished by executive action. Lawful presence was the Obama administration’s interpretation. Although that has been challenged in the courts: whether DACA is even lawful with the extension of a limited lawful presence, as distinguished from a path to citizenship. With respect to the first, these are minors, and so it’s quite different than an individual who enters the country essentially voluntarily, versus an individual who is brought to the country by their parents or an adult and isn’t necessarily making a knowing involuntary selection.

HPR: What about the issue of unaccompanied minors?

AM: We are a nation of immigrants, and we are a nation of laws. An individual who is brought here as an unaccompanied or arrives at the border as an unaccompanied child doesn’t necessarily have a basis to remain. They also have to have a legal basis to remain in the United States. They have to meet certain qualifications. For example, to qualify as a special immigrant juvenile — that’s a construct under immigration law. But let’s take a step back and look at the humanity of the situation and think about the desperation that a parent or parents must feel to send their child. It speaks of the desperation of humans in our world.

HPR: During the Biden administration, there was a lot of public debate over the DHS’s decision to discontinue at one point the “Remain in Mexico” policy. What are your responses to the criticisms of that decision, particularly people who say that it also corresponded with an uptick in attempts at border crossings?

AM: One, that was a campaign promise of presidential candidate Biden at the time, and he fulfilled that promise. That was an executive decision. Secondly, on the evidence that the “Remain in Mexico” policy was a significant factor in the reduction of individuals encountered at the border, the evidence doesn’t necessarily support that.

HPR: Beyond evidence and from a principled standpoint, why shouldn’t we incentivize other countries to accept some sort of responsibility for tackling the immigration crisis?

AM: That’s a very different question, and a very apt question. We did speak to leaders in other countries that were countries of transit, and said, “No, you need to enforce your borders, and you need to develop an asylum system in your country, and you cannot serve as a simple pass through to the United States.” During the Biden years, the subject of immigration was not exclusive to the United States; it was a mass migration globally, a human phenomenon of that magnitude and of that nature, requiring a multilateral response.

HPR: What’s your response to people who are fed up with the situation of ICE raids and have been calling to abolish ICE, specifically as someone who has led in a federal immigration position at DHS?

AM: I agree with the removal of individuals who are unlawfully present in the United States and pose a public safety threat to our communities. I am for immigration enforcement, focused on that priority area and some other priority areas, such as recent border crossers, which we made a priority in the Biden administration. The tactics we have seen employed over the last 18 months raise grave concerns. The focus on enforcement is not based exclusively on certain priority areas, but is casting a wide net, even on people who have been here for many, many years and have been valuable in contributing to our communities.

I do not agree with the notion of abolishing ICE. ICE is a very able immigration and law enforcement agency with varied missions. Homeland Security investigations is a criminal investigative arm within ICE that fights the fentanyl epidemic, the pandemic of online child sexual exploitation and abuse, and investigates and prosecutes customs violations. We need enforcement and removal operations from ICE. We do have people unlawfully present in the United States who pose a risk to our community and should be deported.

HPR: What was your reaction to the political firestorm over the GOP-led impeachment trial of you?

text:
Costa Rica cannot fully meet its human rights obligations to the migrants the United States is deporting here from other countries, according to a report by two international advocacy groups. The report recommends that Costa Rica suspend the arrangement and accept no further transfers unless it can guarantee the resources and safeguards needed to receive more people.

The study, Left in Limbo: Emerging Challenges for Third Country Nationals Forcibly Transferred by the United States to Costa Rica, was published Oct. 1 by Refugees International and the Global Strategic Litigation Council. It was written by Rachel Schmidtke, senior advocate for Latin America at Refugees International, and Natasha Pérez Tümmler, regional litigator for the Americas at the council.

It examines the first months of a memorandum of understanding Costa Rica signed with the United States in March. Under the agreement, Costa Rica accepts up to 25 people a week who are not Costa Rican and who were removed from the United States, with Washington covering costs through funding to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

The report’s central conclusion is that the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería (DGME), the immigration agency, cannot fully meet its national and international human rights obligations toward the people it receives. “Once people are in Costa Rica, the State has a responsibility to ensure that their rights are effectively protected,” Pérez Tümmler said.

Based on 21 interviews with deportees conducted from April through the summer, the groups found that migrants struggle to obtain identity documents, find work, get legal advice and stay in contact with their families. Nine of the 21 had not received Costa Rican identity documents confirming their legal status.

Some of those interviewed held humanitarian migration status and work authorization, but found that employers and banks did not always recognize the paperwork. The authors note that their sample is not representative of everyone received or of every nationality. According to the report, 22 flights had brought 460 people of 39 nationalities to Costa Rica by the time of publication. Of those first 460, 210 were still in here as of Sept. 25, including 37 waiting for assisted voluntary return.

Figures from the immigration agency as of Oct. 2 put the total at 478 people on 23 flights. Of those, 183 remained here, 26 were in the process of returning and 269 had left. They came mainly from Mexico, China, Colombia and Brazil. That marks a steady increase from early September, when government figures showed 424 people had arrived on 20 flights and 187 were still in Costa Rica.

The report argues that the government did not adequately plan for the administrative and financial consequences of receiving people who may need long-term protection. It also says the IOM has become the main point of contact for the deportees, even though responsibility for their rights rests with the Costa Rican state.

The groups also object to limits on outside access. During an official visit by civil society organizations to one of the hotels housing deportees on Aug. 10, the DGME prevented confidential conversations with the migrants, according to the report.

Two days later, Omer Badilla Toledo, vice minister of interior and police and director general of the DGME, notified the organizations by letter that future visits were denied, despite an agreement to hold them monthly. The groups say the restriction cuts migrants off from information and independent legal advice at the moment they are deciding whether to stay, return home or try to move elsewhere.

Badilla rejected the report’s conclusions earlier this month, denying that Costa Rica is failing its human rights obligations. He acknowledged that some people remain here while their immigration status is decided and attributed the buildup to differences in how long each person stays.

Badilla said between 55% and 60% of those received have already left Costa Rica. He said the IOM funds the assistance with U.S. money while his agency supervises the process and remains the regulating authority. He also said a process will be set up to issue DIMEX residency cards to those who stay and announced a U.S.-funded integration program offering Spanish classes, job-search help and housing support that would begin enrolling participants in the coming weeks.

Badilla defended the hotel visit restrictions as a privacy measure, saying migrants are free to speak with journalists outside the hotels. He said the agency has faced no legal proceedings related to deportees received under the agreement, and that he respects the report’s view but does not share it.

The report’s broader recommendation is that the U.S. third-country agreements be ended altogether. Costa Rica is one of several countries taking part in that wider U.S. practice of third-country deportations, though unlike deportees held in some other countries, those sent here are housed in hotels rather than detained and may move around freely.

The call to suspend the agreement comes just as the government prepares to launch its integration program. Whether the people who stay can get the documents they need to work, open bank accounts and rent homes will shape whether Costa Rica remains a transit point or becomes a lasting destination for people the United States has removed.

text:
Written by Lauren J. Mapp, Edited by Kate Morrissey

Sen. Alex Padilla said he observed concerning conditions at the Immigration and Customs Enforcement holding facility in downtown San Diego on Friday morning during an unannounced oversight visit.

Around 8 a.m. at the Edward J. Schwartz Federal Building, where, in the basement, ICE operates holding cells intended for short-term detention, Padilla observed poor light and a cell rendered unusable due to plumbing problems, according to spokesperson Edgar D. Rodriguez.

He said the rooms did not seem appropriate to hold people for extended periods as they lacked proper sleeping accommodations and showers, and supplies seemed to be rundown and outdated.

At a press briefing outside after the visit, Padilla said that members of Congress — including those from San Diego and across California — have visited ICE detention facilities to confirm whether conditions are compliant with safety standards.

“(We) ask all the basic questions about not just access to food and water, but access to medical attention, access to counsel, ability to communicate with families and whatnot to make sure that those fundamental rights are being respected and that facilities are in compliance with the standards that they're supposed to maintain,” Padilla said.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

The senator said that during his visit, there were four people detained in the holding facility who had been brought there Friday morning.

“We understand that we should expect those numbers to go up throughout the course of the day because of the enforcement actions happening after school drop offs,” he said.

Padilla said he was not allowed to speak with any of the people detained there.

Rodriguez said Padilla also raised concerns over accountability at the facility after learning during his visit that ICE contracts with private operators to provide services at the facility rather than managing them directly.

Reports about conditions in ICE detention facilities and a recent increase in immigration arrests in San Diego County prompted Padilla’s unannounced visit.

“The senator remains concerned and is doubtful about whether this facility is adequately equipped to safely and appropriately accommodate individuals in ICE custody,” Rodriguez said via text Friday afternoon.

While ICE hasn’t publicly acknowledged it, media outlets have reported an increase in immigration arrests in San Diego as part of the 45-day “Operation Safe California” leading up to next month’s midterm election.

San Diego activists and immigration advocates have also noticed increased ICE activity locally.

Last week, more than 50 people gathered to protest ICE following recent arrests and ICE sightings at or near schools in City Heights, including Hoover High School, Ibarra Elementary School and John Marshall Elementary School.

Padilla said his office has received a significant uptick in calls related to people being detained by immigration officials in the region, especially during school drop offs.

“That says a lot about the priorities of this administration,” Padilla said. “It is not a focus on the worst of the worst as they so often claim to be. They are picking up people without those dangerous violent criminal backgrounds or records for the sake of meeting those arbitrary goals.”

He said that if Democrats take control of the House of Representatives, Senate or both chambers as a result of the midterm election, he expects legislators to push for more accountability from ICE and the Trump administration.

HERTFORD COUNTY, N.C. (WITN) — An ICE protest and vigil was held at Rivers Correctional Institute on Saturday afternoon, just a month after the previous one, which organizers say kicks off a nationwide plan for protest vigils across the country for the next couple of weeks.

“All the things that’s happening around our nation kind of breaks my heart, and I just didn’t want it to be in my backyard,” Cynthia Stephens said, a Hertford County resident.

Stephens was just one of many protesters marching Saturday afternoon to protest the upcoming reopening of the GEO-owned Rivers Correctional Institute as a detention facility for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The immigration detention facility is set to reopen soon, anticipating a capacity of 1,320 beds, spanning over 257 acres.

Most arrived by bus from places like Raleigh and Durham to participate, including Raleigh resident Randy Jones.

“We’re bringing Raleigh here to say we don’t like this in our state and we’d like them to get out,” Jones said.

Stephens says she’s grateful to see support from across the state in Hertford County.

“It makes me feel wonderful it makes me know that lots and lots of people are feeling the same way I do, and I’m not in this alone,” Stephens said.

National vigil organizer for the Workers Circle, Jessica Burroughs, says this is part of a national movement in honor of the Day of the Dead and lives lost while in detention centers.

“It will take all of us. Locals, North Carolinians and beyond to stand up and say this is not right,” Burroughs said.

Burroughs says her organization plans to hold another vigil here Dec. 5 and says they will continue to hold monthly vigils here until the center closes.

Organizers say 30 cities across the country will hold protest vigils in conjunction with the Day of the Dead or Dia de los Muertos tradition of honoring loved ones.

text:
When footage of a man being hit by federal immigration officers’ SUV in Northern California became public, the Department of Homeland Security responded by saying the man had jumped on the vehicle’s hood.

Local police raised doubts about federal officials’ account as they announced a criminal investigation into Tuesday morning’s incident involving the pedestrian, 37-year-old Antonio Moreida, citing video footage that contradicted DHS’ statement.

Footage from a nearby surveillance camera, a bystander’s cellphone recording and Moreida’s GoPro, which had already been made public at the time of the agency’s statement, told a different story of what happened on a residential street in Woodland, an agricultural city just outside of Sacramento. The incident is the latest in which DHS’ account has been contradicted by officials and video evidence amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Police contradict ICE account

In a statement Wednesday morning, DHS said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers didn’t hit a pedestrian.

“An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement in response to CNN’s request for information. “The agitator slid off the hood. ICE immediately contacted EMS and the Woodland Police Department. Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation,” apparently accusing the man of faking his injuries.

After the incident on Tuesday, Woodland Police Chief Ryan Kinnan said in a statement he found footage of the incident troubling. Investigators were working to gather evidence and statements and to review available audio and video related to the incident, including video taken from multiple perspectives, police said in a Facebook post. Woodland Police didn’t take part in the ICE operation the agents were involved in that morning, police said.

The following day, Woodland Police called DHS’ account “inconsistent.”

“Certain claims made in the DHS statement are inconsistent with the video evidence obtained and reviewed by Woodland Police investigators,” Kinnan said in an update Wednesday. The update said investigators had established, based on video evidence, the pedestrian had been hit by the vehicle driven by ICE agents and that he had not jumped onto the vehicle.

The local police department is conducting a criminal investigation into the events leading up to the collision and the actions of those involved, Kinnan said Wednesday.

By Thursday, in response to follow-up questions about the video footage, federal officials no longer said the person jumped on the hood.

“This individual chose to directly impede a law enforcement action and stand in the middle of an active road,” an ICE spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. “Our officers deliberately attempted to avoid making contact with this anti-ice protestor and drive around him, while also braking. We strongly urge individuals to not stand in the middle of active roadways while a law enforcement vehicle is approaching.”

Footage reviewed by CNN shows Moreida, a Woodland resident, in the middle of the street at around 9:40 a.m. Tuesday. Moreida said he had responded to a call that morning by NorCal Resist, a group which monitors immigration operations, about ICE activity in Woodland, he told CNN on Tuesday, hours after the incident.

He said he was trying to record agents’ unmarked vehicles. He had been recording one vehicle, standing on the car’s driver’s side, when it turned left and drove off, which he said pushed him into the middle of the street.

Video from Moreida’s GoPro shows him following a black Dodge Durango with tinted windows as it drives down the street.

Then, he said he heard a loud engine before seeing the agents’ black Chevy Tahoe drive toward him, which is shown in his GoPro footage, though the video has no audio.

Down the street, the bystander’s cellphone video shows the Durango pass the Tahoe, which has tinted windows, on a residential street. In the video’s background, people can be heard blowing whistles, presumably to alert people nearby of ICE’s presence in the neighborhood.

The ICE agent driving the Tahoe moves toward Moreida and between the cars with its brake lights on, footage shows. In the bystander’s video, Moreida isn’t yet visible.

The SUV’s wheels begin to turn to the left only a few feet from Moreida, a wider angle of surveillance footage from a home shows.

“The individual was standing in the street long enough that a reasonable person should be able to see them and recognize that they were there,” said Ryan Schwank, a former ICE attorney and training instructor who reviewed the videos provided by CNN.

Schwank also took issue with ICE’s characterization that Moreida was standing in the middle of an active road and impeding law enforcement’s actions.

“When we’re looking at Antonio’s actions, he’s not impeding. He’s not standing blocking the vehicle from moving,” he said. “He’s standing and filming, and that’s well within his bounds to do. He’s well within his rights to do what he was doing.”

Moreida’s GoPro appears to show when he’s struck by the front-right side of the vehicle before he drops his camera.

“Before I knew it, it just drove straight into me,” he said. “I took the hood of the car straight to the chest. It initially took the wind out of me and I couldn’t breathe.”

The surveillance footage shows Moreida take a step back when he appears to make contact with the car. He is then seen falling toward the ground, off the front-right side of the car, the footage shows.

In the bystander’s footage from behind, a screeching noise is heard before the Tahoe jolts forward. The SUV veers left before straightening out, the video shows.

The bystander’s angle shows the Tahoe brake lights turn off. Moreida is then visible in the bystander’s video, falling to the ground and rolling, first on his back with his legs swinging above him. He then appears seated upright in the nearby surveillance footage, this time facing the sidewalk.

The SUV’s brake lights turn back on briefly before it drives farther down the street, the surveillance footage shows.

The driver, an ICE agent, stayed near the scene and called local dispatch, Woodland Police said. The agent cooperated with police during the initial investigation, the local agency said.

Moreida said an off-duty EMT provided him aid at the scene before Woodland Police officers arrived. Federal agents didn’t approach him after he was hit by the SUV, he said.

Moreida said he was eventually transported to the hospital. He said he had X-rays taken of his swollen knees, where he said he had the most damage. In addition, he said he has bruises and cuts from the road.

ICE has reduced the amount of training for officers, including in vehicle operations and how to deal with confrontations, said Schwank, who is now an agency whistleblower after resigning in February.

On Saturday, ICE said it is instituting additional training for officers.

“ICE training will now be extending to 72 days. The change, effective June 2, 2026, will apply to all new academy classes beginning July 1, 2026. All graduates of the previous academy curriculum will attend follow-on training at the Advanced Field Officer Training Program,” an ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement to CNN. “As we have said all along, ICE training does not end when recruits graduate from the academy. ICE officers go through a rigorous on-the-job training and mentorship. This additional training is tracked online and monitored closely.”

Local officials call for investigations

Soon after it became public, local officials expressed dismay over the incident, which occurred in a rural Northern California community that’s about half Latino. More than a fifth of the population is foreign-born, according to US Census estimates.

“The lack of truth in the Department of Homeland Security’s statement is evidenced by video taken at the scene,” Woodland Mayor Tom Stallard said in a statement issued Wednesday. “All of us can be assured that the Police Department’s investigation into this disturbing incident will continue to be speedy, fair, and impartial.”

US Rep. Mike Thompson, a Democrat whose district includes Woodland, said ICE’s statements about the facts surrounding the incident were disappointing but not surprising.

“ICE has a history of trying to hide the facts and mislead the public,” he told CNN. “And this is another example of that happening.”

title: The Small-Town Cop Who Helped ICE Deport His Ingram, Texas, Neighbors - ProPublica
authors: Francesca D’Annunzio, McKenzie Funk, Kirsten Luce

Martinez told us about a moment when she watched him detain one of her cousins.
Later that day, Luján saw a Facebook post showing a familiar face in a mug shot: Carranza’s.
