text:
The new patrol officer parked his black Dodge Charger outside a house off Main Street and approached on foot. A Mexican ballad was playing. Someone had called in a noise complaint, claiming it sounded as if people were fighting.

But as the officer, Jaron Alexander, got closer, he found nothing of the sort. A middle-aged woman greeted him as her daughter, Joanna Martinez, petite and visibly pregnant, looked on. “What kind of party are you all having?” she remembers him asking. Behind her were three generations of an extended family. They were celebrating a 3-month-old’s baptism over pozole verde, horchata and beers.

Alexander ran some IDs and found no issues. The music wasn’t even that loud, he thought. He told them to have a good night, and then he left.

That encounter, in early October last year, was the first of many that Alexander and Martinez would have in tiny Ingram, Texas, a 1.5-square-mile town of 1,900 people beside the Guadalupe River. But it was the only one before Ingram signed an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that would roil the town and tear Martinez’s family apart.

“Her and I, at the beginning, I felt like we were running into each other all the time,” Alexander told us, in one of eight conversations over four months that offer a rare window into the thoughts of one of the local police officers on the front lines of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

In a town as small as Ingram, drivable in five minutes end to end, more run-ins were probably inevitable. Later that October, Alexander pulled over a work truck for rolling through a stop sign, and soon there Martinez was, demanding that he let her friends go rather than let immigration take them. He didn’t. He pulled over another driver in November who turned out to be her cousin, the father of the baby they celebrated at the baptism party. Alexander handed him over to immigration agents as well.

He pulled over Martinez herself a few weeks before she was due to give birth, she says, surprising her when he knew her name and the type of car she typically drove. He warned her that the car’s window tint was illegal and let her go. After that, he says, he caught a glimpse of her and her husband and their newborn daughter in the toy aisle at Walmart. Martinez told us she doesn’t think it was even her that day — her baby girl was then just days old, and she couldn’t imagine running errands with her so soon. But in Alexander’s memory, she was shopping for Christmas presents, just like him.

Alexander, who is in his mid-30s, with dirty blond hair already turning gray, says he didn’t come back to Ingram to help deport his neighbors. In his telling, he just ended up making it part of his job. The town was where he started his law-enforcement career years earlier, before he took a better-paying position with the county, as a sheriff’s deputy. But things recently started to fall apart, first in his marriage, next at the sheriff’s office: A 185-page internal investigation found that he had an affair before his divorce was final and used a county vehicle to carry it out, then lied about it all. He says the investigator called him an “embarrassment to the profession.” The sheriff’s office fired him. (Alexander said at the time, and again to us, that he did not have the affair.)

Ingram’s Police Department took him back just when its new chief — its eighth in five years — was under pressure from the City Council to do more: more traffic stops, more citations, more arrests, more numbers. Alexander says he told the chief that the sheriff’s office had a deal with ICE and that Ingram should look into it; maybe it could help the department grow. “Blame me,” he eventually told people. “It’s my fault in a way.”

Donald Trump had retaken the presidency with a promise to carry out “the largest deportation in the history of our country.” America was still figuring out what that meant. Finding and expelling up to 4% of the U.S. population — the 14 million residents who are estimated to be undocumented — wasn’t something a few thousand ICE agents could do on their own.

Underway in Chicago that fall, and soon in Minneapolis, was one version of how the administration could try to do it: masked agents from across the federal government surging into a liberal city to round up immigrants, beating back — even killing — the citizens who tried to stand in their path.

But a quieter kind of surge was spreading across the country at the same time. In September 2025, ICE announced new incentives for a partnership program known as 287(g). The program’s most aggressive form, the so-called task force model, which Ingram opted in to, enlists local police officers as deputy immigration agents, and the new incentives included a $100,000 vehicle stipend, a $7,500 equipment stipend for every participating officer, quarterly performance bonuses and funding to help cover officer salaries and overtime. “By joining forces with ICE,” the announcement read, “you’re not just gaining access to these unprecedented reimbursement opportunities — you’re becoming part of a national effort to ensure the safety of every American family.”

Alexander completed an online course with ICE a few weeks after the baptism party, qualifying him for time-and-a-half pay whenever he helped the agency pick up immigrants. Here in the Texas Hill Country, he soon became the local face of the national crackdown.

Ingram was just starting to recover from its worst natural disaster in a century, the flood that summer that killed at least 139 people up and down the Guadalupe River, including 25 girls at Camp Mystic. In the riverbed, towering bald cypress trees now stood at a lean, their branches swept back by a 30-foot surge of water and mud, their trunks still plastered with debris. As construction workers rebuilding the community traveled to their jobsites via Junction Highway, Ingram’s five-lane main thoroughfare, a black Charger began stopping them before they could get there.

Within three months of the baptism party, Alexander and Ingram’s other patrol officer had delivered at least 70 people to immigration agents, picking off what the police chief called a “dumbfounding” number of undocumented drivers. Within a year, they would hand over the equivalent of 10% of Ingram to ICE.

The weight of what Alexander was doing started to settle on him after Christmas. He says he was out patrolling as one of his new ICE handlers, a man in a ball cap and dark glasses, hovered nearby in an unmarked SUV. Around lunchtime, Alexander followed two Latino men in a 2008 GMC truck for several blocks before stopping them, they recall him saying, for failing to signal a turn.

A young man sat in the passenger seat. Alexander checked his papers along with the driver’s and determined that both were undocumented. The agent in the unmarked SUV rolled up behind them. Alexander realized who the man in the passenger seat was only after Martinez arrived in tears. It was her husband, Ulices Macias, the father of her newborn daughter.

“I don’t normally do this,” Martinez recalls Alexander telling her, “but I’m going to open up the car. I’m going to take the handcuffs off him.” He let the family have a moment together. In a video taken by Martinez’s younger sister, Alexander stood by, expressionless, as Martinez embraced Macias by the rear door of the Charger. He watched Macias cradle his 2-week-old baby girl, swaddled in a white blanket, and hug Martinez’s 4-year-old son, his stepson.

Then the ICE agent put the handcuffs back on Martinez’s husband, wrapped a chain around his waist and led him away. Alexander says Martinez threw herself to the ground and sobbed.

Images of the family he broke up shortly after Christmas would intrude on Alexander’s thoughts for months, he told us. But it didn’t keep him from doing his job. His next shift came a few days after he handed over Macias, and he was back in the Charger, back to stopping cars on Junction Highway.

“Mini Guanajuato”

Alexander says he didn’t always want to be a police officer. He describes himself as “kind of a chameleon.” He grew up in nearby Harper, tried a few different colleges without graduating and spent his 20s cycling though jobs in freight logistics, pest control and insurance.

Still seeking his calling, he arranged a ride-along with a police officer outside Austin. What sold him on policing was the suburban officer’s power to enforce the law as he saw fit. That day, they pulled over a woman who had a warrant out for her arrest. She was coming back from the store with children and groceries in the back seat.

“You can use your discretion,” Alexander recalls the officer telling him. Wouldn’t they be doing more harm if they took her? What would the kids do without their mother? And wouldn’t it all create more paperwork? The officer let her go. Alexander imagined himself making the same kinds of judgment calls. In 2021, he enrolled in the police academy.

Even before the floods, tensions were rising in Ingram. Hundreds of Mexican immigrants and their families had settled there in recent decades as an increasingly militarized border made it harder for seasonal ranch hands and other workers to cross back and forth. Latinos would come to make up 45% of its population, and some residents began affectionately calling Ingram “mini Guanajuato,” after the central Mexican state where many have roots. Yet when Alexander returned, Ingram’s City Council still consisted of six white men.

A council faction led by Claud Jordan, now the town’s mayor, and Rocky Hawkins, now the mayor pro tem, came to power in November 2020, in a revolt against a new sewer project. They abolished Ingram’s city administrator position and took direct control of the Police Department, cycling through chief after chief. Five former city employees say Hawkins regularly used racist slurs for Mexicans. Four say that he pressured the city to go after Latinos through code enforcement or targeted patrols, and two say that Jordan did, too. One of the employees recalls Hawkins complaining that Mexicans were “taking over Ingram.” (Hawkins and Jordan each declined to speak on the record or address detailed questions we sent them by email. In a brief text-message exchange, Hawkins said that none of it was right but declined to offer any specific concerns.)

These were the men the new chief, Dustin Breshears, had to answer to as ICE revived the task force program, which had been shut down for a dozen years until the day Trump returned to office in January 2025. ICE, under President Barack Obama, had phased out the program after some of the first sheriffs to participate in it, including Joe Arpaio of Maricopa County, Arizona, used it to disproportionately target Latinos in their communities. Investigations by the Department of Justice found that deputies in the task force program pulled over Latino drivers at up to nine times the rate of other drivers and that some retaliated violently against people who accused them of racial profiling. But now, under Trump, any law-enforcement agency, no matter how troubled or small, was encouraged to sign up.

Breshears began appearing at City Council meetings armed with statistics: number of arrests since the last meeting, number of traffic stops, number of cleared cases from the backlog of hundreds he inherited — and number of what he called “deportations.” (He later explained this was his imprecise shorthand for “immigration-related enforcement activities.”) At the council’s October 2025 meeting, held a couple of weeks after Alexander showed up at the Martinez family’s baptism party, Breshears reported a remarkable 162 traffic stops by Ingram’s two patrol officers — Alexander and Christian Perez, who was 25 — in just 20 days. (Perez declined to comment.) The officers made more stops in two months than the department had made in the entire previous year. The City Council gave Breshears an $18,000 raise.

Before Breshears arrived and Alexander returned in August 2025, the weekly blotter in The West Kerr Current, the local newspaper, documented the humdrum of community policing: loose dogs, neighborhood disputes, code violations. Then, suddenly, it was filled with drivers stopped for defective brake lights, damaged license plates, cracked windshields, illegal window tints or other unspecified “equipment violations.”

Breshears and Alexander strongly deny targeting Latinos. “It’s honestly not what’s happening,” Breshears says, noting that his half brother, wife and daughters have Mexican heritage. Ingram’s traffic stops were simply up across the board, he says, so more Latinos were getting stopped. He shared statistics showing that stops of Latinos were proportional to their share of the population.

Alexander, who on top of his roughly $70,000 base salary was now logging dozens of hours per month for ICE, told us the same. “I don’t care who’s in the car,” he says. “I really don’t.”

“El Charger Negro”

As the ICE program took hold in Ingram, warnings about Alexander and his black Charger — the department has several — spread through the Hill Country and far beyond. Groups on Facebook and WhatsApp seemed to track his every move. The Charger was outside Rita’s taco shop. The Charger was near Dollar General. The Charger was parked by the church. A member of one particularly active Facebook group texted him screenshots, and he scrolled through blurry photos of himself looming behind work trucks or leaning over car windows.

Many Latino motorists trying to reach worksites up the Guadalupe began driving an extra 90 minutes each day to avoid the section of Junction Highway that Alexander patrolled. Ranch hands began sleeping at their employers’ properties in nearby Hunt, coming to town only when they knew — or hoped — that Ingram’s officers would be off duty. Residents were rattled the day a Customs and Border Protection helicopter hovered above town and the elementary school went into lockdown as the police hunted for a Mexican man who had run from one of Alexander’s traffic stops.

One family notarized guardianship papers, in case the parents were detained and the children left behind. One woman swore Alexander showed up outside a memorial service and asked people for IDs. Another woman said he detained her and her husband when they returned home from church. Parties dwindled. Invite lists shrank. People began to move away, to Kerrville and San Antonio, and Alexander’s reputation reached as far as La Ceja, a village in the mountains of central Mexico, where an elderly resident said he and his neighbors were familiar with the Texas town’s police. “El Charger negro,” he said, with a knowing nod. He estimated that some 20 or 30 people in the village were recent deportees from Ingram.

Alexander’s fortunes seemed to rise as the Martinez family’s fell. With her husband gone, Joanna Martinez couldn’t afford payments on the trailer they shared. She and their infant and her 4-year-old son moved back into her childhood bedroom in her mother’s crowded home, where several relatives and their children also lived. She tried to stay connected with her husband, Macias, via WhatsApp calls while working as much as she could as a house cleaner to keep afloat. “I can’t lock myself up in my room and just cry,” Martinez says.

Winter for Martinez and her family brought a string of dark incidents. The January arrest of her cousin near the carwash as she drove to pick up her children from school. A canceled baby shower for her older sister, Jazmin, over a rumor that the Charger planned to show up. Another cousin, himself the father of a newborn, stopped and taken right in front of her mother’s house as Martinez watched.

A half dozen of the attendees from the October baptism party would soon be gone from Ingram, after being detained and deported or leaving to join relatives who had been. Some people had gotten wind that Alexander was making money off his enforcement. When a Spanish-language Facebook page shared a photo of him questioning the passenger of a beige Ford pickup, someone posted an animated image in the comments: a stack of green dollar bills growing taller and taller in an endless loop.

Alexander received his first ICE payments in early December. In January, as the country’s attention turned to the violent immigration crackdown in Minneapolis, he was often spending three or four hours a day and sometimes entire shifts working on behalf of the federal agency. By the time federal authorities announced a drawdown in Minneapolis on Feb. 12, Alexander had already made $3,264.46 from his task force hours, according to his pay stubs.

Ingram was by then one of more than 750 task force model partners around the country, up from not quite 500 when it signed up in October. At least 43 million U.S. residents, according to an analysis of ICE records by the legal data firm Titus Consulting, already lived in a county with an active task force agreement. Alexander was one of thousands of deputized officers in Texas alone.

In interviews, Alexander described the immigration system he was enforcing as “skewed” and “weird,” but he saw himself as largely separate from these concerns. “If you’re taking federal money to do a job,” he says, “I think you should do the job.”

Still, he seemed to struggle with the contradictions of his role. He told us he sometimes shared his lunch with the people he detained and that he let them hold on to their phones to call loved ones from the rear seat of the Charger. He handcuffed them with their hands in the front rather than the back so they could use their hands.

Martinez told us about a moment when she watched him detain one of her cousins. He allowed the man’s wife and children to hug him goodbye and waited until his 7-year-old daughter wasn’t looking to handcuff him. To Martinez, it seemed as if Alexander was trying to prove to her that he wasn’t a bad person. “But I’m not going to fall for it,” she says.

There was a protest in Ingram the following day against Trump’s mass deportations. Martinez decided to go. As she stood among a few dozen protesters waving a handmade sign with the name “J. Alexander” circled and crossed out, she saw him drive by again and again.

A few weeks later, Katie Winer, the leader of the group that staged the protest, was following the Charger after Alexander detained another immigrant in a traffic stop. He approached her car and threatened to arrest her if she followed him in the future, on charges of interfering with public duties. But he also seemed to want to talk, and she recorded him as they discussed what was going on in Ingram. “I think you guys are making a bigger deal of it than they are,” he said of the people he handed over to ICE. The only outliers were “loudmouths” like Martinez and “her little crew.”

Winer interjected that Martinez’s husband was the family’s breadwinner, and it was Alexander’s actions that tore them apart.

“My actions did not,” Alexander said. “His actions did. I made a traffic stop. He was here illegally. That’s not my fault.”

Still, Alexander’s uncertainty seemed to be growing. In March, another of Martinez’s cousins confronted him outside the taco shop, pressing him about Macias as she filmed with her phone.

“If I’m being 100% honest,” he said, “I don’t enjoy when families are separated, like with the Joanna situation. That kind of fucked me up.”

“I Voted to Get the Bad Guys Out”

A month later, as Ingram’s handoffs to ICE surpassed 100 people, another video of Alexander circulated among a small group of community members. It showed an evening traffic stop, at least the fifth stop Alexander made that day. He had followed a silver Ford F-250 from the highway until it pulled into the gravel driveway of a mobile home. There, the man in the passenger seat, a landscaper named Victor Ramirez Hernandez, tried to hurry inside. Alexander grabbed him before he could get there.

The truck’s driver pulled out his phone and began filming. “Why are you arresting him?” he asked.

“I’m not,” Alexander answered, struggling to place handcuffs on Ramirez as he squirmed. “I’m detaining him.” Then he wrapped his hands around the laborer’s chest, lifted him off the ground and slammed him down on the driveway. “I played nice with you, and now I’m done,” he said. He straddled Ramirez and cuffed his hands behind his back.

“He’s bleeding because you hit him,” the driver said evenly. They argued back and forth.

“You’re an idiot,” Alexander said, his face reddening. “Shut up. The more you talk it’s just making you look stupider.” (Alexander declined to comment on this incident. Breshears, who reviewed body-camera footage, says Alexander’s use of force was justified to control a potentially dangerous situation.)

Acrimony pulsed through Ingram that spring. In the Latino community, family members and neighbors accused one another of snitching, which Alexander says did happen. Young women accused one another of having affairs with him, which he denies, insisting that people just misinterpreted his attempts to be kind. “I’m friendly with the people that I meet,” he says, “especially when they’re friendly to me.”

One subject of these rumors was Martinez. She and her older sister scoffed at them. “He’s taken our whole family at this point,” Jazmin says. “And she’s going to sleep with him? It’s really annoying.” But some in the community, even cousins, stopped speaking with her. “It’s like ‘Hunger Games,’” Martinez says.

As Latinos fled and avoided Ingram, the daily takeout orders at one Mexican restaurant on the edge of town dropped to 50 from 200. A corner store catering to immigrants lost around half its revenue and most of its Latino regulars. Landlords in a mobile-home park just outside town struggled to find tenants.

But it wasn’t just Ingram’s Latino community that was reeling. For Ingram’s non-Hispanic business owners, including many Republicans in a county that voted 77% for Trump in the 2024 election, the immigration crackdown was becoming an outrage. It was taking people they worked with and knew well. It was interfering with flood reconstruction. It was hurting the local economy.

The owner of a heavily damaged strip mall on the western edge of town, Steve Edelstein, lamented the loss of two workers who were helping him rebuild. “Technically local law enforcement is doing their job,” he told a reporter for The West Kerr Current, emphasizing that he supported Trump. “But it isn’t helping the community.” A manager overseeing the rebuilding of Ingram’s Little League field, which was washed away in the flood, made an angry call to the city after two of his workers were picked up, Breshears says. A contractor helping rebuild Hunt’s destroyed post office had his crew reduced to eight workers from 30 — causing what should have been a four-day job to stretch to two weeks.

Among the people who called Jordan, the mayor, to complain was his onetime high school classmate Neal Secor, who describes himself as “one of the most conservative guys you’ll ever meet.” His family business, a cluster of rental cabins called Waltonia on the River, was nearly destroyed by the flood. He was struggling to rebuild. He says that in the spring, in two separate stops, the Ingram police detained four of his workers and handed them over to ICE — the second set as they returned from a job repairing the docks at a nearby youth camp, a favor Secor was trying to do for a neighbor.

Secor says Jordan’s defense was simple: You voted for this. They’d all voted for this.

“Let me tell you something,” Secor says he told Jordan. “I didn’t vote for this. I voted to get the bad guys out.” The two employees detained coming back from the youth camp were like family, his friends and co-workers for over a decade. “There’s still a lot of bad guys here,” he continued. “These guys aren’t them.”

Secor recalls Jordan saying that Ingram’s officers were just following the law. But, Secor wondered, why was it that he could drive 85 every day on the 75-mile-an-hour interstate and police officers just let him pass? He told Jordan he’d put 175,000 miles on his truck and never been pulled over. “It’s a matter of what laws you want to pick and choose,” he recalls telling the mayor. “We all break laws every day if you really want to get down to it.”

“God Wanted Me to Meet You”

On an unpaved side street in the Ingram hills in April, Alexander again faced a decision over whether to separate a young family. This time he had more of a choice; ICE had yet to arrive. A woman named Norma Luján took his hand and said she was praying for him.

Luján, 61, runs a successful housecleaning company based in Ingram. She had heard of Alexander long before she confronted him. She had seen him in the Charger, too: on the side of Junction Highway as she made her way to jobs at vacation homes or youth camps up in Hunt. On the side of the highway on the way back. In her rearview mirror for four excruciating minutes one afternoon as her “girls,” as she called her crew, held their breath and sank into their seats, protected by the tint of her car’s windows and the fact that a license-plate reader would show it was registered to her, a Texas-born U.S. citizen.

In January, at the carwash, Alexander had helped a sheriff’s deputy take one of Luján’s best employees into custody. The woman, Cinthya Carranza, was a single mother and asylum seeker from Guanajuato — and Joanna Martinez’s cousin. Carranza was on her way to get her children from school after she and Luján spent the day cleaning houses. Later that day, Luján saw a Facebook post showing a familiar face in a mug shot: Carranza’s. Luján broke into tears. To her, the arrest was a signal event. The Charger had mostly stopped men up to that point. This was the moment she understood that no one was safe.

Luján started losing workers in droves after Carranza was taken — some to traffic stops, most for fear of having to drive through Ingram. Her crew of 30 people dropped to fewer than 10. She worried for her business, but she worried more, she said, for her workers, the lives they had made in Ingram and the relationships she had built with them. They invited her to parties and baptisms, surprised her with presents on her birthday. She often led them in prayer. “I love them,” she says. She promised she would try to protect them.

When Luján’s employee Maria called that April afternoon to say the officer in the Charger was outside her house, detaining her husband as he returned from work, Luján jumped into action. Maria (who asked to be identified by her middle name because she is undocumented) was eight months pregnant and already terrified that she would have to give birth alone. Alexander had taken her brother a week earlier. Now Maria was hiding behind the curtains of her home, sneaking peeks outside, hoping Alexander would let her husband go.

“Cálmate” — calm down — Luján told herself as she approached the Charger. “Cálmate.” She took a deep breath. She says Alexander was sitting in the driver’s seat with the door propped open, staring at a tablet computer.

“Look, his wife has had a complicated pregnancy,” she told him. (This was true.) “She’s in the hospital.” (For that lie, Luján says, she later prayed for forgiveness.)

Then Luján reached out and grabbed Alexander’s hand. “I pray for your being, for your soul,” she recalls telling him as she cried. “I want you to think about what you’re doing. Feel it. Feel it, please.” She squeezed his hand. “I need you to look inside your heart,” she continued, “and let him go.”

Alexander didn’t react at first, in Luján’s telling. “God wanted me to meet you,” she said. He met her gaze.

“I’m that guy that everyone talks about on Facebook,” she recalls him finally saying. “If you think I don’t lose any sleep, you’re wrong.”

Luján pushed through the lump in her throat to speak. “I’m going to pray for you every night,” she promised him. She says Alexander squeezed her hand back, then pulled away. He walked off to make a call. She couldn’t make out much of what he said. It was quiet, save for the sound of Luján’s sobs and the pebbles from the unpaved road crunching beneath the officer’s feet.

Then he returned to the Charger. “Get him out of the car,” Luján recalls him saying. “Hurry up.”

“God bless you,” Luján said. “God will repay you for this.”

Alexander says he doesn’t remember the details of his interaction with Luján, but he confirms that he let Maria’s husband go, calling it a matter of “human decency.” He knew how hard it was to raise children. “A woman needs rest,” he says. “She needs help.” Maria’s husband “needs to be there helping out.”

At first, nothing seemed to change. Over the next two months, as the Hill Country prepared to welcome summer tourists and campers back after the devastation of the floods, Alexander worked around 100 task force hours, earning close to $5,000 from ICE.

But the next time he ran into Joanna Martinez, he seemed to be having misgivings. It was early June, and he was eight months into the ICE program. He had pulled over another of her family friends on Junction Highway, a person she had known since childhood. Martinez got a phone call and rushed to the scene, as she had so many times before. “I don’t feel good about this,” she recalls him saying when she arrived. “I signed up to be a cop, not an ICE agent.” (Alexander says he remembers that they talked and that he could have said something like that.)

Later that month, he pulled over a young man from Honduras who was on his way to a soccer game with his cousin, a 12-year-old with developmental disabilities. The boy’s father says he and his wife hid across the street watching it all happen, too terrified to step out and claim their son. The parents sent a friend from church, but she was not a legal guardian. Alexander says he had no choice but to hand the boy over to ICE, adding though that if he was one of the parents, he would see it differently. “If I’m in that position, there’s no way I’m letting my kid go,” he told us. “I’m probably fighting someone.”

Within a couple of weeks, Alexander’s task force hours dropped by about 40%, according to his pay stubs. It remains unclear if he tried to step back from immigration work or whether the number of undocumented drivers in Ingram had simply dwindled because of all he had already done.

According to Chief Breshears, Ingram had logged 194 “immigration-related incidents” as of this August. Whether every handover led to a deportation, Breshears couldn’t say. Alexander says he doesn’t know how many of the 194 are people he stopped. But he says he has now let at least 10 people go — many, though not all of them, mothers of young children.

Alexander sees this, and his relationship to the Martinez family, as evidence of his humanity, despite what people say about him. “For context, I’ve deported like six of their family members, and they’re still friendly to me,” he says. “So I’m not the monster they make me out to be.”

On July 16, the skies over Ingram opened again, dropping nearly 19 inches of rain in a single day, and the Guadalupe again overtopped its banks, again destroying businesses and homes. In the predawn darkness in the early hours of the emergency, Alexander began racing toward Ingram in his black Charger to help. He had barely left his house when surging floodwaters consumed the vehicle, destroying the Charger’s engine block. A driver in a pickup truck took him back home, and that’s where he stayed until the storm receded.

“One Free Pass”

Alexander remains only one cog in a deportation machine for which the federal government has now earmarked $240 billion. Today more than 1,900 agencies in at least 30 states have signed up for ICE’s task force model, with more than 29,000 deputized officers. With their help, ICE recently hit a record of immigration arrests, totaling more than 50,000 in August.

On Sept. 11, Alexander met one of us at a taco spot on Junction Highway. Ingram had changed in the year since his return. Whole neighborhoods had emptied out, and residents noticed fewer drivers on the streets. In part because of the money from ICE, the Police Department had hired two additional officers. As a Mexican ballad played over the speakers, Alexander warned against making too much of the leniency he showed to families like Maria’s. “It’s like one free pass, I guess,” he said: If he encountered her husband again during a traffic stop, he would probably hand him over to ICE. He just thought letting the father-to-be go was the right call at the time. “I mean, don’t you?” he asked.

He said he hadn’t made all that much money working with ICE. But city records show that his earnings from the agency already totaled $18,793.25 in nine months, more than a quarter of his base salary. “I think it’s skewed a little bit,” he said, looking at the pay stubs we had gathered.

Alexander said it was hard for him to be out in public anymore. He can’t escape being recognized in Ingram and Kerrville. Sometimes he catches Latinos staring at him, then walking away, visibly uncomfortable. So he tries to do his shopping and errands in another town 30 minutes away.

He blamed the Facebook groups. They had created a climate of “unreasonable fear” in Ingram. “What do they think I’m going to do right now?” he asked, seated at his table in the taco shop. A steady stream of customers, many of them white, approached a counter staffed by two young Mexican sisters. He said their father used to hide out in Hunt to avoid being pulled over in town. Some of their co-workers had quit months before, too uncomfortable to serve Alexander when he came in for breakfast. But when the taco shop owner sees him, he said, she hugs him.

“I know the status of everybody in this room,” he said. He suggested everyone who worked there was undocumented. Whether they disappeared or were allowed to stay was up to him. And today, at least, he was just there for breakfast.

“They’re fine, right?”

Down the street, the bystander’s cellphone video shows the Durango pass the Tahoe, which has tinted windows, on a residential street.
He is then seen falling toward the ground, off the front-right side of the car, the footage shows.
The SUV’s brake lights turn back on briefly before it drives farther down the street, the surveillance footage shows.

text:
(CNN) — When footage of a man being hit by federal immigration officers’ SUV in Northern California became public, the Department of Homeland Security responded by saying the man had jumped on the vehicle’s hood.

Local police raised doubts about federal officials’ account as they announced a criminal investigation into Tuesday morning’s incident involving the pedestrian, 37-year-old Antonio Moreida, citing video footage that contradicted DHS’ statement.

Footage from a nearby surveillance camera, a bystander’s cellphone recording and Moreida’s GoPro, which had already been made public at the time of the agency’s statement, told a different story of what happened on a residential street in Woodland, an agricultural city just outside of Sacramento. The incident is the latest in which DHS’ account has been contradicted by officials and video evidence amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Police contradict ICE account

In a statement Wednesday morning, DHS said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers didn’t hit a pedestrian.

“An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement in response to CNN’s request for information. “The agitator slid off the hood. ICE immediately contacted EMS and the Woodland Police Department. Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation,” apparently accusing the man of faking his injuries.

After the incident on Tuesday, Woodland Police Chief Ryan Kinnan said in a statement he found footage of the incident troubling. Investigators were working to gather evidence and statements and to review available audio and video related to the incident, including video taken from multiple perspectives, police said in a Facebook post. Woodland Police didn’t take part in the ICE operation the agents were involved in that morning, police said.

The following day, Woodland Police called DHS’ account “inconsistent.”

“Certain claims made in the DHS statement are inconsistent with the video evidence obtained and reviewed by Woodland Police investigators,” Kinnan said in an update Wednesday. The update said investigators had established, based on video evidence, the pedestrian had been hit by the vehicle driven by ICE agents and that he had not jumped onto the vehicle.

The local police department is conducting a criminal investigation into the events leading up to the collision and the actions of those involved, Kinnan said Wednesday.

By Thursday, in response to follow-up questions about the video footage, federal officials no longer said the person jumped on the hood.

“This individual chose to directly impede a law enforcement action and stand in the middle of an active road,” an ICE spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. “Our officers deliberately attempted to avoid making contact with this anti-ice protestor and drive around him, while also braking. We strongly urge individuals to not stand in the middle of active roadways while a law enforcement vehicle is approaching.”

What footage shows

Footage reviewed by CNN shows Moreida, a Woodland resident, in the middle of the street at around 9:40 a.m. Tuesday. Moreida said he had responded to a call that morning by NorCal Resist, a group which monitors immigration operations, about ICE activity in Woodland, he told CNN on Tuesday, hours after the incident.

He said he was trying to record agents’ unmarked vehicles. He had been recording one vehicle, standing on the car’s driver’s side, when it turned left and drove off, which he said pushed him into the middle of the street.

Video from Moreida’s GoPro shows him following a black Dodge Durango with tinted windows as it drives down the street.

Then, he said he heard a loud engine before seeing the agents’ black Chevy Tahoe drive toward him, which is shown in his GoPro footage, though the video has no audio.

Down the street, the bystander’s cellphone video shows the Durango pass the Tahoe, which has tinted windows, on a residential street. In the video’s background, people can be heard blowing whistles, presumably to alert people nearby of ICE’s presence in the neighborhood.

The ICE agent driving the Tahoe moves toward Moreida and between the cars with its brake lights on, footage shows. In the bystander’s video, Moreida isn’t yet visible.

The SUV’s wheels begin to turn to the left only a few feet from Moreida, a wider angle of surveillance footage from a home shows.

“The individual was standing in the street long enough that a reasonable person should be able to see them and recognize that they were there,” said Ryan Schwank, a former ICE attorney and training instructor who reviewed the videos provided by CNN.

Schwank also took issue with ICE’s characterization that Moreida was standing in the middle of an active road and impeding law enforcement’s actions.

“When we’re looking at Antonio’s actions, he’s not impeding. He’s not standing blocking the vehicle from moving,” he said. “He’s standing and filming, and that’s well within his bounds to do. He’s well within his rights to do what he was doing.”

Moreida’s GoPro appears to show when he’s struck by the front-right side of the vehicle before he drops his camera.

“Before I knew it, it just drove straight into me,” he said. “I took the hood of the car straight to the chest. It initially took the wind out of me and I couldn’t breathe.”

The surveillance footage shows Moreida take a step back when he appears to make contact with the car. He is then seen falling toward the ground, off the front-right side of the car, the footage shows.

In the bystander’s footage from behind, a screeching noise is heard before the Tahoe jolts forward. The SUV veers left before straightening out, the video shows.

The bystander’s angle shows the Tahoe brake lights turn off. Moreida is then visible in the bystander’s video, falling to the ground and rolling, first on his back with his legs swinging above him. He then appears seated upright in the nearby surveillance footage, this time facing the sidewalk.

The SUV’s brake lights turn back on briefly before it drives farther down the street, the surveillance footage shows.

The driver, an ICE agent, stayed near the scene and called local dispatch, Woodland Police said. The agent cooperated with police during the initial investigation, the local agency said.

Moreida said an off-duty EMT provided him aid at the scene before Woodland Police officers arrived. Federal agents didn’t approach him after he was hit by the SUV, he said.

Moreida said he was eventually transported to the hospital. He said he had X-rays taken of his swollen knees, where he said he had the most damage. In addition, he said he has bruises and cuts from the road.

ICE has reduced the amount of training for officers, including in vehicle operations and how to deal with confrontations, said Schwank, who is now an agency whistleblower after resigning in February.

On Saturday, ICE said it is instituting additional training for officers.

“ICE training will now be extending to 72 days. The change, effective June 2, 2026, will apply to all new academy classes beginning July 1, 2026. All graduates of the previous academy curriculum will attend follow-on training at the Advanced Field Officer Training Program,” an ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement to CNN. “As we have said all along, ICE training does not end when recruits graduate from the academy. ICE officers go through a rigorous on-the-job training and mentorship. This additional training is tracked online and monitored closely.”

Local officials call for investigations

Soon after it became public, local officials expressed dismay over the incident, which occurred in a rural Northern California community that’s about half Latino. More than a fifth of the population is foreign-born, according to US Census estimates.

“The lack of truth in the Department of Homeland Security’s statement is evidenced by video taken at the scene,” Woodland Mayor Tom Stallard said in a statement issued Wednesday. “All of us can be assured that the Police Department’s investigation into this disturbing incident will continue to be speedy, fair, and impartial.”

US Rep. Mike Thompson, a Democrat whose district includes Woodland, said ICE’s statements about the facts surrounding the incident were disappointing but not surprising.

“ICE has a history of trying to hide the facts and mislead the public,” he told CNN. “And this is another example of that happening.”

On the day of the operation, Thompson called on Acting ICE Director David Venturella to investigate the collision, including by preserving evidence and cooperating with local authorities. As of Friday, the congressman had yet to receive a response to his letter, his office told CNN.

text:
Introduction

The US. immigration policies are characterized by their heartless detention conditions and systemic abuses against refugees, especially at the U. S./Mexico border. Sexual and physical abuses, the forced sterilization that occurs in these immigration detention camps, as well as how private prison corporations have been involved in these detentions, are revealed by investigations and publications of Human Rights Watch and ACLU. These recorded cases show gross violations of human rights, dignity, and justice, which are contrary to the principles of liberalism. Moreover, the history of the US. immigration control illustrates a trend of xenophobia and exclusion, indicating that today’s problems are a continuation of an old problem. Given the way migrants and asylum seekers are treated, alongside making a profit out of detained individuals, it warrants rethinking these policies based on justice and human rights ideals.

The Inhumane Conditions of Detention and the Abuse of Asylum Seekers

From horrific conditions bordering the US/Mexico, where migrants and asylum seekers are held, information is becoming more available, exposing the pattern of abuse and neglect involved. Human Rights Watch (2022) has published an all-embracing report that throws light on these “shocking abuses,” which meticulously documents instances of sexual and physical abuse as reported by US asylum officers. These reports are not sporadic but systemic issues constituting a grave breach of human rights and dignity.

For instance, such maltreatments consist of reports on how asylum seekers undergo degrading treatments, physical harm, or psychological torture, among others, which are entirely in stark contrast to the liberal values that stress individual rights (PressTV, 2021). Indigenous ideas about land stewardship, borders, and belonging should be included in contemporary debates on immigration. It underscores the hypocrisy of describing European colonization of Native lands as ‘illegal immigration’ given the historical and cultural aspects associated with Native American roots (Critical Media Project, n.d.). Everyone should be treated fairly and respectfully, regardless of their status or origin.

The Dark Legacy of Coerced Sterilization in Immigration Detention

Immigration detention centers house a sinister history of forced sterilization, which revives a chilling memory of eugenic measures taken against marginalized individuals in the past. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has also noted that immigrant women have been coerced into undergoing involuntary sterilization (Manian, 2020). Here, the practice infringes on the autonomy and reproductive health rights of these women as it also drags behind it the shadowy past of eugenics, which aimed at taming fertility amongst certain groups (Medosch, 2021). It implies that such actions are grave violations of ethical standards and human rights and have serious consequences. The immigration detention system must be reformed immediately if these kinds of coercions are not to be allowed to persist any longer.

The Role of Private Prisons in Exacerbating Injustices

The ethical and legal complexities of private prison corporations’ role in administering immigration detention facilities are enormous. The ACLU National Prison Project has underscored that these entities are driven by profit, which, in turn, implies they pursue the expansion and continuation of detention practices (Cho, 2021). Through securing lucrative contracts with ICE, private prisons have made a business model out of human lives (Schwenk, 2023). This situation is alarming as it brings monetary motives into the context of incarcerating people, thus conflicting inherently with basic liberal notions like justice and fairness.

The idea that justice and legal process should operate impartially and without economic interest is fundamentally incompatible with making money from human bodies. A recently published article emphasizes the pressing need for radical change in the system, noting that enforcement-based immigration strategies have been a historical and ongoing problem (Hernández, 2021). It is worth asking how reliable a system that allows for financial gains to be used in determining how detained people are treated or cared for may be.

The Historical Context of U.S. Immigration Policies

To fully grasp the current United States immigration policies, it is necessary to delve into the historical currents of these laws and views on foreigners. The history of US immigration has been characterized by alternating phases of openness and limitation, reflecting the changing attitudes towards immigrants in society (History, 2022). This backdrop is essential in understanding today’s immigration debates, which have been marked occasionally by xenophobia and exclusion trends influencing public policy. History shows that some present-day policies are not new but reiterations of the long-standing themes of discrimination and fear of the unknown.

Therefore, adopting a more enlightened, humane approach to migration policy becomes necessary, transcending earlier biases to uphold inclusiveness, human rights, and respect (Mercado et al., 2021). Reflecting on this history underscores the urgent need for a comprehensive reform of U.S. immigration policy and detention practices, aiming to establish a framework that emphatically prioritizes justice, dignity, and human rights (Panleft, 2010). Past mistakes must serve as lessons to shape a future that recognizes the dignity of all people, irrespective of race, nationality, or social class.

Conclusion

To summarize, the current situation at the US/Mexico border is characterized by the criminalization of migration and inhumane treatment of detainees, a deeply disturbing moral and ethical crisis. The ill-treatment that has been documented by both Human Rights Watch and ACLU, as well as cases of private prison corporations profiteering from their torment, only indicate how these practices undermine primary liberal values such as human rights, dignity, and justice. It is high time for these policies to be reconsidered based on complete knowledge of past immigrant policies. For instance, America needs laws that are fair to everyone, regardless of immigration status, to allow all humans to live with respect, compassion, and protection of their rights, which are the highest principles of justice and human rights.

text:
Mount Morris, N.Y. (WHAM) — Dozens of Mount Morris residents took to the streets Saturday to protest the arrest of longtime local business owner Dian Zhao Lin, calling for his release and return home.

Lin was arrested by ICE agents on Tuesday. ICE officials said he had been in the United States illegally for nearly 30 years.

Among those demonstrating Saturday was Lin’s daughter, Yujin Lin, who described her father as the glue that kept the family together.

“I really miss my dad's presence around us. You know him just being there, even if he's telling me to go wash the dishes, even though I hate doing the dishes. I want to do the dishes for him,” Yujin Lin said.

A video captured during the arrest was later posted to social media.

Community members said they were also upset about Lin’s arrest. Lenny Palermo, a Mount Morris community member, said Lin was like a brother to him.

“I've known this family since they've come here, they fed my family almost every week because Monica is friends with Izzy here. She calls me Grandpa too. They call me Uncle. Mr. Lin is the hardest working, most valuable person we have in Mount Morris,” Palermo said.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said Lin’s arrest was part of a targeted enforcement operation, adding that he had been in the country illegally for nearly 30 years and was ordered removed by an immigration judge in 1999.

“I think that people need to stop looking at this as a left and right issue, more as a humanity issue. Like this isn't about like how you feel about politics. This is how you you express empathy,” Isabele Palermo said.

The arrest sparked outrage and calls for Lin’s release, with his family saying it has been difficult to cope without him.

“It has taken a toll on our mental health, our physical health, and it is extremely, extremely hard for us to be able to proceed with life as normal if we do not have my dad next to us. We are not able to be at peace if we are not able to see our dad here,” Lin’s daughter said.

The Lin family is asking people to sign a petition demanding Lin’s release. ICE officials said he will remain in custody pending removal.

In Colorado, Secretary of State Jena Griswold said the DOJ is seeking to send election monitors to Adams County, a northeast part of Denver.
What can poll monitors do?
text:
Georgia is a battleground state featuring intense elections between Democrats and Republicans this cycle at the Senate and gubernatorial levels. GOP candidate Rick Jackson is rivaling Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms in the gubernatorial race, while Mike Collins (R-GA) is challenging Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) in the Senate race.

Revelations that poll monitors will be deployed to the Peach State in November come after Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, announced in August that the DOJ would send 1,000 observers nationwide, in what she termed “the largest monitoring effort” in the agency’s history.

Monitoring elections is a normal part of the DOJ’s duties. The department under former President Joe Biden sent roughly 400 monitors to 64 jurisdictions across around two dozen states on Election Day in the last midterm year, 2022.

However, the latest effort marks a substantial expansion of that effort, with more than double the election monitors to be sent nationwide. It’s unclear which jurisdictions or how many the department plans to monitor this November, with the DOJ telling NPR such details will be released closer to the election.

Where are poll monitors going?

States that have suggested the arrival of poll monitors include: Oregon, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Georgia, Colorado, Florida, Minnesota, Texas, Washington, Utah, and Kansas. The DOJ has sent monitor notifications to seven Texas counties, Washington state’s King County, Florida’s Miami-Dade County, and Minnesota’s Hennepin and Ramsey counties, among other jurisdictions nationwide.

For instance, in Pennsylvania, four counties are set to be monitored by federal observers—in Philadelphia, Allegheny, Luzerne, and Lehigh.

In Colorado, Secretary of State Jena Griswold said the DOJ is seeking to send election monitors to Adams County, a northeast part of Denver. The Democratic official panned the effort, saying she believes it is aimed at trying to intimidate people. Adams County includes part of the state’s toss-up 8th Congressional District, which could determine party control of the House.

Some officials believe the DOJ is being weaponized to intimidate voters and destroy the integrity of the election process, the opposite of what the Trump administration has framed it as. Other officials have said the ramped-up observing effort is little more than a symbolic gesture.

Scott Schwab, Kansas’ Republican secretary of state, told PBS News this week that the DOJ’s effort is likely little more than a “feel-good” initiative. He confirmed he has heard from the DOJ in recent days about plans to monitor Kansas, but said personnel are “going to be looking from afar,” with monitors “normally half a building away from the elections processing and monitoring center.”

David Becker, a former voting attorney in the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, said the scale of this year’s monitoring efforts is “not normal, but I’m not particularly concerned,” adding that the agency does not have “blanket authority to be everywhere” and monitors must follow local and state laws about whether they are allowed inside a polling location.

What can poll monitors do?

Monitors are fairly restricted in what they are legally allowed to do. They can observe for potential violations during the election process, document what happened, and then report it to DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, which performs more of the enforcement and investigative follow-up action.

“They’re neutral observers. They have no role in stepping in and helping,” Dhillon said during an August interview with RealClearPolitics. “They can’t step in and change it.”

ABDUL EL SAYED HAS STABILIZED HIS MICHIGAN SENATE CAMPAIGN. CAN THE DEMOCRAT HOLD THE GAINS?

The DOJ has framed monitors as necessary to ensure “transparency, ballot security, and compliance with federal law.” It says monitors must follow the same rules that apply to voters at the polling place.

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

The Department of Homeland Security agreed in a settlement with the state to alert city officials at least 30 days before environmental permitting would get underway.

No new Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centers are slated for construction in Newport, Oregon, anytime soon, and the federal government will provide at least a month’s notice to city officials before any environmental permitting would get underway.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security agreed to those terms through Aug. 1, 2027, as part of a settlement with the Oregon Department of Justice filed in federal court in Eugene on Friday.

“ICE doesn’t get to skirt the law to build a facility for locking up and deporting our neighbors,” said Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, in a news release. “Oregon stood up, we made the federal government answer for its plans in court, and now they have to follow the law.”

The possibility of a new ICE detention center coming to Newport arose last fall amid concerns that federal immigration authorities were scouting the Oregon Coast for a long-term holding facility, including at Newport’s U.S. Coast Guard municipal airport site.

Newport’s city leaders went public with their concerns shortly after, and strong opposition grew from residents and the state’s Democratic leaders, who also took issue with the temporary removal of a life-saving rescue helicopter from the city’s Coast Guard facility.

Rayfield successfully sued the Homeland Security Department over the helicopter’s removal, securing a court order that it be returned to Newport, and asked a federal judge to halt any construction on an immigration detention facility at the site.

In that case, which is behind the recent settlement, lawyers for Oregon’s Justice Department argued that the federal government had been skirting federal environmental and coastal land use regulations by trying to build a facility on the municipal airport site without providing advanced notice to state and local leaders. The Oregon Justice Department agreed to drop the case following the federal government’s commitment to providing advance notice should efforts to build a detention center in the area resume.

The notice period required in the lawsuit does not apply to other Oregon cities, though the settlement notes ICE is not planning to expand or create any detention facilities or processing centers in the state.

text:
Earlier this year, the Post Falls Police Department entered into an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that allows the agency to perform immigration duties.

The Kootenai County Sheriff's Office did the same, as did the Idaho State Police. And most recently, the Spirit Lake Police Department. Other Idaho counties, including Franklin, Caribou, Washington, Bonneville, Bingham and Owyhee counties, previously came on board.

Post Falls was the first city in Idaho to join the federal 287(g) program, which allows trained local police officers to perform specific immigration enforcement functions under the supervision and direction of ICE.

“We are proud to continue our partnership with federal law enforcement to keep our city safe and we reiterate our commitment to enforcing the law,” said Post Falls Mayor Randy Westlund. “This partnership advances these goals and strengthens our community.”

Post Falls Police Chief Mark Brantl said that by participating in the program, officers will gain additional tools to address serious criminal activity linked to immigration violations.

"This agreement enables us to work more effectively with federal partners to remove dangerous individuals from our community, while continuing to focus on community-oriented policing," he said

Spirit Lake PD Chief Michael Morlan said: “All this is allowing is access to databases and to work in cooperation with ICE.”

Morlan said sharing resources with other law enforcement agencies is vital, especially for a smaller agency, and that the training will be valuable.

Coeur d'Alene, however, isn't so sure about the benefits of partnering with ICE.

The agency has been criticized for its handling of arrests and accused of poor training, physical abuse, civil rights violations and harassment. On the other hand, some praise them for their courage, dedication, professionalism and fairness.

The Coeur d’Alene Police Department does not intend to join the 287(g) task force program or partner with ICE, Chief Greg Yeager previously told the Press.

“It’s a tool that some agencies use,” he told the Coeur d'Alene Press in an email last month. “But not one we’ve had need of.”

Mayor Dan Gookin told The Press that “our police department isn’t interested in the program for various reasons.”

Council member Christie Wood expressed concerns about the local police department working with ICE agents, questioning whether they’re “well-trained” and whether the city would be left “cleaning up the mess.” She said she would support passing a resolution, but the city’s police department would comply with federal law.

The differing views of the mayors and police chiefs of Kootenai County's largest cities are interesting and highlight a debate.

Supporters see the 287(g) program as a practical tool that strengthens cooperation with federal authorities and helps remove dangerous criminals. Critics question whether the benefits outweigh the risks, including potential liability, training concerns and the impact on community trust.

One side is embracing closer cooperation with ICE as a commonsense public safety measure. The other sees little need for the program and worries about its potential consequences.

Right now, we don't know who's right.

As more Idaho agencies sign on, the real test will be whether these partnerships make communities safer without creating unintended problems. The Press, and the public will be watching.

title: ICE Will Decide Who Lives and Who Dies - Austin Kocher
description:
As you may have heard, there was another detention death this week, this time in Folkston, Georgia.
In response to the hunger strike, ICE has approved forced-feeding, a method that experts say amounts to torture.
One grotesque, perverse conclusion is that the best way to get medical attention is to stage a hunger strike.
But this also illustrates the economy of indifference inside detention facilities.
We don’t know for sure whether Sandoval was part of the hunger strike.
text:
The purpose of the U.S. deportation system is not merely to enforce immigration laws on the books; it is, more fundamentally, to construct an apparatus that generates humiliation, dehumanization, and the perception of the expendability of non-citizens, particularly non-white immigrants whose bodies, whether citizen or not, remain differentially excluded from the body politic.

My colleague Nancy Hiemstra has written about the use of the term “body” in her book Detain and Deport. Detention center staff refer to a person as a body, to a group of detained people as bodies. “We just booked in 17 bodies.” “No, we don’t have that body here, they transferred out three days ago.” As plenty of social theorists have observed, the term “body” uniquely points to a human being without revealing whether that person is living or dead.

This indeterminacy is not an accident or a weakness in the term. Rather, this indeterminacy does political work by revealing and enacting a consequential ambivalence over whether the body is alive or dead. To refer to people as bodies is to treat their lives as matters of material inputs and outputs, objects of logistical management like Amazon packages, rather than persons who enjoy certain minimum standards of ethical care.

The rise in the number of deaths inside immigrant detention centers under the current administration is cause for concern. One form that this concern takes for me is not only whether the agency cares about migrants’ lives (it seems clear that they don’t), but how the agency operationalizes its indifference towards migrants’ lives through attention and inattention to migrants’ well-being.

These questions are not abstract. As you may have heard, there was another detention death this week, this time in Folkston, Georgia. A Salvadoran man named Luis Sandoval died from what is currently reported as consistent with suicide — although a full investigation is needed to understand the whole story. ICE’s official announcement here.

This happened inside the same facility where a group of detained people are on a hunger strike to protest detention conditions, including “moldy food, foul-smelling water, freezing cells, sleep deprivation, untreated dental pain and months-long waits for care,” according to Migrant Insider (read the full article below). In response to the hunger strike, ICE has approved forced-feeding, a method that experts say amounts to torture.

All of this came to mind when I talked to José Olivares from The Guardian today for the story that just came out this evening: “Man detained at Georgia immigration detention center dies as hunger strike continues.” In my comment to José, I emphasized what I saw as the embodiment of the central tensions within our deportation system’s dehumanizing mission.

Pause with me for a moment on the absurdity that ICE would force-feed hunger strikers who are protesting rotten food and malnutrition. Hunger strikes are a tactic that people use when they have nothing left to fight with other than the basic materiality of their own body — an indication that the person has already been reduced to a state ambiguously between life and death. Forced-feeding as an intervention is a way of taking away what little agency people have left, while refusing to address the substance of the underlying complaint. It’s as if ICE intends to send a message: “we will not let you escape humiliation by suffering or dying on your own terms when that suffering and death contain within them a clear political message.”

ICE’s sudden urgency to insist on life-giving care runs in direct contradiction to its increasing death toll. Let’s not forget that nearly every reported death under this administration, and administrations before it, is accompanied by stories of people repeatedly begging for medical attention and being turned away. As long as these bodies are breaking down on their own and not as part of an explicit attempt to expose detention conditions, the agency is indifferent to these deaths. One grotesque, perverse conclusion is that the best way to get medical attention is to stage a hunger strike.

But now we are forced to factor in the death of Luis Sandoval. If it was indeed a suicide, we first should remember that suicides, too, are often the result of systems, not simply individuals, and that when a suicide happens inside of a controlled facility, it represents a systemic failure of one kind or another. But this also illustrates the economy of indifference inside detention facilities. We don’t know for sure whether Sandoval was part of the hunger strike. And yet it appears that ICE and the private contractor GEO Group that runs the facility were far more concerned about keeping alive people who wanted little more than basic care than preventing the deaths both here and throughout the rest of the massive detention archipelago across the country.

In short, the juxtaposition of when ICE forces people to live and when ICE allows people to die or even sets up the conditions for people to want to die does more than just reinforce the agency’s view that migrants’ bodies are expendable. It’s a warning that what should be a relatively minor federal sub-agency doing civil case management has chosen to embody a dangerous type of sovereign authority over life and death for which we have no mechanisms of even basic oversight and accountability.

text:
Immigrants detained in the U.S. by President Donald Trump’s administration have no constitutional right to a bond hearing, a federal appeals court ruled Friday.

According to Reuters, the ruling came out of the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans.

Fewer rights for detained migrants

What we know:

The court’s conservative majority ruled 10-7 that the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment does not apply to immigrants who are detained and seeking a bond hearing.

What they're saying:

"To the extent petitioners seek to vindicate a liberty interest to be ​free from physical restraint in the most abstract sense, they can do so at any moment by ​agreeing to leave the country," US Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote.

READ MORE: 6 charged in decade long, multi-million dollar marriage fraud ring

In a social media post, James Percival, general counsel for the US Department of Homeland Security, called the decision a "big win in the 5th Circuit on mandatory detention ​for illegal aliens."

What we don't know:

It’s unclear whether the ruling will stand; the Supreme Court has agreed to take up the issue as federal courts are flooded with lawsuits by migrants who say they’ve been unflawfully detained. Lower courts remain divided on what rights migrants should have amid the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

Big picture view:

If the ruling stands, detained migrants in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi (the 5th Circuit’s jurisdiction) will have fewer avenues to lobby for their release.

Local perspective:

Texas and Louisiana house more immigrant detainees than any other state.

‘Devastating consequences’

The other side:

"Unchecked, executive authority to ​arrest and detain, indefinitely, echoes fearfully from history," US Circuit Judge Dana Douglas, one of the dissenting judges, wrote in the opinion.

"This ruling opens ​the door to more people being locked up for no reason, with devastating consequences ​for them, their ⁠loved ones and their community," Ellie Norton, a lawyer for the non-US citizens in the case at the National Immigration Project, said in a statement to Reuters.

text:
The arrests last week of ICE observers Madison Crabill, 25, and Adilene Tonoco, 33, by Santa Ana Police triggered community protests as well as rebukes from City Council members.

The Orange County District Attorney’s Office confirmed today that no criminal charges would be filed against the two activists who were accused by Santa Ana Police of suspicion of stalking, conspiracy and resisting or obstructing a peace officer. The incident began Oct. 13 when two off-duty federal agents reported that the women were following them and that they feared for their safety.

Activists and supporters of the two ICE observers held a press conference the next day condemning the arrests as unlawful interference in Constitutionally protected activities and a possible violation of state law prohibiting cooperation with federal immigration authorities. Under California’s Sanctuary laws, local police do work with federal agents in arresting suspects with criminal convictions, specific criminal histories and conditions, or judicial warrants. Crabill and Tonoco have clean records.

The controversy brought a vocal protest to Tuesday night’s City Council meeting, where residents and activists criticized the arrests during much of the nearly two hours spent on public comments. Crabill addressed the council, recounting the encounter and calling for a public apology and police accountability.

“Our unjust arrest is another example of intimidation designed to allow ICE’s illegal agenda to continue without oversight,” said Crabill during public comments at the City Council meeting. “This incident should serve as a reminder of what the undocumented community goes through with ICE and collaborating agencies.”

Santa Ana Police Chief Robert Rodriguez defended his officers in an Oct. 16 statement, saying investigators established probable cause for the arrests. He said the department was responding to allegations of criminal conduct and was not participating in immigration enforcement.

In their remarks from the dais, Council members Thai Viet Phan and Jessie Lopez expressed skepticism with the validity of the arrests and the claim agents made that they were fearful.

“If that is the standard and the standard our police department is using to justify these charges, then it would, I think, obliterate any type of ability for us to hold these ICE agents, and officers accountable for what they’ve been doing in our city,” said Phan.

Council member Jessie Lopez remarked that even those who support what ICE is doing should not try to criminalize the ability to observe what federal agents are doing in the community.

The statement received by the Observer today from the DA’s Office regarding the case submitted by Santa Ana Police short: “We reviewed the evidence and found insufficient evidence to prove a crime was committed beyond a reasonable doubt based on the evidence presented to us.” Case closed.

text:
Quick Take

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrived at the Santa Cruz Main Jail on Saturday morning seeking to take someone into custody, but left without detaining anyone, the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office said. Volunteers monitoring ICE activity reported that agents came and went throughout the day.

The Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office confirmed that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents were conducting enforcement activities at the Santa Cruz Main Jail on Saturday morning.

Federal immigration agents had arrived at the facility in an attempt to take an individual into custody, but left without detaining anyone, according to a department social media post.

“The Sheriff’s Office remains committed to protecting public safety, maintaining community trust and carrying out its responsibilities in accordance with California law and applicable county policies governing cooperation with federal immigration authorities,” the department said.

Despite the department’s statement that agents had left, a black Nissan Pathfinder and a red Jeep SUV, each carrying two ICE agents, remained outside the jail into the afternoon. Both vehicles left the parking lot by 2:30 p.m. Volunteers said agents had come and gone repeatedly throughout the day. It remained unclear where the agents went or whether they would return, but some volunteers reported following some of the agents up northbound Highway 17.

Mayoral candidate Ami Chen Mills and former Santa Cruz city councilmember Sandy Brown were at the scene.

Sheriff Chris Clark has previously told Lookout that his department does not cooperate with immigration enforcement.

The sheriff’s office did not respond to Lookout’s request for comment.

Your Allied Rapid Response, an ICE watchdog group, first reported the presence of immigration officials at 9:30 a.m. Saturday. The group’s legal observers, who document ICE activity, were on scene until agents left the jail.

Nearly 20 YARR volunteers remained at the jail as of midafternoon Saturday.

According to Joliene Gatlin, co-director of jail ministry for Profits of Hope — a group that gathers at the jail three times a month on Saturday to provide coffee, food, clothing and other resources to visiting families of inmates headed for release — one of their members either saw or heard ICE agents and notified YARR. She added that the jail closed down its lobby and halted visitation for the day.

Gatlin and other volunteers are likely to return on Sunday, in case ICE agents return.

This story is developing. Check back for updates.

text:
A Nashville judge temporarily blocked Tennessee health officials from requiring immigration status checks of HIV-positive individuals enrolled in a healthcare safety-net program.

Chancellor I'Ashea L. Myles issued the temporary restraining order late Wednesday. The order prevents the Tennessee Department of Health from moving forward with a demand that organizations revise their contracts to include immigration status verification as a condition of serving patients in the Ryan White HIV/AIDS program.

The order extends to a companion program known as HOPWA, or Housing Opportunities for People with AIDS. Myles set a Nov. 4 hearing in the case.

The decades-old, federally-funded Ryan White program provides millions of dollars to every U.S. state to serve low-income individuals living with HIV/AIDS. States in turn distribute funding to healthcare and other providers who work directly with patients.

On Oct. 1, the Tennessee health department sent a memo to these providers citing new state law that requires verifying anyone seeking federal, state or local public benefits to be lawfully present in the United States. The law also comes with criminal penalties for employees who fail to verify patient status.

Nashville CARES, one of the Tennessee's largest participants in the program, filed suit challenging the mandate earlier this week. The federal government does not require immigration status checks as a condition of receiving services through Ryan White or HOPWA and federal law exempts such checks for programs targeting communicable diseases, it noted in legal filings.

Hundreds of its patients would be at risk of losing life-saving medical, prescription drug and support services -- including financial assistance that pays the costs of private health insurance, Nashville CARES said in legal filings.

Represented by attorneys with the Tennessee Justice Center, the organization said the mandate violated state rule-making procedures and federal law.

Attorneys representing the Tennessee Department of Health objected to a temporary injunction in a legal response to Nashville CARES' initial petition. They argued that Nashville CARES was "essentially (asking) the Court to intervene in a contract dispute." State attorneys also disputed the right of Nashville CARES to broadly challenge the state's imposition of the new contract rules on all Tennessee organizations that participate in Ryan White program, arguing the case should focus only on Nashville CARES' dispute.

Myles' temporary restraining order applies to all organizations that contract with the state to provide Ryan White services.

The order blocks any effort to require immigration or citizenship status verification for any individual currently enrolled in the program, and any new applicant. Myles also blocked the state from restricting enrollment only to those able to provide proof of legal immigration or citizenship status.
