text:
LAKEWOOD – Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen (CO-07) and Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08) today led an effort demanding answers from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) following reports the agency has used local police to gain backdoor access to a nationwide license plate surveillance network, allowing the federal government to track private citizens’ movements. In the Members’ letter to Acting Director David Venturella, which was signed by 33 other Democrats, the Members press ICE to disclose whose movements it is tracking, what legal authority it relies on, and what safeguards protect the public from abuse.

“Reports that ICE is using local police as a backdoor to track people’s movements is terrifying and should alarm every single one of us. Especially during the Trump administration, which is looking for every opportunity to track and deport even law-abiding people,” said Congresswoman Pettersen. “I’m demanding answers about who ICE is tracking, how this information is being used, and what is stopping agents from abusing it. ICE does not get a blank check to spy on families and communities.”

“ICE’s use of local police as a backdoor to access Flock’s license plate cameras and secretly track Americans’ movements is an outrageous abuse of power,” saidCongressman Raja Krishnamoorthi. “The Trump administration cannot use local law enforcement to circumvent the Fourth Amendment and evade accountability. We are demanding answers about who ICE has been tracking, how this information has been used, and whether anyone has been detained or arrested as a result of this surveillance.”

A recent investigation uncovered more than 4,000 searches of Flock Safety camera data by state and local law enforcement conducted for federal authorities or with a potential immigration focus. The reporting described how ICE obtained access through local law enforcement despite having no formal contract with Flock governing that access.

Flock’s automatic license plate readers capture vehicle information and locations, allowing law enforcement to search records across camera networks. Access to those records can reveal incredibly personal details about people’s daily routines and whereabouts, raising concerns about privacy and the potential misuse of information collected in communities across the country.

“Such chilling, unrestrained surveillance obtained without judicial authorization, contractual safeguards, or public transparency, represents far more than a procedural lapse—it represents the quiet expansion of a federal surveillance system operating out of sight and beyond any meaningful public oversight,” the Members write in the letter.

The letter requests answers by November 20, 2026, including:

How often ICE has accessed Flock camera data, directly or through state and local partners and for what purposes.

How many people have been detained, arrested, or subjected to other enforcement actions as a result.

What legal authority and internal policies govern ICE’s access to and use of this information.

Whether ICE has reviewed these practices for compliance with federal privacy protections, the Fourth Amendment, and Department of Homeland Security policy.

Whether ICE intends to establish a formal agreement with Flock safety or another license plate reader vendor .

Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen has consistently fought back against the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement overreach and defended due process. In the Colorado legislature, she helped pass legislation ensuring local law enforcement agencies do not serve as an extension of ICE. In Congress, she voted against legislation that would force Washington, D.C. police to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement and condemned ICE operations in schools, churches, and hospitals. This letter builds on her work to protect immigrant communities and demand accountability for federal enforcement practices that threaten people’s rights.

The full text of the letter can be found HERE and below.

Dear Acting Director Venturella:

We write with serious concern regarding reports that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been accessing data from Flock Safety automatic license‑plate‑reader (ALPR) cameras, an AI‑powered surveillance system, with no formal contract or governing agreement in place, creating serious concerns around data privacy and overreach. According to recent reporting, ICE has used state and local law‑enforcement agencies to conduct more than 4,000 searches of Flock camera data on its behalf, enabling ICE personnel to obtain personally identifiable information without a criminal warrant.

Not only is this protocol potentially illegal, exploiting this information side-door allows ICE personnel to query ALPR cameras deployed across multiple states – in effect granting federal agents access to a nationwide, continuously updated surveillance grid capable of tracking the movements of millions of people in real time. Such chilling, unrestrained surveillance obtained without judicial authorization, contractual safeguards, or public transparency, represents far more than a procedural lapse — it represents the quiet expansion of a federal surveillance system operating out of sight and beyond any meaningful public oversight.This is a serious breach of privacy and a clear departure from federal law and agency policy. The ability of federal agents to access vast quantities of location‑tracking data, without judicial authorization and without public disclosure, constitutes an unprecedented intrusion into the privacy of the general public, and must be explained immediately.

Please provide a response to the following no later than November 20, 2026:

How many times has an ICE agent obtained data from Flock Cameras, whether directly or through state or local law‑enforcement partners?

For what purpose is ICE accessing and obtaining data from Flock Cameras?

Have any individuals been detained, arrested, or otherwise subjected to enforcement actions as a result of information obtained from Flock Cameras? If yes, please provide that number.

What authority or legal statute is ICE purporting to operate under when accessing Flock Camera data? Please provide that authority or legal statute.

Does ICE maintain any internal policy governing the use of ALPR data obtained through third‑party or indirect means? If so, please provide that policy.

Has ICE conducted any legal review regarding whether accessing ALPR data through state or local partners complies with federal privacy protections, the Fourth Amendment, or DHS policy? If so, please provide that review. If not, please indicate whether the agency plans to do so.

Does ICE intend to formalize a contract or memorandum of understanding with Flock Safety or any other ALPR vendor?

We look forward to your prompt response.

text:
The full Fifth Circuit upheld the Trump administration’s policy of mandatory detention for noncitizens, saying in a split decision Friday that constitutional due process protections didn’t entitle three migrant men to bond hearings in immigration court.

While the petitioners have Fifth Amendment rights, they haven’t been admitted to the US and so aren’t entitled to procedures beyond what’s spelled out in immigration statutes, wrote Trump-appointed Judge Cory Wilson in an opinion joined by eight of his colleagues. A ninth, Judge Priscilla Richman, concurred with the result of the majority opinion.

Echoing a point frequently made by Trump administration officials, Wilson wrote that noncitizens can be released from detention “at any moment by agreeing to leave the country.”

Furthermore, the length of their stay in immigration detention “presented no constitutional issues” warranting their release, Wilson wrote.

Seven judges, all appointed by Democrats or Republican President George W. Bush, dissented, with Judge Leslie Southwick saying the majority built “an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents.”

The decision marks another significant Fifth Circuit win for the Trump administration, which has used the detention policy as a legal cornerstone of its mass-deportation efforts. Thousands of immigrants are detained in Fifth Circuit states, particularly Texas and Louisiana, and the court is an outlier among appellate circuits in upholding the policy.

Only one other circuit has blessed the policy, while nine have ruled against it.

The Supreme Court has agreed to consider whether Trump’s mandatory detention scheme correctly interprets the statute, a separate legal question than the Fifth Circuit considered in Friday’s decision.

Attorneys for the noncitizen petitioners castigated the decision in a statement Friday.

“At a time when conditions in immigration detention are increasingly dangerous, this ruling opens the door to more people being locked up for no reason, with devastating consequences for them, their loved ones, and their community,” said Ellie Norton of the National Immigration Project.

The Fifth Circuit previously found there’s no statutory right to a bond hearing in such cases. Congress has significant power over immigration issues and is free to make rules for noncitizens that wouldn’t be acceptable for citizens, Wilson wrote.

“Controlling illegal immigration is, no doubt, an important and controversial issue of public policy. But the Constitution entrusts broad authority to delineate immigration policy, and to design proceedings to effectuate those policy choices, to Congress — not courts,” Wilson said. “Neither we nor the district courts are free to ignore that bedrock principle and rewrite the immigration policy Congress has enacted.”

Last year, in a departure from nearly three decades of practice, the Trump administration began to classify noncitizens who have long lived within US borders as “seeking admission,” the same as noncitizens who’d just entered the country — a legal interpretation that denied them bond hearings.

That helped spark a flood of immigrant habeas corpus petitions in which noncitizens argued they were being illegally detained.

In a concurrence, Judge James Ho wrote that courts, unlike Congress, shouldn’t have a say over immigration policies.

“These habeas petitions, far from affirming American liberty, are profoundly un-American — because they send the message that the only people who are above the law in our country are the ones who violated our laws to get in,” said Ho, a Trump appointee.

Judge Andrew Oldham, another Trump appointee, wrote a lengthy response to Judge Dana Douglas’ assertion that the majority opinion relies on “sham history.”

The writ of habeas corpus doesn’t define “the strike zone,” which is left up to “Congress, and Congress alone,” he said. “Congress can expand it or contract it, as it has over time. But what Congress says goes, and the Constitution does nothing to change what counts as a ball or a strike.”

In dissent, Southwick said that while detention can be a valid part of deportation proceedings, there’s no support for the idea that a noncitizen can be locked up for as long as they’re pending, “however delayed,” with no option for possible release. Southwick was joined by Douglas and Judges Carl Stewart, James Graves Jr., Stephen Higginson, Irma Carillo Ramirez.

Under longstanding Supreme Court precedent, Southwick wrote, a noncitizen’s “presence and residence” in the country — not their technical “admission” to it — entitles them to due process.

Judge Catharina Haynes said she agreed with Southwick’s “basic points” but stressed that his logic should apply only to residents like the petitioners, who’ve been in the country for more than a decade, have no criminal history, and have US citizen relatives.

Douglas also wrote a separate dissent, joined by Stewart, Graves, Higginson, and Ramirez. The majority opinion “detonates the core of the Due Process Clause,” she wrote.

“A country where a roaming police force must seek out millions of noncitizens for mandatory detention without meaningful process or recourse to even a rudimentary hearing is a less decent place for people like Petitioners who have led law-abiding lives, committed no crimes, and raised United States citizens,” she wrote.

Higginson wrote separately, joined by five fellow dissenters, to say that the court was wrong in the first place when it upheld the Trump detention policy on statutory grounds. The en banc court should have revisited the statutory question and interpreted the law in a way that doesn’t raise such significant constitutional concerns, he said.

Ho’s concurrence in particular “implies that any judicial inquiry into the constitutionality of executive immigration detention impermissibly injures Congress,” Higginson wrote. “That proposition cannot be true.”

The due process question came to the court after district court judges began granting noncitizen habeas claims even after the Fifth Circuit panel upheld the Trump policy on statutory grounds.

When the government challenged those grants at the Fifth Circuit, a panel agreed that due process required bond hearings. But the en banc court threw out that decision and agreed to hear the due process arguments as a full court.

Noncitizen petitioners are also represented by American Immigration Council and Garza & Narvaez PLLC.

text:
A federal appeals court has revived a lawsuit filed by FaithWorks and more than two dozen other religious organizations to prevent immigration enforcement actions in houses of worship and other sensitive locations.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia released a divided opinion Oct. 20 concluding plaintiffs offered sufficient proof their congregations and ministries faced imminent threats from immigration agents and therefore could move ahead with Mennonite Church USA, et al. v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

The action stems from the Trump administration’s January 2025 decision to roll back a decades-old sensitive locations policy directing immigration agents as much as possible from operating on the properties of schools, places of worship and hospitals. The revised policy removes those limits and simply asks agents to “use their discretion along with a healthy dose of common sense” when operating at or near sensitive locations like churches.

The lawsuit contends the new approach violates the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, the First Amendment’s guarantee of freedom of religion and the Administrative Procedures Act which governs the federal government’s rule-making processes.

In April, U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich denied the preliminary injunction sought by the faith-based groups, concluding they lacked standing to bring the lawsuit and the negative consequences anticipated from the updated policy had occurred in insufficient numbers.

But judges Florence Pan and Robert Wilkins ruled the plaintiffs have standing to proceed by representing “millions of worshippers, including Baptists, Brethren, Catholics, Conservative Jews, Episcopalians, Evangelicals, Mennonites, Quakers, Pentecostals, Presbyterians, Reconstructionist Jews, Reform Jews, Unitarian Universalists, United Methodists, and Zion Methodists.”

In addition to concerns about disruptions and fears caused by immigration raids, the litigants also demonstrated harms to ministries nationwide, the majority wrote. “In their complaint, every plaintiff alleges that at least one of its member congregations provides support to undocumented immigrants — some of whom are members of the congregations, and others of whom benefit from their charitable work.”

The 2-1 ruling also took into account incidents of federal agents spying on congregations and other controversial enforcement actions that have occurred since the lawsuit was filed in February.

“Given the ‘credible threat’ of impending enforcement activity at or near plaintiffs’ members’ premises, plaintiffs ‘should not be required to await and undergo (further enforcement) as the sole means of seeking relief,’” the majority wrote, citing relevant case law.

“Plaintiffs’ members likely face imminent harm from increased enforcement at their houses of worship; that harm is traceable to the new enforcement policy; and the relief requested will likely redress their injury, at least in part.”

But in her dissent, Judge Neomi Rao argued that even restoring the policy to its previous form would not redress plaintiffs’ alleged harms: “The memo simply discouraged immigration enforcement in protected areas but imposed no actual restriction on enforcement authority or discretion. Enforcement priorities and policies are the exclusive purview of the executive branch, and supervising these choices is beyond the judicial province.”

The appellate decision reversed Friedrich’s ruling and remands the case back to the district court where plaintiffs can again seek a temporary restraining order while the litigation continues.

Stephen Reeves, executive director of FaithWorks (formerly Fellowship Southwest), expressed gratitude for the ruling and said the ministry will continue to defend the right for people to serve their neighbors without fear from Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“We hope this decision will result in an injunction so that our immigrant neighbors will know their faith community is free from the threat of ICE enforcement and that our partner churches can continue exercising their faith by serving neighbors regardless of immigration status,” he said. “While this injunction would not prevent enforcement in most places, it would guarantee that houses of worship are truly sanctuaries. It’s the very least we can offer them: a refuge in times of trouble.”

Nothing less than freedom of religion is at stake in the case, said Bishop Thomas Bickerton, leader of the New York and New England conferences of the United Methodist Church.

“It’s inherent in our Wesleyan DNA to fight for justice for those that are marginalized and those that are oppressed, and this is an accentuated case,” he said.

Bickerton also cited the long history of New York’s Methodist congregations welcoming immigrants into membership. “They are our people, and we’re standing with them at all costs.”

The Unitarian Universalist Association, also a plaintiff, said faith groups have to be diligence given the Trump administration’s disregard for individual rights and sacred spaces.

“As the threats to our sanctuaries — including documented instances of surveillance of UU congregations — and religious practices intensify, we will continue our practice of faithful dissent against such oppression, and we look forward to being a part of the next step of the legal process.”

The Mennonite Church USA cautioned members that the ruling is not victory in the lawsuit itself, but an important moment in the struggle for the right to serve those targeted by the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.

“We’re asking the government to not interfere with our right to practice our faith freely, which is protected by the Constitution,” said Michael Danner, associate executive director for church vitality in Mennonite Church USA and executive director for the Mennonite Education Agency. The lawsuits asks the federal government “to enforce laws in ways that don’t stop us from following Jesus’ command to love our neighbors.”

Mennonite Church v. DHS is one of multiple lawsuits filed against the administration’s focus on houses of worship for immigration enforcement raids.

In August, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit upheld a lower court’s injunction blocking DHS operations on the sites of Cooperative Baptist Fellowship and other plaintiffs’ properties in Philadelphia Yearly Meeting of the Religious Society of Friends v. DHS. A district court in Massachusetts issued a preliminary injunction in February for American Baptist Churches USA, the Alliance of Baptists and other faith groups in New England Synod, Evangelical Lutheran Church in America v. DHS.

However, the decisions, which apply only to the groups that filed the lawsuits, have not discouraged DHS and ICE from conducting immigration operations near and on plaintiffs’ church properties. In August, University Baptist Church in Minneapolis learned that ICE agents had entered its facilities at least four times, including in May, to secretly record conversations between worshipers. The congregation is affiliated with the Alliance and ABCUSA, both plaintiffs in New England Synod.

The intrusions possibly violated the restraining order in that case and a contempt-of-court motion was filed in response to complaints of “egregious violations of the preliminary injunction, including deploying an undercover ICE agent into one of plaintiffs’ protected churches to surveil and record people inside.”

The spying at UBC and other churches was part of DHS efforts to crack down on activists and demonstrators opposed to ICE operations in Minnesota.

title: How the DHS voter-fraud probe reached San Diego's registrar and got reined in by a judge

text:
A federal judge in California ordered Department of Homeland Security officials to halt operations and interviews targeting voter fraud in nine states Wednesday, saying the effort is based on a highly flawed data analysis that has ensnared people whom federal officials “know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens.”

Court declarations by Nicolas Bartell, an official with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which operates within DHS, connect the voter-matching operation criticized in Wednesday’s injunction with a list of more than 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters the Trump administration is separately seeking to have reviewed and possibly withheld by the state of California in a lawsuit.

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin stayed her order until Friday at 5 p.m. to allow the government time to appeal in a case that has captured national attention in the waning days of the election. Early voting is well underway, and ballots are being cast between now and Nov. 3.

Court records, along with subpoenas first obtained by inewsource, show how an escalating probe by Homeland Security Investigations — an agency within DHS created after 9/11 that has traditionally focused on preventing terrorism and fighting transnational crime — led to federal prosecutors accessing voting records in San Diego and Imperial counties this summer and filing criminal charges against 28 people this week.

“Anybody who knowingly commits voter fraud should be prosecuted,” Rep. Mike Levin, D-San Juan Capistrano, told inewsource. “For the sake of argument, let’s say those 28 all had acted improperly. Out of 23 million, it’s certainly the opposite of any sort of evidence of widespread fraud.”

In an interview Wednesday, Levin said, “I think what Trump wants to do is cast doubt on millions of lawful votes by spotlighting isolated allegations of wrongdoing.” He said he thought Trump is trying “ultimately to lay the groundwork to challenge results that he doesn’t like.”

Federal prosecutors said they used subpoenaed voter records from county registrars alongside Homeland Security information to build the cases they announced Monday.

In four situations involving San Diego County voting, HSI agents relied on voter-registration forms and ballot envelopes; three federal complaints explicitly reference records from the San Diego County registrar.

The Imperial County registrar received a summons and a subpoena from HSI agents, records obtained by inewsource show.

At a press conference in Los Angeles on Monday, Kevin Murphy, the HSI special agent in charge of San Diego, thanked all four California U.S attorneys assembled there.

“Their close coordination with HSI has been critical to today’s successful operations,” he said.

At that news conference, Acting Deputy U.S. Attorney General Trent McCotter pushed back on critics like Levin who say the president is trying to sow doubt in the election, saying, “I don’t see how trying to remove noncitizens from elections would sow doubt. All that ensures is that the votes of citizens count as they should.”

The operation began in March 2025 and, after a slew of lawsuits in other states, culminated with the Trump administration filing a lawsuit against the state of California last week that demanded the state comb through and potentially set aside 20,000 ballots that the federal government alleges belong to noncitizens.

In August, DHS directed HSI to focus on sending agents into the field to question people about voter eligibility in the nine states of California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

DHS created lists of individuals to target in these field operations by combining a variety of sources, including publicly available information and data from state and local governments.

The judge called the pooled data set “voluminous and unreliable” and said some records from independent sources were of “questionable provenance.”

An HSI internal memo directed agents to document their investigations beyond normal operating procedures so that DHS could use it for “media and reporting.” These appear to have been used by HSI in its many social media posts showing agents knocking on doors and making arrests.

Federal officials then took public or state-supplied voter rolls and used artificial intelligence tools to identify suspected noncitizens, creating a list that had a high likelihood of error and was “widely known to inadvertently include U.S. citizens,” Judge Martínez-Olguín wrote in her ruling.

The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services said in court filings that errors in identifying citizenship can result from “similar names, outdated citizenship information, clerical errors and other circumstances.”

There is no comprehensive up-to-date federal database that tracks citizenship.

HSI agents were ordered to complete a minimum of 40 manual reviews in no more than 12 minutes by searching through commercial databases, which the judge found increased the risk of error.

The California Nurses Association, the lead plaintiff in the case, said that its voter mobilization activities made it clear to them that the investigations were intimidating eligible voters — and the judge found “substantial evidence” of “a reasonable fear of harm to those assisting and mobilizing voters.” The judge said the CNA was likely to succeed on a claim the Voting Rights Act had been violated in ruling that the federal operation should stop.

A footnote in the ruling says, “Though the Court makes no findings related to the extent of the threat of voter fraud, it notes that other courts have found that the federal government has failed to establish that significant fraud threatens the reliability of upcoming elections.”

What’s next?

If the government doesn’t appeal successfully, the judge’s order would go into effect after business hours on Friday and stay in place until after polls close on Nov. 3.

California and Los Angeles County officials are asking a federal judge to dismiss the Justice Department lawsuit that could keep thousands of Californians’ ballots from being counted.

The department wants election officials to set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 people it identified as “likely noncitizens” until their citizenship can be verified, but California and the county moved to dismiss the case Wednesday, arguing that federal officials lack authority to impose those demands.

The list of 20,000 people was generated using the same methods the judge found faulty in court, according to declarations by federal officials.

Los Angeles County’s preliminary review also raises questions about the list.

Of 200 sampled records with county addresses, 112 had canceled or inactive registrations and had not been sent general-election ballots, according to declarations filed by county election officials.

County officials also warned that verifying citizenship and setting aside ballots could prevent eligible voters’ ballots from being counted before election deadlines.

DOJ attorneys say an immediate court order is necessary because ballots cannot be traced back to voters once opened and processed.

California has declined to give the federal government access to its full unredacted voter rolls or set aside ballots. It provided records on 300 subpoenaed voters.

Last September, the Trump Administration issued a proclamation introducing a $100,000 fee for certain H-1B visa petitions.

text:
Last September, the Trump Administration issued a proclamation introducing a $100,000 fee for certain H-1B visa petitions. This substantial fee only applied to new H-1B visa petitions for individuals located outside the United States – in other words, petitions that would ultimately require consular processing. Petitions requesting a change of status or extension of status for individuals already living in the United States were not impacted by this fee.

On-going Litigation

In June 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the $100,000 fee nationwide, finding the executive branch lacked authority to impose the fee. The federal government has appealed this decision, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit declined to keep the fee in effect while litigation proceeds. The appeals process is ongoing.

Similarly, in September 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California also vacated the fee nationwide, finding the federal government failed to follow mandatory rulemaking procedures, thereby creating a second, independent basis for blocking enforcement. The administration will need to overcome both this court order as well as the earlier decision from Massachusetts through a successful appeal before the fee can go back into effect.

Current Status of the $100,000 Fee

Despite the court order(s) vacating the $100,000 fee, immigration attorneys nationwide reported significant delays in the adjudication of H-1B visa petitions for individuals located outside the United States. Despite USCIS’ guarantee it will take adjudicative action on H-1B visa petitions filed under premium processing within a 15-business day window, impacted H-1B visa petitions were effectively placed on an indefinite hold for several weeks.

Finally, as of October 2026, it appears that USCIS is adjudicating these H-1B petitions again, and attorneys report seeing H-1B visa petitions filed between June and August 2026 under premium processing being adjudicated for individuals located outside the United States, without requiring payment of the $100,000 fee.

The Trump Administration issued a new proclamation, extending the $100,000 fee until September 21, 2027, but the ongoing court orders block the government from collecting the fee, and the new proclamation currently has no effect.

A Proposed $103,265 Fee

If implemented, this fee would not only apply to H-1B cap-subject petitions requesting consular processing – it would apply to all H-1B petitions submitted under the annual H-1B cap registration (“lottery”), including petitions requesting a change of status, such as those filed for recent graduates in F-1 status.

Notably, this fee would not apply to cap-exempt petitions, such as those filed by institutions of higher education, affiliated nonprofit entities and nonprofit/government research organizations.

This proposal is still in the rulemaking process and has not yet become final, so at this time, the $103,265 has not yet been implemented.

text:
Wisconsin election officials are divided over how to handle the possibility of unarmed federal immigration or law enforcement agents arriving at polling places this November and asking to observe voting.

The disagreement centers on a passage in new Wisconsin Elections Commission guidance intended to help local election officials navigate encounters with law enforcement at the polls. Among other instructions, the guidance says that agents from ICE, the FBI and other federal agencies who want to observe voting must follow the same rules as other election observers.

But officials in Dane County, home to Madison and one of Wisconsin’s most Democratic strongholds, warn that the language could lead poll workers to admit federal agents in violation of federal law. Federal law bans U.S. officials from sending troops or armed agents to the polls except under extremely limited circumstances, and a different law bans voter intimidation.

In an Oct. 15 email to the commission, the county’s attorney argued that the guidance could be read as permitting armed ICE agents to observe voting, despite federal restrictions.

Dane County officials have spent months preparing for the possibility of federal interference in the election. The commission, meanwhile, approved its guidance less than three weeks before Election Day, after receiving what it said was hundreds of questions from local clerks seeking clarity about federal law enforcement at the polls.

Clerks and attorneys interviewed by Votebeat were divided over whether the guidance provides the clarity they need. Some praised it as helpful and others said it came too late or warned that its language could lead election inspectors to misunderstand the limits of federal law.

On page three, the guidance instructs election officials to contact their clerks and the commission if federal agents arrive to observe voting. If federal officials are present “just to observe, they still have to check in like regular observers and are subject to the observer rule,” it states. The guidance does not, at that point, distinguish between armed and unarmed federal agents.

It then discusses circumstances in which armed, uniformed local officers might observe voting.

Only two pages later does the commission explain the federal law restricting armed personnel in federal service from polling places.

The structure of the advice, Dane County attorney David Gault told Votebeat, “creates the implication it’s okay for ICE to be there and observe, and I just don’t think that’s the case.”

“If they’re armed, it’s clearly prohibited,” he said. “If they’re unarmed but still in some kind of a uniform designating them as a federal agent, I think the law is still pretty clear they’re not supposed to be there.”

Dane County officials object to commission guidance

Election officials across Wisconsin have been preparing for months for the possibility of federal law enforcement at the polls, but the concern is particularly acute in the state’s largest, heavily Democratic counties. In Dane County, the state’s second-largest, officials say listening to the commission’s guidance could complicate their efforts to keep federal agents from interfering with voting.

The guidance lays out steps for election officials to take when federal agents appear. Chief inspectors are instructed to immediately notify their municipal clerk, who must then contact the county clerk and commission staff. Agents carrying out legitimate law enforcement duties, rather than observing voting, are treated differently. In those cases, election officials are told to request identification and any warrants, document the encounter and ask officers to conduct their business outside the voting area when possible.

The commission also tells election inspectors they can remove observers if they have a reasonable basis to believe they are, or are about to, intimidate or disrupt voters. In its instructions addressing local law enforcement officers who insist on observing while armed and in uniform, the guidance leaves inspectors to determine whether their presence crosses that line.

Dane County Clerk Scott McDonell took issue in particular with the statement that if federal agents wish to observe, they can check in like regular observers.

“It’s inaccurate,” said McDonell, a Democrat. “It’s confusing. It doesn’t reflect what the law is.”

If a back-office ICE employee who’s unarmed wants to observe, that might be fine, McDonell said. “But that’s not how I think anyone would read that,” he said, saying clerks may assume the sentence is referring to armed federal agents.

Sharing McDonell’s concerns, Gault, the Dane County in-house attorney, sent an email to Wisconsin Elections Commission Administrator Meagan Wolfe on Oct. 15, the same day the commission finalized the guidance.

Gault said that while armed ICE agents are clearly banned from the polls under federal law, a separate federal law bars a person acting under the color of law from intimidating voters. Gault argued that it would ban even an unarmed but uniformed ICE agent from observing at the polls.

“There is no legitimate reason for ICE to be at a polling place,” he told Wolfe. “Everyone there is presumptively a US citizen. I don’t think WEC’s guidance should imply that an ICE agent can be a legitimate observer.”

Commission attorney supervisor Angela O’Brien Sharpe disagreed, saying federal law doesn’t address every situation that may bring federal agents to the polls. “If federal law enforcement wishes to observe an election, then they are permitted to do so,” she said, adding that they would be subject to Wisconsin observer rules.

She emphasized that the guidance does not authorize armed federal observers, and was intended to help pollworkers “manage how to respond to varying situations like these” including deciding whether an officer’s presence constitutes intimidation or a disturbance.

Gault was unsatisfied, calling the guidance “confusing at best.”

“If asked, this office will advise election officials and law enforcement in Dane County that armed federal agents should not be at a polling place under any circumstances,” he wrote. “If they are there legitimately to vote they should at a minimum be unarmed.”

Local attorneys can offer advice to city and county election offices that contradicts the commission’s, Sharpe said.

Little precedent for federal agents observing elections

Federal election monitors from the Justice Department have observed voting for decades, but the prospect of ICE or FBI agents arriving at polling places specifically to monitor voting presents a largely untested legal question.

Justin Levitt, an election law specialist at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who worked in the White House under President Joe Biden on voting rights issues, said the commission’s guidance is “legit and accurate,” adding that it’s “straight down the middle of providing lawful advice without picking a fight.”

“I understand why Dane County wants a different emphasis,” Levitt said. “I don’t think that means they were right and the state was wrong. I think that just means they’ve got different interests here.”

He said the commission and Dane County agree more than they disagree: They both agree that armed agents are banned at the polls, and that chief inspectors can kick out anyone intimidating voters.

Had the commission gone further and said ICE was banned from the polls entirely, he said, “That would actually be getting Wisconsin in trouble because you cannot single out federal officials for special treatment.”

Sterling Knoche, a staff attorney at the University of Wisconsin Law School-based State Democracy Research Initiative, similarly said the guidance provides clerks with good instructions for minimizing disruptions at the polling place while instructing them to consult the people who could seek a court injunction if necessary.

Knoche said the commission may not have had a sound legal basis to categorically prohibit unarmed federal agents in uniform from observing. Whether their presence is lawful would depend on their conduct and the circumstances, he said.

In Milwaukee on Monday, Wolfe drew a similar distinction. She said that federal and state law prohibits armed federal agents from showing up at the polls, but said the legality of unarmed agents observing is less clear. In that case, she said, chief inspectors and poll workers must determine whether their presence intimidates or disturbs voters.

How clerks are preparing to apply the guidance

Local officials offered differing assessments of how useful the guidance would be, even as some agreed that federal agents in uniform could intimidate voters.

Marathon County Clerk Kim Trueblood, a Republican, said the guidance was “fine.” She said county clerks have been coordinating with their local sheriffs, who would be their first call if federal agents do show up at the polls. If she were an inspector, she said, she would not allow federal law enforcement agents to register as observers if they’re in uniform, even if they were unarmed.

“We would be on a very strong legal footing to say, ‘You standing there in your FBI vest is intimidating to voters, and so we’re not going to allow that,’” she said.

In an interview, Green Bay Police Chief Chris Davis told Votebeat that the guidance was quite helpful and would be instructive in the unlikely situation that federal agents show up at a city polling place.

“We have to make a decision about what to do fairly quickly,” he said, “so any time we can get guidance like this from an authority, it helps us do that.”

Green County Clerk Arianna Voegeli, a Democrat, said the commission’s guidance came late but was consistent with the guidance that she already had given to local election officials. She agreed that the mere presence of federal officers in uniform could constitute voter intimidation, though she said it’s a legal gray area if they’re unarmed.

“I’m not too concerned about issues here in Green County, just because we’re a smaller county,” she said, though she’s discussed the issue with law enforcement and feels prepared. Larger counties, she said, have likely developed their own plans already.

McDonell, the Dane County clerk, said this guidance might add to the confusion for some clerks instead of taking away from it.

“It would have been better if they hadn’t sent this out,” he said. “It’s at minimum badly worded.”

Alexander Shur is a reporter for Votebeat based in Wisconsin. Contact Alexander at ashur@votebeat.org.

text:
44

(OSV News) — Vice President JD Vance is used to being confronted by questions from the press. He recently faced questions from a Catholic sister.

Sister Nancy Sylvester, of the Sisters, Servants of the Immaculate Heart of Mary of Monroe, Michigan, was among attendees at an Oct. 15 town hall event in suburban Detroit featuring the vice president, where she was able to ask him a question about immigration. The event aired on CBS Oct. 17.

“We are sisters who minister at the southern border in the United States, as well as here around Detroit, and they are constantly seeing families who are affected by our immigration policies,” Sister Nancy told Vance in the video from CBS News. “They see the trauma of children who are separated from their parents, sometimes on a moment’s notice — they go to school and they come back and (the parents are) not there.”

She went on, citing the “fear and violence” of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers.

“How would you justify to people of faith, especially those of us who try to follow the Gospel, how the behavior of the ICE men and women can constantly be justified in terms of the kind of values we want to live by?” asked Sister Nancy, who is a senior contributor for Global Sisters Report. “And also, what policies would you advocate to try to promote more compassionate and respective behavior toward our immigrant sisters and brothers?”

Vance: ‘Trying to strike a balance’

Vance, who is Catholic, began his answer by saying he appreciates her “and hopefully I’ll be in your prayers as you’ll certainly be in mine.” He said the federal government is “trying to strike a balance” between the need for law enforcement and acting humanely.

Despite the host’s efforts, Vance did not address specific instances of alleged violent incidents by ICE officers, such as shooting American citizens, but allowed that mistakes have been made.

“Most of them are amazing people who are patriots and they want to do a good job protecting their country. Sometimes you have some people who make mistakes, sometimes you have some people who really screw up, and obviously we have a responsibility to prosecute, investigate when people do screw up,” Vance said.

Incidents where ICE officers have been ordered to receive more training or discipline may not be advertised, Vance said, but that does not mean it is not happening.

“We believe people have to be judged in a court of law and through a normal investigatory process,” he said. “We don’t jump in and try to accuse people just again because of what we’ve seen in a news media article.”

Vance says ICE has ‘done a good job’ overall

Vance seemed to imply that the government has had to be aggressive because of policies under the administration of President Joe Biden, saying, “What we saw over the last five years, before we came in, I mean is, we have to talk about the fact that drug cartels were sex trafficking thousands and thousands of children, thousands of thousands of girls who were sold into sex slavery. Of course, the fentanyl trade which killed a lot of people in Michigan.”

“Despite what some people say in the press, I promise you that we wake up every day and we try to balance law enforcement with humane law enforcement,” he said. “And of course, when you’re dealing with hundreds of thousands of law enforcement officials, you’re never going to get everything perfect, but I think the men and women of ICE, by and large, have done a good job and where there are people who’ve screwed up, of course they should suffer consequences.”

Sister Nancy is founder and director of the Institute for Communal Contemplation and Dialogue, has served in leadership of her own religious community and in the presidency of the Leadership Conference of Women Religious, and is a columnist for GSR. Previously, she was national coordinator of Network, a Catholic social justice lobby.

text:
McAllen, Texas — Benny Melendez, the owner of a small construction company along this stretch of the U.S.-Mexico border, says he's been forced to take drastic measures to protect his immigrant workers.

"If I don't install fences, ICE is going to come into my property and take my workers away," Melendez said as he showed CBS News the fencing he's set up at one of the several construction sites he manages in South Texas.

Melendez says the fencing is designed to prevent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from arresting his workers, and to require them to have judicial warrants before entering his job sites.

Local officials say construction is one of the industries hardest hit by President Trump's sweeping crackdown on illegal immigration. Construction company owners like Melendez say they're struggling to find workers, with some having been detained by ICE and many scared of showing up to work and getting arrested. Building a home, he said, is now taking his team a year due to manpower issues — up from an average of four months before the Trump administration's crackdown began.

"We're blessed that we have two workers today," Melendez said.

The South Texas resident, who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after supporting President Biden in 2020, said ICE operations have also made him rethink his vote.

"I regret my vote for Biden. Now I regret my vote for Trump," Melendez said. "What other options do we got? They're not working for us, neither party."

Melendez's disillusionment is emblematic of broader concerns among some Latino voters — including some who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 — who believe his mass deportation crackdown has gone too far. A recent CBS News poll found nearly 60% of Latinos believe the Trump administration has deported more people than they expected.

Democrats are hoping those concerns will help them in key races in the midterm elections in November, as they try to retake control of Congress. That bet will be put to the test in Texas, where Mr. Trump and Republicans saw huge gains among Latinos in 2024, especially in communities along the southern border directly affected by the migration crisis there under the Biden administration.

Democratic state representative James Talarico and Ken Paxton, Texas' Republican attorney general, are in a hotly contested race for an open Senate seat. In Texas' 15th congressional district, Tejano singer Bobby Pulido, a Democrat, is hoping to unseat Republican Congresswoman Monica De La Cruz.

Javier Villalobos, the Republican mayor of McAllen, the largest city in that congressional district, warned that his party is now at risk of losing some of the gains it made in Latino border communities. He called concerns about ICE's crackdown the No. 1 issue among his constituents.

"Inflation, the economy, everything is important. But what hits you immediately, what hits personally is the crackdown, when you see the ICE agents, masked, and pulling people out of vehicles," Villalobos told CBS News. "It is not a good picture."

Villalobos noted that local residents supported efforts to bolster border security and deport violent criminals in the U.S. illegally. But he said many now see ICE's deportation campaign as "a crackdown on the Hispanic community," one he believes has instilled fear in his city, including among American citizens.

CBS News has reached out to the White House for a response. Trump administration officials have routinely defended ICE's enforcement efforts, noting the president ran on expanding deportations and cracking down on illegal immigration.

"I particularly don't care about midterms," White House border czar Tom Homan told CBS News earlier this month when asked about criticism of ICE by some Republicans. "My job as a border czar is to keep that border secure and enforce immigration law."

Jessica Vuittonet, a coffee shop owner in San Benito, roughly a 45-minute drive from McAllen, said she voted for Mr. Trump two years ago, mainly because of her religious views. But she says she now regrets that decision, citing cases of local residents getting detained by ICE.

"I know he was going to start deporting people but not innocent people — not hardworking people," she said.

text:
By Nate Raymond

Oct 23 (Reuters) – A US appeals court ruled on Friday that President Donald Trump’s administration is not required under the US Constitution to give detained immigrants a chance to seek release on bond.

In a 10-7 ruling powered by its ​conservative majority, the New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals decided that the Constitution’s ‌Fifth Amendment due process protections do not require that immigration detainees receive bond hearings.

“To the extent petitioners seek to vindicate a liberty interest to be free from physical restraint in the most abstract sense, they can do so at any moment by agreeing to leave the country,” US Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote in ‌the ​decision.

The ruling, if left to stand, would eliminate a key ⁠avenue for detained migrants in the ⁠three states under the 5th Circuit’s jurisdiction — Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi — to argue for release, especially if the US Supreme Court decides the administration’s detention practice complies with immigration law.

The Supreme Court this month agreed to consider the issue, which has divided lower courts. Numerous ​lawsuits by migrants arguing they were being unlawfully detained have flooded the courts as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, implemented Trump’s mass deportation agenda.

The Supreme Court is considering only ⁠whether such hearings are required by statute, not by the ⁠Constitution, the issue the 5th Circuit addressed with Friday’s decision.

While the 5th ​Circuit in February had adopted the administration’s reading of immigration law as requiring mandatory detention, a 2-1 ​panel of the court in July held that ICE could not constitutionally detain ‌people for more than 90 days without providing hearings to argue for release on bond.

The decision, which came in lawsuits by two Mexican citizens and one Honduran, carried particular importance because Texas and Louisiana, within the 5th Circuit’s jurisdiction, house the nation’s largest numbers of immigration detainees.

But the full ⁠5th Circuit agreed to rehear the case, and on Friday reversed course, concluding that detained immigrants are not constitutionally entitled to proceedings in immigration court beyond what Congress provided by statute.

“This ruling opens the ⁠door to more people being ‌locked up for no reason, with devastating consequences for them, their ⁠loved ones and their community,” Ellie Norton, a lawyer for the non-US ​citizens in ‌the case at the National Immigration Project, said in a statement.

James ​Percival, the ⁠general counsel for the US Department of Homeland Security, in a social media post hailed what he called a “big win in the 5th Circuit on mandatory detention for illegal aliens.”

Among the dissenting judges was US Circuit Judge Dana Douglas, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, who wrote that “unchecked, executive authority to arrest and detain, indefinitely, echoes fearfully from history.”

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; editing by David ​Bario and Will Dunham)

title: ICE Detains Special Needs Student, U.S. Citizen Near Santa Maria High School
authors: Ryan P. Cruz, Adam Echelman, Elaine Sanders, Jean Yamamura, Indy Staff, Tyler Hayden, Tiana Molony, Sergio Olmos, Wendy Fry, Nick Welsh
description:

“I want to reassure you that the Santa Maria Joint Union High School District is committed to maintaining safe, protected, and welcoming spaces for all students, families, and staff,” Garcia said.

text:
A Santa Maria High School student with special needs was detained by federal immigration enforcement less than a half mile from the school campus on Thursday morning. The student, who was described as non-verbal, was on his way to school when he was apprehended for matching the description of another person. Witnesses at the scene said he was aggressively tackled, restrained, and questioned before being left with multiple injuries, including a broken wrist.

Volunteers with the 805 Rapid Response Network have been on the ground every morning in Santa Barbara County, documenting verified ICE activity and alerting the community through the 24/7 hotline. The Rapid Response team reported the incident immediately and confirmed the details with eyewitnesses and Santa Maria Joint Union High School District staff. Nearby security camera footage also confirmed ICE was involved in the incident.

When ICE officers left the student on the street, he made his way to the campus, and school staff arranged for an ambulance to provide medical attention. School administration said the student’s injuries included lacerations, bruising, and a wrist that required surgery.

In a statement posted to social media, representatives from the Rapid Response Network said the student was one of several community members stopped and questioned by ICE that same morning “without probable cause other than their skin color.”

“No person, regardless of their place of origin, should be beaten and left without medical care,” the group wrote.

District Superintendent Antonio Garcia sent out a message to students and their families, in which he said the Santa Maria Police Department was also called and has passed along information about the incident to the District Attorney, the California Attorney General, and ICE’s regional office in Los Angeles.

“I want to reassure you that the Santa Maria Joint Union High School District is committed to maintaining safe, protected, and welcoming spaces for all students, families, and staff,” Garcia said.

An ICE spokesperson addressed the incident in a statement provided to the Los Angeles Times, which confirmed that the agency was conducting a “targeted enforcement operation” in Santa Maria on October 21 when officers “encountered an individual they believed matched the description” of their target.

The ICE spokesperson said that when the student “resisted officers, refused lawful commands, and assumed a fighting stance with clenched fists, they relied on their training to safely control the situation until they could confirm his identity, whereupon he was released.” According to ICE, the 20-year-old special needs student “never requested medical assistance.”

Santa Maria Councilmember Gloria Soto, who has been outspoken in her criticism of ICE enforcement in the city, called the recent incident “unacceptable.” She asked Mayor Alice Patino to call a special council meeting to address the community’s concerns and questioned the explanation provided by ICE’s unidentified spokesperson.

“ICE’s own statement admits agents stopped the wrong person,” Sotos said. “A student walking to school ended up in surgery, and saying he ‘never requested medical assistance’ doesn’t change the fact that he was hurt. Reports state he had his ID on him the whole time and was never asked for it. This kind of brutality is not okay. There needs to be an independent investigation into how a case of mistaken identity ended with a student hurt this badly.”

Soto noted that the incident is just the latest in what has been two years of increasingly aggressive enforcement operations on the Central Coast. More recently, Rapid Response volunteers reported a surge in ICE enforcement believed to be part of a statewide initiative known as “Operation Safe California,” with more than 175 community members being arrested in the span of two weeks, according to 805 UndocuFund.

Notably, Santa Maria has been one of the hardest hit communities. ICE activity has been reported almost every day this month, including at the North County Branch Jail, workplaces, and near schools. On October 5, the father of a student at Allan Hancock College was arrested while dropping his daughter off in the campus parking lot.

In response to the incident, a coalition of immigrant rights groups and nonprofits such as 805UndocuFund, CAUSE, Future Leaders of America, The Fund for Santa Barbara, MICOP, and Santa Maria Indivisible are asking local leaders to increase pressure for an independent investigation of the incident and full accountability for officers involved.

The groups are also calling on city officials to disclose any coordination with ICE to ensure that no city resources, funds, or facilities are being used to assist in further federal enforcement operations .

On Saturday, October 24, 805 Undocufund will be holding a rally in Santa Maria starting at 5 p.m. on South McClelland Avenue.

text:
Press releases are posted on Independent.com as a free community service.

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today co-led a multistate coalition in filing an amicus brief in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests. Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk. The brief highlights the widespread harms that unlawful immigration enforcement practices have inflicted on communities across the country, including in California.

“The Trump Administration has engaged in an aggressive, militaristic mass deportation program with no regard for people’s humanity and dignity,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Federal immigration agents are arresting people without the requisite probable cause determination, often while masked, wearing armor, and carrying lethal weapons. California will not stand by while this Administration creates fear in our immigrant communities. We will continue to fight back, defend our neighbors, and stand up for the rights and dignity of every person.”

Across the country, federal immigration agents have escalated their enforcement activities, disrupting communities and undermining public health, safety, education, and local economies. California has seen these harms firsthand, as aggressive immigration enforcement tactics have kept students out of school, disrupted agricultural work, discouraged people from seeking medical care, undermined families’ financial stability, and weakened the relationship between immigrant communities and local law enforcement. Federal agents’ use of ski masks, dark sunglasses, plainclothes, and unmarked vehicles, and refusals to identify themselves while carrying out operations, has further contributed to fear and uncertainty in affected communities.

Today’s brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction.

Attorney General Bonta has consistently fought against unlawful federal immigration enforcement practices across the country. Earlier this month, he filed a lawsuit challenging the Trump Administration’s policy and practice of carrying out civil immigration enforcement in and around state courthouses. He also supported challenges to unlawful federal immigration enforcement practices in several cases:

United Farm Workers v. Noem: He filed an amicus brief in support of a challenge to DHS’s “Operation Return to Sender” in Kern County, where roving patrols and warrantless arrests kept children out of school and workers at home.

Vasquez Perdomo v. Noem: He led a multistate coalition in filing an amicus brief challenging suspicionless stops during “Operation at Large” in Los Angeles, which disrupted local businesses and led to the cancellation of community events.

Ramirez Ovanda v. Mullins: He co-led a multistate brief in support of plaintiffs challenging ICE’s policy and practice of carrying out unlawful warrantless arrests in Colorado.

In filing the brief, Attorney General Bonta, District of Columbia Attorney General Brian Schwalb, and Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser lead the attorneys general of Arizona, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

description:
A federal appeals court has handed a legal victory to churches, synagogues and other religious organizations challenging the Trump administration’s decision to permit immigration enforcement operations at places of worship.
The legal dispute centers on the administration’s removal of federal guidelines that previously limited immigration enforcement at locations considered sensitive, including religious institutions and schools.

text:
A federal appeals court has handed a legal victory to churches, synagogues and other religious organizations challenging the Trump administration’s decision to permit immigration enforcement operations at places of worship.

In a 2-1 ruling issued Tuesday, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reversed a lower court’s decision rejecting the religious groups’ request for a preliminary injunction. The case now returns to the district court for further review.

The legal dispute centers on the administration’s removal of federal guidelines that previously limited immigration enforcement at locations considered sensitive, including religious institutions and schools.

Judge Florence Y. Pan, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, authored the majority opinion, finding that the religious organizations had demonstrated sufficient grounds to pursue their legal challenge. Their lawsuit raises constitutional and statutory claims under the First Amendment, the Religious Freedom Restoration Act and the Administrative Procedure Act.

“Plaintiffs’ members likely face imminent harm from increased enforcement at their houses of worship; that harm is traceable to the new enforcement policy; and the relief requested will likely redress their injury, at least in part,” Pan wrote.

Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee who dissented from the majority, questioned whether the religious organizations had established a sufficient connection between the revised policy and the injuries they alleged. She argued that returning to the earlier guidelines would not necessarily prevent immigration operations or reverse declines in religious service attendance.

“It is purely speculative that returning to the policies set forth in the Mayorkas Memo will either reduce enforcement activity near plaintiffs’ places of worship or reverse attendance declines at those places,” Rao wrote.

The controversy began in January 2025, when the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) eliminated restrictions governing immigration enforcement at sensitive locations. Those protections were initially established during the Obama administration in 2011 and subsequently broadened under the Biden administration in 2021.

“Criminals will no longer be able to hide in America’s schools and churches to avoid arrest. The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement, and instead trusts them to use common sense,” DHS stated at the time.

In response to the policy change, a coalition of 27 religious organizations representing multiple Christian denominations and Jewish communities initiated legal action seeking the restoration of the previous restrictions.

The plaintiffs include Mennonite Church USA, The Episcopal Church, the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.), the Union for Reform Judaism and the United Synagogue of Conservative Judaism, among other religious bodies.

Although the appeals court ruled in favor of the religious groups on the preliminary injunction appeal, the decision does not itself prohibit immigration enforcement at houses of worship. Instead, it directs the lower court to reconsider whether temporary restrictions should be imposed while the lawsuit proceeds.

description:

text:
Increased support from Latino voters is considered to be one of the reasons Donald Trump won the 2024 election. Now, as the 2026 midterms approach, Lisa Magaña looks at Latinos’ falling support for Trump in Arizona and in the US more widely. She writes that as Republicans target Latino immigrants, this can become personal for Latinos, prompting them to politically mobilize, including forging new political inroads to groups like first-time voters.

This article is part of our ‘The 2026 Midterms‘ series curated by Peter Finn (University of Greenwich). The series explores the run-up to the 2026 US midterm elections at the state and national levels. If you are interested in contributing to the series, contact Peter Finn (P.D.Finn@greenwich.ac.uk).

Over 68 million people in the United States currently identify as Hispanic or Latino, making this population the nation’s largest ethnic minority. It includes those with Mexican, Puerto Rican, Dominican, Cuban, Central American, South American and Spanish roots. The proximity to Mexico and Central America makes the United States a prime destination for Latin American immigration. As a result, if Latinos in the United States had their own country, it would be the third largest Latin American population in the world, after Mexico. Two-thirds of all Latinos in the United States are of Mexican origin, and of that, 31 percent are foreign born.

More Latinos voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election

In the 2024 election, exit polls suggested that in states like Texas, Florida and Arizona there was an increase in Latino voter turnout for Trump. This was surprising to some because of Trump’s rhetoric on immigration and towards Latinos generally. Exit polls suggest that those Latinos that voted for Trump did so because they thought he was the better candidate at handling the economy. According to polling, white voters also thought that Trump would be better than Kamala Harris on economic issues. Unlike many Latino voters, however, white voters voted for Trump because they believed that he would be better at handling immigration issues and be generally tougher on immigrants.

According to Nate Cohn of the New York Times, the president’s popularity with Latino voters in the 2024 election helped him with the popular vote, He also maintained that the Republican Party may have done a better job than the Democratic party at wooing Latino voters.

Latinos appear to be swinging away from Trump ahead of the 2026 Midterm elections

With only a few weeks until the midterm elections, exit polls suggest a significant decline in support of Trump. As of October 2026, Nate Cohn notes that Trump’s approval ratings among Latino voters have fallen to the mid-20s, and Latinos prefer Democrats by 35 percentage points when asked who they will support for Congress. This is a significant change, since Kamala Harris led Trump by only seven percentage points among Latino voters in the 2024 election. Polls are not always accurate, but these data indicate that there is probably going to be an extraordinary shift in the electoral map, meaning trouble for Republican incumbents.

The voting patterns of Latinos in the United States are not all the same. That is, the political party they align with, their country of origin, the state they reside in, their generational status and level of education, to name but a few factors, all influence how Latinos will vote. In the past both parties have been guilty of “Hispandering.” This is when pundits explicitly try to target Latino voters with inauthentic marketing, or outreach based on stereotypes of Latinos.

“Voto Latino” (CC BY-SA 2.0) by quinn.anya

According to National Public Radio (NPR), in the upcoming midterm elections, some swing states with large Latino districts can potentially mean the difference between winning back the majority in both congress and senate. The Hispanic Congressional Caucus, through an initiative called the BOLD PAC is trying to woo those Latinos voters. Using innovative approaches, the BOLD PAC is using the talent of social media influencers to get the word out to Latinos about their potential political impact. BOLD PAC maintains it does not directly pay influencers for their efforts but rather will cover travel and related expenses for events that help Latino candidates. This is a smart “non-Hispandering” approach to outreach because the Pew foundation finds that 30 percent of younger Latinos get their information from social media influencers.

The backlash to Republicans’ anti-immigration policies from Arizona’s Latino voters

Republicans believe they have a winning political strategy when they criticize and scapegoat Latinos and immigrants. Republicans should remember that in Arizona there has been a major political backlash by a wide range of traditional and nontraditional political players to the decades-long wave of anti-immigrant and, more generally, anti-Latino proposals. In 2020, the state flipped to Joe Biden, the first presidential win for a Democrat there since 1996. The traditional power players among Latinos in Arizona include a mix of new and longstanding Latino elected officials and community leaders, while nontraditional constituencies include Latino high school students, working-class Latino voters, church members, and a diverse array of grassroots organizations.

In the 2016, 2018 and 2020 elections, we saw the impact of the “New American Majority”. These are groups that previously came together to oppose anti-immigration policies and rhetoric and have forged important new inroads into other non-traditional voters. Simply put, when Republicans push anti-immigrant legislation, target and/or scapegoat Latino immigrants, we see the political response as new political players, such as first-time voters, forge new political pathways.

There are obvious demographic reasons to explain why anti-immigration agendas mobilize Latinos. First, Latinos are very likely to either be immigrants or to have family members or friends affected by immigration. Studies show that anti-immigrant rhetoric has politically rallied Latinos because anti-immigration policies often manifest themselves as anti-Latino. Some studies have also shown that the general experience of discrimination of Latinos has centered around immigration, whether the Latino was a US citizen or not. Latinos, regardless of their citizenship status, have experienced some type of discrimination based on racial profiling due to immigration concerns. It is important to reiterate that, in a political context, immigration is much more than a talking point; it is personal.

It appears the Republican Party is pushing its anti-immigrant agenda once again, and it is unlikely to be successful in the long run. In a survey conducted on Latino voters in Arizona, researchers found the following: Seventy percent of Latinos thought the Trump administration was not doing enough on the economy. Top concerns for Latinos in Arizona are inflation, housing, healthcare and jobs. Eighty two percent of Latino voters in Arizona want Congress to limit the president’s political power. And most interesting, the Republican agenda of mass immigration enforcement and Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) have made Latinos that voted for Trump no longer want to support him. They feel the actions of ICE affect themselves personally or someone that they know. And these anti-immigrant actions by the Trump Administration only serve to galvanize Latinos.

title: Anti-ICE activists ejected from Philly courthouse as they protest immigration arrests
description:

text:
A dozen No ICE Philly protesters were quickly ejected from the Criminal Justice Center on Friday morning as they called for greater protections for immigrants who go to the courthouse.

Group members entered the Center City building through different doors, then gathered in the center of the main-floor lobby to read a statement insisting all people be kept safe ― before being cut off by sheriff’s deputies.

The demonstrators wore matching red T-shirts that said, “Signs are not enough! We need policy now!”

That referred to small notices posted at the courthouse and elsewhere in the wake of city “ICE Out” legislation, which say the property is city-owned or controlled and that using it as a staging or processing area for civil enforcement operations is prohibited.

People who were in the courthouse lobby on other business seemed not to realize what was happening when the activists formed a line in the middle of the hall.

The protesters left when directed to do so, continuing their demonstration on the sidewalk outside. No one was arrested.

They urged people to phone and demand action from President Judge Nina Wright Padilla and Sheriff Rochelle Bilal.

For months, No ICE Philly has demanded that the court administration and the Sheriff’s Department take strong action to stop ICE from using the courthouse as “a hunting ground.”

Arrests there have increased since January 2025, when the Trump administration eliminated Biden-era restrictions on immigration enforcement at courthouses amid its ongoing, full-scale deportation agenda.

Immigration arrests take place as people are trailed outside by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and taken into custody on the sidewalk. Attorneys with the Defender Association of Philadelphia have described agents hanging out at courthouse entrances, in the lobby, and in hallways and courtrooms, always dressed in plain clothes and without visible badges or identification.

Many immigrants who go to the courthouse are not criminal defendants ― they are witnesses, victims, friends, or family members. But some have been targeted and arrested by ICE, immigration attorneys and government officials say, causing witnesses and victims to stay away from court and hindering the administration of justice.

“We are demanding that the court have a specific policy that keeps ICE out of the courthouse,” said Carrie Rathmann, a No ICE Philly member who helped lead the Friday event. “It’s a perversion of justice to have people fearful and not coming to the courthouse.”

Other places have created specific, enforceable policies, she said, and there’s no reason that can’t happen in Philadelphia.

“We’re not going to let up,” she added.

Efforts to reach spokespeople for Sheriff Bilal and the First Judicial District were not immediately successful.

No ICE Philly and other groups have previously rallied outside the courthouse and at the Sheriff’s Office itself.

They say First Judicial District leadership has declined to update policies to offer protections that extend beyond the courthouse doors, in some cases leading to people being arrested the moment they set foot outside the building. Bilal, according to No ICE Philly and other groups, maintains that the Sheriff’s Office’s responsibility for security lies within the courthouse, not on the public streets and sidewalks.

No ICE Philly is part of local ICE Out of Courts coalition that includes Juntos, Asian Americans United, Victim Witness Services, HIAS Pennsylvania, ACLU Pennsylvania, the Public Interest Law Center, and the Defender Association.

They say ICE has been allowed free run of the courthouse, even while other U.S. cities have embraced policies to prevent that.

In Chicago, for instance, the top Cook County judge barred ICE from arresting any party, witness, or potential witness while going to court, including arrests that might be made inside courthouses but also in parking lots, entryways, and surrounding sidewalks.

Much of the ire over ICE arrests at the courthouse has been directed at Bilal. No ICE Philly and others say that by not barring ICE, she has helped enable the arrest of scores of immigrants in the last year or so.

The sheriff has said her office does not cooperate with ICE, does not assist in ICE operations, and does not share information with the agency. In January, the First Judicial District said authority for managing ICE’s presence at the Criminal Justice Center rested with the sheriff, and that decisions around that were her sole responsibility.

On Friday, No ICE Philly members rallied outside after being ejected.

“ICE out! ICE out!” they shouted.

“Our goal was to be disruptive and get the information out,” said one group member who declined to be named, “and to make sure that we let our leaders know that we want ICE out of the courthouse right now.”
